When the preposition was dropped, the well-known disagreement between al-Khalīl and Sībawayh about the position of «أَنْ» applies; and His saying {قُلْ إِنَّ الهدى هُدَى الله} is a parenthetical clause. Al-Zamakhsharī said, in establishing this view, with which he began: "«ولا تُؤْمِنُوا» is connected with His saying «أَنْ يُؤْتَى أحد», and what is between them is a parenthesis, i.e. do not display your belief that anyone will be given the like of what you were given except to the people of your religion, not to others. They meant: keep secret your acknowledgement that the Muslims have been given the like of what you were given, and do not divulge it except to your partisans alone, not to the Muslims, lest it increase them in firmness, and not to the polytheists, lest it call them to Islam. «أو يُحاجُّوكم» is conjoined to «أَنْ يُؤْتَى». The pronoun in «يُحاجُّوكم» refers to «أحد», because it has the sense of a plural, meaning: do not believe for anyone other than your followers, for the Muslims will argue against you before your Lord with the truth and overcome you before Allah. If you say: what is the meaning of the parenthesis? I say: its meaning is that guidance is the guidance of Allah; whomever He wills to show kindness to, so that he embraces Islam or increases in firmness, that happens, and your scheming, your stratagems, and your keeping your acknowledgement hidden [Translator's note: printed «وزيُّكُم», apparently for «وزَيُّكم» / «وزَوْيُكم», "your withholding"] from the Muslims and the disbelievers do not avail. Likewise His saying {قُلْ إِنَّ الفضل بِيَدِ الله يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشَآءُ}: He means guidance and success (tawfīq)." I say: these are good words, were it not for what he intends by their inner meaning [Translator's note: an allusion to al-Zamakhsharī's Muʿtazilī reading of "kindness" (luṭf)]. On this view His saying {إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ} is excepted from something omitted, the implied meaning being: "do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you were given, to anyone of the people, except to your partisans, not to others". This clause — I mean His saying «ولا تُؤْمِنُوا» to its end — is then part of the speech of the group (ṭāʾifa) mentioned before, i.e. "a group said such-and-such, and also said: and do not believe …", while the clause {قُلْ إِنَّ الهدى هُدَى الله} is the speech of Allah alone.

The second is that the lām in «لِمَنْ تَبعَ» is redundant, and it is excepted from the later «أحد», the implied meaning being: "do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you were given except one who follows your religion"; so «مَنْ تَبعَ» is accusative as excepted from «أحد». On this view Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted three views on the position of «أن يؤتى»: the first and second are the doctrines of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, which have preceded; the third is the accusative as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), its implied form being «مخافَةَ أَنْ يُؤْتَى» (for fear that … be given). This second view is not sound either in meaning or in grammatical technique. As for the meaning, that is clear. As for the technique, it involves placing the excepted before the thing from which it is excepted and before its governing word, and it also involves placing something within the ṣila of «أَنْ» before it, which is not permissible.

The third is that «أَنْ يُؤْتَى» is genitive by the particle of cause, namely the lām, the thing explained by the cause being omitted, its implied form being: «لأنْ يُؤْتَى أحدٌ مثلَ ما أُوتيتم قلتم ذلك ودَبَّرتموه، لا لشيء آخرَ» (because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, you said that and plotted it, and for nothing else). On this view the speech of the group is complete at His saying {إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ}. Let us clarify this view by what al-Zamakhsharī said. He said, may Allah have mercy on him: "Or the speech is complete at His saying {إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ}, in the sense: do not believe with this outward belief — namely their believing at the beginning of the day — except for one who follows your religion, i.e. except for those who were followers of your religion among those of you who embraced Islam; because their return was more hoped for, in their view, than the return of others, and because their Islam was more vexing to them. His saying {أَن يؤتى أَحَدٌ} means: because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, you said that and plotted it, and for nothing else; that is, the envy and transgression in you — that anyone should be given the like of what you were given of the excellence of knowledge and the Book — called you to say what you said. The proof of this is the reading of Ibn Kathīr «أَأَن يُؤْتَى أحد» with the addition of the interrogative hamza for affirmation (taqrīr) and rebuke, in the sense «ألأنْ يُؤْتَى أحدٌ؟» (is it because anyone should be given …?). If you say: what then is the meaning of His saying «أو يُحاجُّوكم» on this view? I say: its meaning is: you plotted what you plotted because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, and because of what is connected with it, upon your disbelieving in it, namely their arguing against you before your Lord."

The fourth is that «أَنْ يُؤْتَى» is accusative by an implied verb indicated by {وَلاَ تؤمنوا إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ}, as though it were said: "Say: guidance is the guidance of Allah, so do not deny that anyone should be given the like of what you were given"; «فلا تُنْكِرُوا» governs «أنْ» and what lies within its scope in the accusative, because His saying {وَلاَ تؤمنوا إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ} is a denial that anyone should be given the like of what they were given. Al-Shaykh [Translator's note: Abū Ḥayyān] said: "This is far-fetched, because it involves omitting the particle of prohibition and omitting what it governs, and that has not been preserved from their speech." I say: whenever there is evidence indicating the governing word, its omission is permissible in whatever state it is.

The fifth is that «هدى الله» is a badal (substitute) from «الهدى», which is the noun of «إنَّ», and the khabar (predicate) of «إنَّ» is {أَن يؤتى أَحَدٌ}, the implied meaning being: "Say: the guidance of Allah is that anyone be given …", i.e. the guidance of Allah is the giving to anyone of the like of what you were given; and «أو» means «حتى» (until), the meaning being: until they argue against you before your Lord, overcome you and refute your argument before Allah. On this view «أَوْ يُحاجُّوكم» is not conjoined to «أَنْ يُؤتى» nor included within the scope of «أَنْ».

The sixth is that «أَنْ يُؤْتَى» is a badal from «هدى الله», the meaning being: "Say: guidance is the guidance of Allah, and it is that anyone be given the like of what has come to us"; and His saying «أو يُحاجُّوكم» means "or let them argue against you, for they will overcome you". Ibn ʿAṭiyya said this. It is open to question, because it leads to omitting the particle of prohibition [Translator's note: so printed; the lām of command is meant] while keeping its effect.

The seventh is that the negating «لا» is implied before «أَنْ يؤتى», having been omitted because the speech indicates it, and «أو» means «إلاَّ أَنْ» (unless). The implied meaning is: "do not believe anyone in anything except one who follows your religion, in that it is not the case that anyone will be given the like of what you were given except one who follows your religion and brings its like and supports it; for that is not given to anyone other than you, unless they argue against you" — as in your saying «لألْزَمنَّك أو تقضيَني حقي» (I will stick to you until/unless you pay me my due). It is weak in that it omits the negating «لا», and what they mentioned about the speech indicating it is not evident.

The eighth is that «أَنْ يُؤْتى» is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi. The precise form of this view is that you make His saying {أَن يؤتى أَحَدٌ مِّثْلَ مَآ أُوتِيتُمْ أَوْ يُحَآجُّوكُمْ} not included under His saying «قل», but part of the completion of the group's speech, connected with their saying: "do not believe except one who comes with the like of your religion, for fear that anyone be given of prophethood and honour the like of what you were given, and for fear that they argue against you before your Lord through your having acknowledged them, if you do not persist in it". This saying of theirs is the fruit of their envy and disbelief despite their knowing the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ. When al-Mubarrad implied the mafʿūl li-ajlihi here, he implied the muḍāf: «كراهَة أن يُؤتَى أحدٌ مثلَ ما أوتيتم» (out of dislike that anyone be given the like of what you were given), i.e. of those who opposed the religion of Islam, because Allah does not guide one who is a liar and an ingrate, so the guidance of Allah is far from those other than the believers; and the address in «أوتيتم» and «يُحاجُّوكم» is to the community of the Prophet ﷺ. Some judged this weak and said: its being a mafʿūl li-ajlihi on the implied form «كراهةَ» requires implying a governing word for it, and implying it is difficult, since before it is a clause in which the explanation of the predication by dislike of the said giving is not evident.

The ninth is that the «أَنْ» with fatḥa comes for negation just as «لا» does; some reported this explicitly from al-Farrāʾ. He made «أو» mean «إلا», the implied meaning being: "no one is given the like of what you were given unless they argue against you", for his being given what you were given is coupled with overcoming you or arguing against you before your Lord, because whoever Allah has given revelation must argue against them before their Lord concerning their not following him. So His saying «أو يُحاجُّوكم» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) necessary in terms of meaning, since Allah does not give revelation to a messenger except that he argues against those who oppose him. This view is worthless, since it has not been established in the speech of the Arabs.

They differed concerning the clause «ولا تُؤْمِنُوا»: is it part of what the group said, or part of what Allah the Exalted said — in the sense that Allah the Exalted addressed it to the believers to make their hearts firm and calm their spirits, lest they doubt when the Jews confused matters for them and falsified? Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported consensus of the people of interpretation that it is part of what the group said, but that is not correct, given the disagreement that people have reported.

«أحد» in the noble verse may be one of the nouns bound to negation, or may not be, but rather mean «واحد» (one). The difference between the two has preceded: the one bound to negation has an original hamza, while the one not bound to negation has a hamza substituted for a wāw. On making it bound to negation, the pronoun referring back to it in the plural is evident, out of regard for its meaning, since what is meant by it is generality; on this is His saying {فَمَا مِنكُمْ مِّنْ أَحَدٍ عَنْهُ حَاجِزِينَ} [al-Ḥāqqa: 47], where He made the khabar plural since «أحد» has the sense of a plural. On making it the one not bound to negation, the plural pronoun in «يُحاجُّوكُم» is with regard to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and his followers. In some of the preceding views it is valid to make the «أحد» mentioned the one bound to negation, namely when the speech is in the sense of denial; and when the speech is in the sense of affirmation, as has passed in some views, it is impossible to make it the one bound to negation. The matter is clear from what has preceded.

Ibn Kathīr read «أأن يؤتى» with an interrogative hamza, in keeping with his rule of easing the second hamza bayna bayna without lengthening between them. This reading has been explained in several ways. The first: «أن يُؤتى» is with the preposition omitted, namely the lām of cause, the thing explained being omitted, its implied form being: «أَلأنْ يؤتى أحدٌ مثل ما أوتيتم قلتم ذلك ودَبَّرتموه» (is it because anyone should be given the like of what you were given that you said that and plotted it?). I have given its verification; in that case the two views on the position of «أَنْ» are acceptable, I mean the accusative, the doctrine of Sībawayh, and the genitive, the doctrine of al-Khalīl.

The second: «أَنْ يُؤتَى» is in the position of the nominative [Translator's note: printed «رفعب», a misprint for «رفع»] as a mubtadaʾ (subject), the khabar being omitted, its implied form being: "Is it that anyone, O company of Jews, should be given the like of what you were given of the Book and knowledge, that you believe in, or acknowledge, or mention to others, or spread among people?" and the like of what may fittingly be implied. This is on the view of whoever says «أزيد ضربته», and it is the less preferred view. So al-Wāḥidī implied it, following al-Fārisī. Better than this implied form, because it is the original, is: «أإتيان أحدٍ مثلَ ما أُوتيتم ممكنٌ أو مُصَدَّقٌ به» (is the giving to anyone of the like of what you were given possible, or believed in?).

The third: it is accusative by an implied verb which this latent verb explains, the question belonging to the chapter of ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb), the implied form being: «أَتَذْكُرون أَنْ يُؤْتَى أحد تذكرونه» (do you mention that anyone be given — do you mention it?), so «تذكرونه» explains the first «تذكرون», in the manner of «أزيداً ضربته»; then the last, explaining verb was dropped because the speech indicates it, and it is as though it were pronounced, and because it is equivalent to what is pronounced it can explain an implied verb. This question is explicitly stated in the texts. This is preferable to the view before it, because it is like «أزيداً ضربته», which is preferred on account of the element that requires a verb [Translator's note: i.e. the interrogative hamza]. Similar to the omission of this implied verb, because what precedes the interrogative indicates it, is the omission of the verb in His saying {آلآنَ وَقَدْ عَصَيْتَ} [Yūnus: 91]; it was said its implied form is: «الآن آمنت ورَجَعْتَ وتُبْتَ» (now you believe, return and repent?) and the like.

Al-Wāḥidī said: "If it is said: how is the entry of «أحد» found in this reading, when it has been cut off from negation and interrogation, and when the speech is cut off as affirmation and confirmation the entry of «أحد» is not permissible? It is said: it is possible that «أحد» in this place is the «أحد» found in e.g. «أحد وعشرين» (twenty-one), and this occurs in affirmation; do you not see that it means «واحد»? Abū al-ʿAbbās said: «أحد», «وَحَد» and «واحد» have one meaning."

His saying «أو يُحاجُّوكم»: «أو» in this reading means «حتى», the meaning of the speech being: "Is it that anyone be given the like of what you were given — you mention it to others, until they argue against you before your Lord?" Al-Farrāʾ said: "Similar in ordinary speech is: «تَعَلَّقْ به أو يُعْطِيَكَ حقك» (cling to him until he gives you your due); and similar is the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:

1335 - فَقُلْتُ له: لاَ تَبْكِ عَيْنُكَ إنما ... نحاوِلُ مُلْكاً أو نموتَ فَنُعْذَرَا
(I said to him: let your eye not weep; we only seek a kingdom, or [until] we die and are excused.)

i.e. «حتى». From this is His saying {لَيْسَ لَكَ مِنَ الأمر شَيْءٌ أَوْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْهِمْ} [Āl ʿImrān: 128]." He said: "This is one view; better than it is to make it conjoined to the interrogative, the meaning being: is it that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that anyone argue against you before Allah, that you believe him?" All this is the sense of al-Fārisī's statement. It is also possible that «أن يؤتى أحد» is accusative by an implied verb, not by way of explanation but by mere indication of meaning, its implied form being «أتذكرون أو أَتَشِيعونَ أَنْ يُؤْتَى أحدٌ» (do you mention, or do you spread abroad, that anyone be given …); al-Fārisī mentioned this too. This is the fourth view.

The fifth: «أَنْ يؤتى» in his reading is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, on the basis that it is included under «قل» [Translator's note: printed «تحت القول»], not part of what the group said; this is more evident than making it part of what the group said.

Al-Fārisī judged the reading of Ibn Kathīr weak, saying: "This is a place where the reading of those other than Ibn Kathīr ought to be preferred over the reading of Ibn Kathīr, because it is not regular in singular nouns that they indicate multiplicity."

Al-Aʿmash and Shuʿayb ibn Abī Ḥamza read «إنْ يؤتى» with kasra on the hamza, and al-Zamakhsharī explained it as the negating «إنْ». He said: "On the basis of the negating «إن», and it is connected with the speech of the People of the Book, i.e. do not believe except one who follows your religion, and say to them: no one is given the like of what you were given until they argue against you before your Lord — meaning they are not given its like, so they will not argue against you."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This reading allows the speech to be an address from the group that said it, and their saying «أو يحاجُّوكم» means 'or let them argue against you', this being on the firm resolve that no one is given the like of what was given; or it may mean 'unless they argue against you', this being on the allowance that someone may be given that if the proof is established for him." So it appears from what Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned that «أو» in this reading may keep its proper sense of choice and variety, or may mean «إلاَّ»; except that it involves omitting the jussive particle while keeping its effect, which is not permissible. On the view of others it means «حتى».

Al-Ḥasan read «أَنْ يُؤْتى أحدٌ» with the verb in the active voice [Translator's note: so vocalized in print; the active voice would be «يُؤْتِي»]. When some reported this reading they did not specify «أن» with fatḥa or kasra, like Abū al-Baqāʾ; others did specify it, with kasra on «إنْ», and explained it as the negating «إنْ». The apparent meaning is that Allah's bestowal of favour is not resembled by the favour of any of His creatures, and it is an address from the Prophet ﷺ to his community. The object is omitted, its implied form being «إنْ يؤتي أحدٌ أحداً مثلَ ما أوتيتم» (no one gives anyone the like of what you were given); the first object, «أحداً», was omitted because the meaning indicates it, and the second was kept.

This is the summary of what people have said about this verse, with its differences, and praise belongs to Allah. Al-Wāḥidī said: "This verse is among the difficult passages of the Qurʾān and the hardest of it to interpret. I have reflected on the statements of the exegetes and the scholars of meanings (maʿānī) concerning this verse, and I have not found a view that runs consistently through this verse from its beginning to its end while explaining the meaning and keeping the composition sound."

semin-durr:37-37.t:
The words of the Exalted: {فَتَقَبَّلَهَا}: the majority read «تَقَبَّلها» as a past verb on the pattern tafaʿʿala, with the middle radical doubled, and «ربُّها» is its fāʿil (agent). Tafaʿʿala allows two aspects. The first: that it has the meaning of the bare verb, i.e.: and He accepted her (qabilahā), meaning He was pleased with her in place of the vowed male, and He had not accepted a vowed female like Maryam — so it came in the exegesis. Tafaʿʿala comes with the meaning of the bare faʿila, as in تَعَجَّب and عَجِب "to wonder at such-and-such", and تبرَّأ and بَرِىء "to be clear of it". The second: that tafaʿʿala has the meaning of istafʿala, i.e.: and her Lord received her (istaqbalahā); one says استقبلْتُ الشيء, i.e. I took it at its first instance. The meaning is that Allah took charge of her at the beginning of her affair and at the time of her birth. Of this are his words — he is al-Quṭāmī:
1244 - وخيرُ الأمرِ ما استقبَلْتَ منه ... وليس بأَنْ تَتَبَّعَه اتِّباعاً
(The best of a matter is what you take up from its start, not by following after it.)
And of it is the proverb: «خُذِ الأمر بقَوابله» ("take the matter at its beginnings"). Tafaʿʿala with the meaning of istafʿala is frequent, as in تَعَظَّم and استعظم, تكبَّر and استكبر, تَقَصَّيْت الشيء and استقصَيْتُه, تَعَجَّلَته and استَعْجَلْتُه.
The bāʾ in His words {بِقَبُولٍ} has two aspects. The first: that it is redundant (zāʾida), i.e.: قَبولاً; on this view «قبولاً» is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun) that came with the additional letters dropped, for had it come according to تقبَّل, it would have been said تَقَبُّلا, as in تكبَّر تكبُّرا. Qabūl is one of the maṣdars that came on faʿūl with a fatḥa on the first radical; they were mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqara. One says: قَبِلْتُ الشيء قَبولاً. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj allowed a ḍamma on the qāf of «قبول», and that is the analogical form, like الدُّخول and الخُروج. Ibn al-Aʿrābī reported it from the Arabs: قبلته قَبولاً وقُبولاً, with fatḥa and ḍamma on the qāf, as heard from the Arabs; and «على وجهه قُبول» ("there is acceptability on his face") and nothing else, meaning it is said here only with ḍamma. They recited:
1245 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . والوجه عليه القُبول
(… and the face has acceptability upon it.)
with ḍamma on the qāf; so some reported it.
Al-Zajjāj said: "This «قبولاً» is not accusative by this verb so as to be a maṣdar not following its verb; rather it is accusative by a verb that corresponds to it, i.e. a bare one." He said: "The implied form is: so He received her with a fine reception (يتقبُّل حسن «[Translator's note: so in the text; evidently بتقبُّل]») and accepted her with a fine acceptance (قَبِلها قَبولاً حسناً), i.e.: He was pleased with her." And there is a remoteness in it.
The second aspect: that the bāʾ is not redundant but remains in its sense, and what is meant by al-qabūl here is a noun for that by which a thing is accepted, like «اللَّدود» for what is administered into the side of the mouth, and al-saʿūṭ for snuff. The meaning thereby is His singling her out by setting her in the place of the male in the vow.
His words: {وَأَنبَتَهَا نَبَاتاً}: نبات is also a maṣdar not following its verb, since the analogical form is إنبات. It was also said: rather it is accusative by a concealed verb that likewise corresponds to it, its implied form being: so she grew a fine growing.
His words: {وَكَفَّلَهَا}: the Kufans read «وكَفَّلَها» with the middle radical doubled and «زكريا» with the short ending, except Abū Bakr, who read it with the long ending like the rest, but in the accusative, while the rest read it nominative, as will come.
Mujāhid read «فتقبَّلْها» with a vowelless lām and «ربَّها» accusative, «أنبِتها» with kasra on the bāʾ and a vowelless tāʾ, and «كَفِّلْها» with kasra on the fāʾ and a vowelless lām. Ubayy read «وأَكْفَلَها», like «أَكْرَمَها», as a past verb.
ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī read «وكَفِلَها» with kasra on the fāʾ and without doubling.
As for the reading of the Kufans, they made the verb transitive to two objects by the doubling, the second of them being «زكريا». Those who read it short, like the two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) and Ḥafṣ, have it with an implied accusative, and those who read it long, like Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, show the fatḥa on it; and that is how I recited it.
As for the reading of the rest of the Seven, كَفَلَ is light according to them and transitive to one object, namely the pronoun of Maryam, and its fāʿil is «زكريا». There is no contradiction between the two readings, because when Allah made him her guardian, he became her guardian. In their reading it is long and nominative as the fāʿil.
As for the reading «أَكْفَلَها», he made it transitive by the hamza just as others made it transitive by doubling, as in خَرَّجْته and أَخْرجته, كَرَّمته and أَكْرمته. This is like the reading of the Kufans in meaning and parsing: the fāʿil is Allah the Exalted, the first object is the pronoun of Maryam, and the second is «زكريا».
As for the reading «وكَفِلها» with kasra on the fāʾ, it is a dialectal form of كَفَلَ. One says كَفَلَ يَكْفُل, like قَتَل يقتُل, which is the widespread form, and كَفِلَ يَكْفَلُ, like عَلِمَ يَعْلَم, on which this reading is based. Its parsing is like that of the reading of the majority, with «زكريا» as the fāʿil.
As for the reading of Mujāhid, all of it is in the wording of a prayer from Maryam's mother to Allah the Exalted that He do for her what she asked of Him. «ربَّها» is accusative as one addressed in the vocative, i.e.: so accept her, O her Lord, and make her grow and give her into guardianship, O her Lord. «زكريا» in this reading is likewise a second object, as in the reading of the Kufans.
Ḥafṣ and the two brothers read «زكريا» with the short ending wherever it occurs in the Qurʾān, and the rest of the Seven with the long ending. The long and short endings in this name are two widespread dialectal forms from the people of the Ḥijāz. It is a foreign noun, so they ought to have said of it: it is a diptote because of being a proper name and foreign, like its counterparts; yet they said only: it is a diptote because of the presence of the feminine alif in it, either the long one as in حَمْراء or the short one as in حُبْلى. What seems to have compelled them to that is that they saw it treated as a diptote both when definite and when indefinite. They said: if its diptote status were because of being a proper name and foreign, it would be declinable when indefinite, since one of the two causes of prevention would be gone; but the Arabs treated it as a diptote when indefinite, so we knew that the preventing cause is something else, and there is nothing here that is fit to prevent its declension except the feminine alif. They mean the likeness to the feminine alif; otherwise this is a foreign noun of which no derivation is known, such that it could be claimed that the alif in it is feminine. Moreover, Abū Ḥātim held that it is declinable when indefinite, as though he regarded in it what I set out earlier, foreignness and being a proper name; but they judged him mistaken and wrong in that.
Al-Fārisī said, discussing it at length: "The hamza in it must be either for the feminine, or for annexing to a pattern (ilḥāq), or changed from another letter. It cannot be changed, because the change must be either from a root letter or from a letter of ilḥāq. It cannot be from a root letter, because yāʾ and wāw are not root letters in what consists of four letters; nor can it be from a letter of ilḥāq, because there is nothing among the root patterns to which this could be annexed. Once that is established, it is established that it is for the feminine; and the same is said of the short alif."
What Abū ʿAlī said is sound if it were among words of which a derivation is known and which admit morphological inflection; but they treat foreign nouns the way Arabic ones are treated, in the sense of: if this occurred in the tongue of the Arabs, what would its rule be?
Beyond that there are two other dialectal forms of it. One of them: زَكَرِيٌّ, with a doubled yāʾ at its end only «[Translator's note: the text has فقد, evidently for فقط, "only"]», without alif; in this dialect it is declinable. Abū ʿAlī explained it, saying: "The account of it is that the two yāʾs that were in it, in the long and short forms, and what came after them were dropped, and the two yāʾs of relation (nisba) were attached." He said: "What shows that is the declension of the noun; had the two yāʾs been the ones that were in it, it would have had to be a diptote because of foreignness and definiteness." This dialect I have mentioned is the dialect of the people of Najd and those adjoining them. The second: «زَكْرٍ», on the pattern of عَمْرٍو; al-Akhfash reported it.
Al-kafāla is originally surety (al-ḍamān); then it is borrowed for joining (to oneself) and taking (into care). One says from it: كَفَل يكفُل and كَفِلَ يكفَل, like عَلِمَ يعلَم, كَفالة and كَفْلاً, so he is كافِل and كفيل.
His words: {المحراب}: there are two well-known aspects in it. The first, which is the position of Sībawayh, is that it is accusative as an adverb (ẓarf), and it departs from all its fellows specifically after «دخل». He means that every specified adverb of place is reached by the verb only through «في», as in «صَلَّيْت في المحراب» ("I prayed in the miḥrāb") — you do not say المحرابَ — and «نمت في السوق» ("I slept in the market") — you do not say السوقَ — except specifically with «دخل», as in دَخَلْتُ السوقَ والبيت ("I entered the market and the house"), and except other words which I mentioned in books of grammar. The second is the position of al-Akhfash: that what comes after «دخل» is accusative as a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), not as an adverb; so your saying «دخلت البيت» is like your saying «هَدَمْتُ البيت» ("I demolished the house") in that each is accusative as a direct object. This is the less preferred view, as shown by the fact that if «دخل» were applied to something other than a specified adverb, it would have to reach it through «في»: you say «دخلْتُ في الأمر» ("I entered into the matter") and not دخلت الأمر; this shows that it does not pass to a direct object by itself.
Al-miḥrāb: Abū ʿUbayda said: "It is the noblest of sitting places and the front of them, and it is so with respect to the mosque." Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: "It is the palace, because of its height and nobility." Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "It is the upper chamber," and he recited, from Imruʾ al-Qays:
1246 - وماذا عليه أَنْ ذكرتُ أوانساً ... كغِزْلانِ رملٍ في محاريبِ أَقْيالِ
(What harm is it to him that I mentioned gentle maidens like the gazelles of the sands, in the chambers of princes?)
They said: its meaning is: in the upper chambers of princes. Another recited, from ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa «[Translator's note: the text has ربعية, a slip for ربيعة]»:
1247 - رَبَّةُ مِحْرابٍ إذا جئتُها ... لم أدْنُ حتى أَرْتَقِي سُلَّما
(Mistress of a high chamber: when I come to her, I cannot draw near until I climb a ladder.)
It was also said: it is the miḥrāb of the known mosque, and that is most fitting for the verse. As for what I mentioned from those before, they mean by it the miḥrāb as such; as for this verse, no disagreement appears among them [over] its being the familiar miḥrāb. It was said: its derivation is from al-ḥarb (war), because people fight over it.
Ibn Dhakwān from Ibn ʿĀmir read «المحراب» with imāla (inclination of the alif) in two places in this sūra without disagreement, because the cause of imāla is strong in it: the alif is preceded by a kasra and followed by another kasra, so the motive for imāla is strengthened. This is unlike «المحراب» when not genitive, for both aspects are transmitted from Ibn Dhakwān in it, imāla and its absence, as in His words {إِذْ تَسَوَّرُواْ المحراب} [Ṣād: 21]: the reason for imāla is the preceding kasra, and the reason for full pronunciation (tafkhīm) is that it is the original. The difference has been given to you between its being genitive, where no disagreement is reported from him, and its not being genitive, where the disagreement applies. Likewise the disagreement from him also applies in «عمران», for the reason I mentioned, namely the preceding kasra.
His words: {وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقاً}: this «وَجَدَ» means "to come upon, meet, encounter", so it is transitive to one object, namely «رزقاً». «عندَها» is evidently an adverb of the finding. Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed it to be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «رزقاً», because it is fit to be an adjective of it originally; on this view it is attached to an omitted element. «وَجَدَ» is what puts كلما in the accusative, since it is adverbial; this has been verified earlier. Abū al-Baqāʾ called it its apodosis, because in his view it resembles a condition, as will come.
His words: «قال: يا مريم»: there are two aspects in it. The first: that it is resumptive. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It cannot be a badal (substitute) from «وَجَدَ», because it does not have its meaning." The second: that it is conjoined with fāʾ, and the conjunction was omitted. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "As it is omitted in the apodosis of a condition, as in His words {وَإِنْ أَطَعْتُمُوهُمْ إِنَّكُمْ لَمُشْرِكُونَ} [al-Anʿām: 121], and likewise the words of the poet:
1248 - مَنْ يَفعلِ الحسناتِ اللهُ يَشْكرها ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them …)
This place resembles the apodosis of a condition, because «كلما» resembles a condition in requiring an apodosis." End. I say: what he said is questionable, in that he imagined that in the words of the Exalted {وَإِنْ أَطَعْتُمُوهُمْ} the apodosis is «إنكم لمشركون» itself, with the fāʾ dropped from it. That is not so; rather the apodosis is omitted, and «إنكم لمشركون» is the answer of an implied oath before the condition — the verification of this question has preceded. So this is not at all among the cases where the fāʾ of the apodosis is dropped. How can he claim that and equate it with the line mentioned, when that is permissible only under poetic necessity? Furthermore, what appears is that the clause «وَجَدَ» is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the fāʿil of «دخل», and the apodosis of «كلما» is «قال» itself, the implied form being: whenever Zakariyyā entered upon her, finding provision with her, he said. This is very clear. «رزقاً» was made indefinite to magnify it, or to indicate by it a certain kind of it.
His words: {أنى لَكِ هذا}: أنَّى is a fronted khabar (predicate) and «هذا» a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject). The meaning of «أنى» here is "from where"; so Abū ʿUbayda explained it. It was also said: it may be a question about the manner, i.e.: how was this made ready for you? Al-Kumayt said:
1249 - أنَّى ومِنْ أين آبَكَ الطربُ ... مِنْ حيثُ لا صبوةٌ ولا رِيَبُ
(How and from where has longing come back to you, from where there is neither youthful passion nor doubts?)
Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed «أَنَّى» to be accusative as an adverb by the "being established" (al-istiqrār) contained in «لك», with «لك» making «هذا» nominative — he means as a fāʿil; there is no need for that. The discussion of «أنَّى» has preceded in al-Baqara.
{إنًّ الله يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَآءُ}: its like has preceded. It may be resumptive [from the words of Allah the Exalted, or it may be from the words of Maryam, so that it is in the accusative position].

semin-durr:75-75.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {مَّنْ إِن تَأْمَنْهُ}: «مَنْ» is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and «من أهل» its khabar (predicate), placed before it. «مَنْ» is either a relative noun or an indefinite noun. «إِنْ تَأْمَنْهُ يُؤدِّه» — this conditional clause is either a ṣila (relative clause), and so has no grammatical position, or an adjective, and so its position is nominative.

Ubayy read «تِئْمَنْهُ» in both places, and {مَا لَكَ لاَ تَأْمَنَّا} [Yūsuf: 11], with kasra on the prefix of the imperfect; so too Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī, except that these two replaced the hamza with yāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya made that the dialect of Quraysh, and al-Shaykh [Translator's note: Abū Ḥayyān] held him to be mistaken. We have already discussed the kasra of the imperfect prefix and the condition for it in Sūrat al-Fātiḥa at full length, so let it be consulted there.

«الدينار» is originally «دِنَّار» with two nūns; the succession of two identical letters was felt heavy, so they replaced the first of them with a weak letter for lightness, because of its frequent use on their tongues. What indicates that is its returning to the two nūns in the broken plural and the diminutive, in their saying «دَنانير» and «دُنَيْنِير». Similar is «قيراط», originally «قِرَّاط», as shown by «قراريط» and «قُرَيْرِيط»; just as they said «تَظَنَّيْت» and «قَصَّيْت أظفاري» (I clipped my nails), meaning «تَظَنَّنْت» and «قَصَّصت» with three nūns and three ṣāds. «الدينار» is an Arabicized word. They said: its weight has never varied at all; it is twenty-four qīrāṭs, each qīrāṭ being three medium barley-grains, so the total is seventy-two barley-grains.

Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read «يُؤَدِّهْ» with sukūn on the hāʾ in both places; Qālūn read «يُؤَدِّهِ» with kasra on the hāʾ without extension (ṣila); and the rest with kasra on it extended by a yāʾ. From Hishām there are two ways: one like Qālūn, the other like the majority.

As for the reading of Abū ʿAmr and those mentioned with him, they explained it in several ways. The best of them is that the hāʾ of the pronoun was given sukūn by treating continuous speech like the pause; this is a wide chapter of which you have already met something, such as {يَتَسَنَّهْ وانظر} [al-Baqara: 259] and {أَنَا أُحْيِي وَأُمِيتُ} [al-Baqara: 258], and you will meet more of it, if Allah the Exalted wills. Ibn Mujāhid recited in support of this:

1336 - وأشربُ الماءَ ما بي نحوه عطشٌ ... إلا لأنَّ عيونَه سيلُ وادِيها
(I drink the water though I have no thirst for it, only because its springs are the torrent of her valley.)

and al-Akhfash also recited in support of it:

1337 - فَظَلْتُ لدى البيتِ العتيقِ أُخيلُه ... ومِطْواي مُشتاقان لَهُ أَرِقانِ
(I remained by the Ancient House watching it, while my two companions were yearning for it, sleepless.)

except that some restrict this to poetic necessity, and it is not as he said, for reasons that will come.

Some attacked this reading. Al-Zajjāj said: "This sukūn reported from these readers is a clear error, because the hāʾ ought not to be made jussive, and since it is not made jussive it does not take sukūn in continuous speech. As for Abū ʿAmr, I think he used to pronounce the kasra in a snatched way (ikhtilās), and it was misreported from him, as it was misreported from him in {بَارِئِكُمْ} [al-Baqara: 54]. Sībawayh — who is precise in matters like this — reported from him that he used to pronounce a hidden kasra", meaning that in «بارئكم» he pronounced a hidden kasra, and the transmitter thought it sukūn. I say: this rebuttal from al-Zajjāj is nothing, for several reasons. Among them: he fled from sukūn to ikhtilās, yet the one who stated explicitly that sukūn is not permissible also stated that ikhtilās is not permissible; indeed he made sukūn in poetic necessity better than ikhtilās, saying: "so that continuous speech is treated fully like the pause", and he made the poet's saying «عيونَهْ سيلُ واديها» better than his saying:

1338 - . . . . . . . . . . ... ما حَجَّ ربَّه في الدنيا ولا اعتمرا
(… he never made the Ḥajj to his Lord in this world, nor the ʿUmra.)

since he gave sukūn in the first and ikhtilās in the second.

Among them: this is an established dialect of the Arabs, preserved by the eminent imams such as al-Kisāʾī [Translator's note: printed «السكائي», a misprint] and al-Farrāʾ. Al-Kisāʾī reported from Banū ʿUqayl and Banū Kilāb {إِنَّ الإنسان لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ} [al-ʿĀdiyāt: 6] with sukūn on the hāʾ and with kasra without full extension, and they say «لَهْ مال» and «لَهُ مال» with sukūn and with ikhtilās. Al-Farrāʾ said: "Among the Arabs are those who make the hāʾ jussive [Translator's note: i.e. give it sukūn] when the letter before it is vowelled, so they say «ضربتهْ ضرباً شديداً» (I hit him hard), giving the hāʾ sukūn just as they give sukūn to the mīm of «أنتم» and «فمنهم», whose original is ḍamma." And he recited:

1339 - لمَّا رأى أَنْ لا دَعَهْ ولا شِبَعْ ... مالَ إلى أرطاةِ حِقْفٍ فالطَجَعْ
(When he saw there was no ease and no fill, he turned to an arṭā-shrub of a sand-dune and lay down.)

I say: this is strange of al-Farrāʾ — how could he recite this verse in this context? For this hāʾ is substituted for the feminine tāʾ which is present in continuous speech, and he changed it into a quiescent hāʾ in continuous speech by treating it like the pause; whereas our discussion concerns only the pronominal hāʾ, not the feminine hāʾ, because the feminine hāʾ has no share at all in vowelling, and for that reason rawm and ishmām are impossible for it in the pause; they stated this explicitly. Al-Zajjāj was weak in lexicography; for that reason he rejected things in Thaʿlab's «فصيح» which he denied came from the Arabs, and people rebutted his rejection, saying: the Arabs said them; Thaʿlab preserved them and al-Zajjāj did not. So let this be one of those.

Some claimed that since the verb is jussive and the hāʾ has taken the place of its final radical, there applies to it what applies to the final radical of the verb, namely sukūn for the jussive; this is not sound.

As for the reading of Qālūn, they recited in support of it:

1340 - لَهُ زَجَلٌ كأنه صوتُ حادٍ ... . . . . . . . . . .
(It has a clamour like the voice of a camel-driver …)

and the saying of another:

1341 - أنا ابنُ كِلابٍ وابنُ أوسٍ فَمَنْ يَكُنْ ... قناعهُ مَغْطِيَّاً فإنِّي لَمُجْتَلِي
(I am the son of Kilāb and the son of Aws; whoever has his veil covering him, I am indeed one who shows himself openly.)

and the saying of another:

1342 - وأغبرُ الظَّهْرِ يُنْبي عن وَلِيَّتِه ... ما حَجَّ ربه في الدنيا ولا اعتمرا
(One dusty of back, whose saddle-cloth reveals that he never made the Ḥajj to his Lord in this world, nor the ʿUmra.)

It has already been mentioned that it is also the dialect of ʿUqayl and Kilāb.

As for the reading of the rest, it is clear. Al-Zuhrī read «يُؤَدِّهو» with ḍamma on the hāʾ followed by a wāw; it has preceded that this is the original form of the hāʾ of the pronoun. Sallām read likewise, except that he left out the wāw and so pronounced it with ikhtilās. These two are counterparts of the two readings «يؤدهي» [Translator's note: printed «يؤد هي»] and «يؤدهِ», with full extension and with ikhtilās, with kasra.

Know that whenever this hāʾ comes after a jussive verb, or an imperative with a weak final letter, these three ways apply to it — I mean sukūn, ikhtilās and full extension. That is as in {نُؤْتِهِ مِنْهَا} [Āl ʿImrān: 145], {يَرْضَهُ لَكُمْ} [al-Zumar: 7], {نُوَلِّهِ مَا تولى} [al-Nisāʾ: 115], {وَنُصْلِهِ جَهَنَّمَ} [al-Nisāʾ: 115] and {فَأَلْقِهْ إِلَيْهِمْ} [al-Naml: 28]. The three ways have come in the readings of the Seven in some of these words, while in some only two ways have come; this will come in detail in their sūras, if Allah the Exalted wills. The secret of it is that when the pronominal hāʾ is preceded by a vowelled letter, the most eloquent practice is full extension, as in «إنه», «به», «له»; and if it is preceded by a quiescent letter, the best-known practice is ikhtilās, whether that quiescent letter is sound or weak, as in «فيه» and «منه»; some distinguish between the weak and the sound. I have dealt thoroughly with that at the beginning of the book. Once that is known, we say: these words referred to, if we look at the pronunciation, occur after a vowelled letter, so their due is to have their vowel fully extended, joined to yāʾ or wāw; and if they take sukūn, it is for the reason given, of treating continuous speech like the pause. If we look at the original form, a quiescent letter has preceded it, namely the weak letter dropped for the jussive, and for that reason ikhtilās is permissible. This is a useful principle that will hold good for you whenever you come near these words in this book.

His saying: «بدينار»: there are several views on this bāʾ. The first is that it keeps its original sense of adhesion (ilṣāq), but this is awkward. The second is that it means «في», and an omitted muḍāf is necessary, i.e. «في حفظِ دينارٍ» and «في حفظ قنطار» (in the keeping of a dinar / of a qinṭār). The third is that the bāʾ means «على»; the verb is often made transitive by it: {لاَ تَأْمَنَّا على يُوسُفَ} [Yūsuf: 11] and {هَلْ آمَنُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ إِلاَّ كَمَآ أَمِنتُكُمْ على أَخِيهِ} [Yūsuf: 64]. It is likewise in «بقنطار».

His saying: {إِلاَّ مَا دُمْتَ عَلَيْهِ قَآئِماً}: an emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh) from the general adverbial, since the implied meaning is: he will not render it to you at any period or time except during the period of your continuing to stand over him, keeping charge of him. This «دُمْتَ» is the defective (nāqiṣa) one, putting in the nominative and putting in the accusative. The condition for its governing is that it be preceded by the adverbial «ما», as in this verse, since the implied meaning is «إلا مدةَ دوامك» (except for the duration of your continuing). It is not conjugated [Translator's note: i.e. it has no imperfect in this use]; as for their saying «يدومُ», it is the imperfect of the complete (tāmma) «دام» meaning «بقي» (to remain). Because it is the ṣila of the adverbial «ما», it necessarily needs another statement so that it can govern the adverbial, as in «لا أصحبُك ما دمت باكياً» (I will not keep your company as long as you are weeping); and if you said «ما دام زيد قائماً» (as long as Zayd is standing) with nothing else, it would not be a complete utterance.

Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that this «ما» be merely maṣdariyya, the maṣdar (verbal noun) cast from it and from «دام» being in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial); it is then also an emptied exception, from the general implied states, the implied meaning being: «إلاَّ في حال ملازمتك له» (except in the state of your keeping close to him). On this view «دام» here is complete, because of what has preceded, namely that the precedence of the adverbial «ما» is a condition for its governing; and if it is complete, «قائماً» is accusative as a ḥāl.

One says «دامَ يدوم» like «قام يقوم», and «دُمت قائماً» with ḍamma on the first radical; this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. Tamīm say «دِمت» with kasra; so read Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Ibn Waththāb, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa and al-Fayyāḍ ibn Ghazwān. Al-Farrāʾ said: "This is the dialect of Tamīm, and they agree in the imperfect, saying «يدوم»", meaning that the Ḥijāzīs and the Tamīmīs agree that the imperfect has ḍamma on the middle radical, whereas the analogy for Tamīm would have been to say «يَدام», like «خَاف يخَاف» and «مات يمات». So its pattern according to the Ḥijāz is faʿala with fatḥa on the middle radical, and according to the Tamīmīs faʿila with kasra. This is al-Farrāʾ's report. Others reported from Tamīm that they say «دِمْت أدام» like «خِفْت أخاف»; Abū Isḥāq [Translator's note: al-Zajjāj] reported that, and others such as al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī and Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī.

The origin of this root is the indication of fixity and stillness. One says «دام الماء», i.e. the water was still; and in the ḥadīth: «لا يبولَنَّ أحدُكم في الماءِ الدائمِ» ("Let none of you urinate in still water"), and in some versions with the addition «الذي لا يجرى» ("which does not flow"), which is an explanation of it. «أَدَمْتُ القِدْرَ» and «دوَّمْتُها»: I stilled its boiling with water. From it is «دام الشيء» when a long time extends over it, and «دَوَّمَتِ الشمس» when the sun stands still in the middle of the sky. Dhū al-Rumma said:

1343 - . . . . . . . . . . ...
والشمسُ حَيْرَى لها في الجَوِّ تَدْويمُ
(… while the sun is bewildered, having a standstill [or: circling] in the sky.)

So al-Rāghib recited this hemistich with this meaning, while others recite it with the meaning that «الدوام» expresses circling around a thing. From this is «الدُّوام», which is the vertigo that seizes a person in his head so that he sees things revolving. He also recited with it the saying of ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada:

1344 - تَشْفي الصُّداع ولا يُؤْذِيك صالِبُها ... ولا يُخالطُها في الرأسِ تدويم
(It cures the headache, its heat does not harm you, and no dizziness mixes with it in the head.)

From it is «دَوَّم الطائرُ» when the bird soars and circles.

His saying: {عَلَيْهِ} is attached (mutaʿalliq) to «قائماً». What is meant by «القيام» (standing) is keeping close, because most often the claimant stands over the head of the one from whom he claims; then it was made an expression for keeping close, even if there is no standing there.

His saying: {ذلك بِأَنَّهُمْ}: a mubtadaʾ and khabar. «ذلك» refers to their regarding as lawful [Translator's note: i.e. others' property] and to there being no blame, as they claimed; i.e. that regarding as lawful is deserved or permitted by their saying «ليس علينا في الأميين سبيل» (there is no way against us concerning the unlettered).

His saying: {لَيْسَ عَلَيْنَا}: it is possible that in «ليس» there is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), which is its noun; in that case «سبيل» may be a mubtadaʾ and «علينا» the khabar, the clause being the khabar of «ليس». It is also possible that «علينا» alone is the khabar, with «سبيل» nominative by it as fāʿil (agent). It is also possible that «سبيل» is the noun of «ليس», the khabar being one of the two prepositional phrases, I mean «علينا» or «في الأميين»; and «في الأميين» may be attached to the notion of being established to which «علينا» is attached.

Some permitted that it be attached to «ليس» itself; Abū al-Baqāʾ and others reported this. This report is open to question, because there is disagreement about these defective verbs governing adverbials, and they based the disagreement on the disagreement about whether they indicate an event: whoever said they indicate an event permitted their governing the adverbial and what resembles it, and whoever said they do not indicate an event prohibited their governing. They agreed that «ليس» does not indicate an event at all, so how could it govern? This is something inconceivable. It is possible that «في الأميين» is attached to «سبيل», because it is used in the sense of blame, liability and the like; and it is possible that it is a ḥāl of it, and so attached to an omitted word.

His saying: {عَلَى اللَّهِ الكذب}: «على الله» may be attached to «الكذب», even though it is a maṣdar, because latitude is allowed with the adverbial and its equivalent [Translator's note: the prepositional phrase] that is not allowed with other things. Whoever prohibited that attached it to «يقولون», which includes the sense of «يفترون» (they fabricate), so it is made transitive in the way that verb is. It may also be attached to an omitted word, as a ḥāl of «الكذب».

His saying: {وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ} is a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. The object of the knowing is omitted, either by restriction (iqtiṣār), i.e. "while they are among those who possess knowledge", or by abbreviation (ikhtiṣār), i.e. "they know their lying and fabrication", which is uglier for them.

semin-durr:38-38.t:
The words of the Exalted: {هُنَالِكَ دَعَا}: «هنا» is the noun, the lām is for distance and the kāf is a particle; it is on the measure of «ذلك». It is accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf makānī) by «دعا», i.e.: in that place where he saw what he saw of Maryam's affair. It is an adverb that is not freely inflected but is bound to the accusative as an adverb, though it may be made genitive by «مِنْ» and «إلى». The poet said:
1250 - قد وَرَدَتْ مِنْ أَمْكِنَهْ ... مِنْ ههنا ومِنْ هُنَهْ
(They have come down to water from places — from here and from there.)
Its rule is the rule of «ذا» in that it may be stripped of the particle of attention and of the kāf and lām, as in هنا; it may be accompanied by the «ها» of attention, as in ههنا, and rarely with the kāf, as in «ها هناك»; combining hā and the lām is forbidden. Its sisters are: هَنَّا with a doubled nūn, with fatḥa or kasra on the hāʾ, and ثَمَّ with fatḥa on the thāʾ; and هَنَّتْ is sometimes said. These point only to what is distant specifically, and هنالك and what was mentioned with it point only to places.
Some claimed that «هناك», «هنالك» and «هَنَّا» are for time. Among the occurrences of «هنالك» meaning time, according to some, is this verse, i.e.: at that time; similar is {هُنَالِكَ ابتلي المؤمنون} [al-Aḥzāb: 11]; and of it are the words of Zuhayr:
1251 - هنالك إنْ يُسْتَخْبَلُوا المالَ يُخْبِلُوا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Then, if they are asked to lend wealth, they lend it …)
The evident view is that it keeps its sense of place. Of the occurrence of «هناك» are his words:
1252 - وإذا الأمورُ تعاظَمَتْ وتشابَهَتْ ... فهناك يعترفون أين المفزَعُ
(When matters grow grave and confused, then they acknowledge where the refuge lies.)
And of the occurrence of هَنَّا are his words:
1253 - حَنَّتْ نَوارِ ولاتَ هَنَّا حَنَّتِ ... وبدا الذي كانت نوارِ أَجَنَّتِ
(Nawār yearned, when it was no time for yearning, and what Nawār had concealed came to light.)
because «لات» operates only on times; and there is a longer discussion of the line than this. In the wording of al-Sajāwandī, «هناك» is for place and «هنالك» for time; that is an oversight, because it is for place whether it is bare, or joined to the kāf and lām together, or to the kāf without the lām.
His words: {مِن لَّدُنْكَ}: two aspects are permissible in it. The first: that it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «هَبْ», «مِنْ» being for the beginning of the extent figuratively, i.e.: grant me from Your presence. The second: it may be attached to an omitted element, being originally an adjective of ذرية; when it was put before it, it became accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). The discussion of لدن, its rules and its dialectal forms has preceded. His words {سَمِيعُ الدعآء}: an intensive form converted from «سامِع» (hearer), and it does not mean «مُسْمِع» (one who causes to hear), because the meaning would be corrupted.
His words: {طَيِّبَةً}: if by «ذرية» he meant the genus, the feminine in «طيبة» is in consideration of the femininity of the group; and if he meant by it a single male, the feminine is in consideration of the wording. Al-Farrāʾ said: "He made «طيبة» feminine because of the feminine wording of «الذرية», as the poet said:
1254 - أبوكَ خليفةٌ وَلَدَتْهُ أخرى ... وأنت خليفةٌ، ذاك الكمالُ
(Your father is a caliph whom another (caliph) begot, and you are a caliph — that is perfection.)"
This is in what does not intend a specific individual; if a specific individual were intended, considering the wording would be prohibited, as with Ṭalḥa and Ḥamza. The poet combined masculine and feminine in his words:
1255 - فما تَزْدَري من حَيَّةٍ جَبَلِيَّة ... سُكاتٍ إذا ما عَضَّ ليس بِأَدْرَدَا
(You do not despise a silent mountain serpent which, when it bites, is not toothless.)
because what is meant by حيَّة is the generic noun, not a specific individual.

semin-durr:39-39.t:
The words of the Exalted: {فَنَادَتْهُ الملائكة}: the two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) read «فناداه» without the feminine tāʾ, and the rest «فنادَتْه» with the feminine tāʾ. Masculine and feminine are by consideration of the broken plural: in the verb ascribed to it the masculine is permissible in consideration of the plural, and the feminine in consideration of the group. Similar is {إِذْ يَتَوَفَّى الذين كَفَرُواْ الملائكة} [al-Anfāl: 50], read with tāʾ and with yāʾ, and likewise His words {تَعْرُجُ الملائكة} [al-Maʿārij: 4]. Al-Zajjāj said: "The feminine attaches to it because of the word 'group', and it may be expressed with the masculine wording, because one says: the plural (jamʿ) of angels; this is like His words {وَقَالَ نِسْوَةٌ} [Yūsuf: 30]." End. What made the omission good here is the separation between the verb and its fāʿil (agent).
Some were bold against the reading of the generality, saying: "I dislike the feminine because of its agreement with the claim of the Jāhiliyya, since the Jāhiliyya claimed that the angels are female." And Abū al-Baqāʾ was bold against the reading of the two brothers, saying: "Some people disliked the feminine reading because of its agreement with the Jāhiliyya; so whoever read «فناداه» without tāʾ read it for that reason. Reading it so is not good, because الملائكة is a plural; and the reason they gave is nothing, because there is consensus on keeping the tāʾ in His words {وَإِذْ قَالَتِ الملائكة} [Āl ʿImrān: 42]." These two statements, issuing from Abū al-Baqāʾ and others, are not good, because they are two mutawātir readings, and neither should ever be rejected.
The two brothers follow their principle of imāla (inclining the alif) in «فناداه»; the script allows both readings together, I mean the masculine and the feminine.
The majority hold that what is meant by the angels is one, namely Jibrīl. Al-Zajjāj said: "The call came to him from this genus, who are the angels, as in your saying «فلان يركب السفنَ» ('so-and-so rides ships'), i.e.: this genus." Similar is {الذين قَالَ لَهُمُ الناس} [Āl ʿImrān: 173], and they are Nuʿaym ibn Masʿūd; and His words «إنَّ الناس» mean Abū Sufyān. And since Jibrīl is the chief of the angels, He reported about him as one reports about a group, to honour him. It was also said: "A chief must have followers, so He reported about him and about them, even though the call issued only from him." Supporting that the caller was Jibrīl alone is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) — and so it is in his Muṣḥaf: «فناداه جبريل» ("so Jibrīl called him"). The conjunction with fāʾ in His words {فَنَادَتْهُ} signals that the supplication was immediately followed by the good tidings.
His words: {وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ}: a circumstantial clause from the object of the call. «يصلي» allows several aspects. The first: that it is a second khabar (predicate), according to those who hold that multiple khabars are allowed without restriction, as in «زيدٌ شاعرٌ فقيه» ("Zayd is a poet, a jurist"). The second: that it is a second ḥāl (circumstantial) from the object of the call, this too according to those who allow multiple ḥāls. The third: that it is a ḥāl from the latent (mustatir) pronoun in «قائم», so that it is a ḥāl from a ḥāl. The fourth: that it is an adjective of قائم.
His words: {فِي المحراب}: attached to (mutaʿalliq) يُصَلِّي. It may be attached to قائم if we make «يُصَلِّي» a ḥāl from the pronoun in «قائم», because what governs it and what governs the ḥāl are then one thing, so no separation results. But if we make it a second khabar, or an adjective of قائم, or a ḥāl from the object, separation between the governing element and what it governs by a foreign element results. This is the sense of the Shaykh's (Abū Ḥayyān's) words. What appears is that the question may be of the type of contention (tanāzuʿ), since each of قائم and يصلِّي can properly have power over «في المحراب»; and that is permissible on any of the aspects of parsing given above.
His words: {إِنَّ اللَّهَ}: Nāfiʿ, Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir read «إنَّ» with kasra, and the rest with fatḥa. The kasra, according to the Kufans, is because calling is treated like saying, so it takes kasra with it; according to the Basrans it is on the concealment of saying, i.e.: so they called him and said. The fatḥa is on the omission of the preposition, its implied form being: so they called him with (the news) that Allah…; when the preposition is omitted, the two well-known aspects apply to its position.
In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: «فنادَتْه الملائكة: يا زكريا»; his words «يا زكريا» are the object of the call, and on this reading the kasra of «إنَّ» is required, and its fatḥa is not permissible, because the verb has taken its full complement of governed elements, namely the pronoun and that with which Zakariyyā was called.
His words: «نُبَشِّرُك»: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim — the five — read in this sūra {إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكَ}, in two places, in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ {وَيُبَشِّرَ المؤمنين} [verse: 9], and in Sūrat al-Kahf {وَيُبَشِّرَ المؤمنين} [verse: 2] likewise, with ḍamma on the yāʾ, fatḥa on the bāʾ and kasra on a doubled shīn, from بَشَّره يُبَشِّره. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim, the three of them, read likewise in Sūrat al-Shūrā, namely {ذَلِكَ الذي يُبَشِّرُ الله عِبَادَهُ} [verse: 23]. All except Ḥamza read likewise in Sūrat Barāʾa: {يُبَشِّرُهُمْ رَبُّهُم بِرَحْمَةٍ مِّنْهُ} [verse: 21], and in the first (occurrence) in al-Ḥijr in His words {إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلامٍ عَلِيمٍ} [verse: 53]; there is no disagreement that the second, namely His words {فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ} [al-Ḥijr: 54], is with the doubled form. Likewise all except Ḥamza read so in Sūrat Maryam in two places: {إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ} [Maryam: 7] and {لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ المتقين} [Maryam: 97]. Everyone not mentioned with these as reading with the stated specification reads with fatḥa on the imperfect prefix, a vowelless bāʾ and ḍamma on the shīn.
If you want to know how to master this section, know that the places in which the said disagreement occurs are nine words, and the readers are of several grades in them. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read all of them doubled, and Ḥamza read all of them light. Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read all of them doubled except the one in Sūrat al-Shūrā, in which they agreed with Ḥamza. Al-Kisāʾī read five of them light and four doubled: he read light the two words of this sūra and the words of al-Isrāʾ, al-Kahf and al-Shūrā.
It has preceded that there are three dialectal forms of this verb: «بَشَّر» with doubling; بَشَر with the light form, on which is what al-Farrāʾ recited:
1256 - بَشَرْتُ عيالي إذ رأيتُ صحيفةً ... أَتَتْكَ من الحَجَّاجِ يُتْلَى كتابُها
(I gave good news to my household when I saw a letter that came to you from al-Ḥajjāj, its writing being read out.)
and the third: «أَبْشَرْتُ», as a quadriliteral, on which is the reading of some «يُبْشِرُك» with ḍamma on the yāʾ. Of al-tabshīr is the other's words:
1257 - يا بِشْرُ حُقَّ لوجهِك التَّبْشِيرُ ... هَلاَّ غَضِبْت لنا وأنتَ أَميرُ
(O Bishr, your face deserves good tidings — why did you not grow angry for us when you were a governor?)
There is consensus on places of these forms, such as {فَبَشِّرْهُم بِعَذَابٍ} [Āl ʿImrān: 21], {وَأَبْشِرُواْ} [Fuṣṣilat: 30] and {فَبَشَّرْنَاهَا بِإِسْحَاقَ} [Hūd: 71]; so the disagreement occurs only in the imperfect, not in the past or imperative. The meaning of al-bishāra and its derivation have preceded in Sūrat al-Baqara.
The words of the Exalted: {بيحيى}: attached to يُبَشِّرُكَ. A muḍāf must be omitted, i.e.: of the birth of Yaḥyā, because essences are not objects of good tidings. And the speech must contain [something] to which the context returns, its implied form being: of the birth of Yaḥyā from you and from your wife; the circumstantial context and the course of the speech indicate that.
«يحيى» has two views. The first, which is the well-known one among the exegetes, is that it is transferred from the imperfect verb (yaḥyā, "he lives"); they have often named with verbs, as in يعيش, يعمر and يَمُوت. Qatāda said: "He was named Yaḥyā because Allah gave him life through faith." Al-Zajjāj said: "He lived through knowledge." On this view it is a diptote because of being a proper name (al-ʿamaliyya «[Translator's note: so in the text; evidently al-ʿalamiyya]») and the verbal pattern, as in «يزيد», «يشكر» and «تغلب». The second: that it is foreign with no derivation, and this is the evident view; so it is a diptote because of being a proper name and personal foreignness. On both views its plural is يَحْيَوْن, with the alif dropped, as in «مُوسَوْن», with the alif dropped and the fatḥa remaining to indicate it. The Kufans said: "If it is Arabic, transferred from the verb, the matter is so; and if it is foreign, what precedes the wāw takes a ḍamma and what precedes the yāʾ a kasra, treating it like the defective noun (manqūṣ), as in «جاء القاضون» and «رأيت القاضين»." This is the Shaykh's report from them. Ibn Mālik reported from them that if the noun's alif is additional, what precedes the wāw takes ḍamma and what precedes the yāʾ kasra, as in «جاء حُبْلُون» and «رأيت حُبْلِين»; and if it is radical, as in «رَجَوْن», the letter before the two letters must take fatḥa. They said: "If it is foreign, both aspects are permissible, because its alif may be radical or additional, since no derivation is known for it." Yaḥyā is diminished as «يُحَيَّى». There was recited to me, from the Shaykh Abū ʿAmr Ibn al-Ḥājib, on that:
1258 - أيُّها العالم بالتصريفِ لا زلت تُحَيَّا ... إنَّ يَحْيى إنْ يُصَغَّرْ فيُحَيَّا ... وأبى قومٌ وقالوا ليسَ هذا الرأيُ حَيّا ... إنما كان صواباً أَنْ يُجيبوا بيُحَيَّا ... كيف قد رَدُّوا يُحَيَّا ... والذي اختارُوا يُحَيَّا ... أتراهم في ضلالٍ أم ترى وجهاً يُحَيَّا
(O scholar of morphology, may you ever be greeted: Yaḥyā, if diminished, becomes yuḥayyā; but some refused and said this opinion is not alive — the right answer would have been to reply with yuḥayyā. How could they reject yuḥayyā, when what they chose is yuḥayyā? Do you think them in error, or do you see a view to be saluted? — a riddle playing on the different spellings of the diminutive.)
I say: this runs like riddles on the diminutive of this word, and that differs with morphology and its working: when three yāʾs come together at the end of a diminished noun, there is a disagreement among the grammarians regarding dropping and keeping, and the root of the question is the diminutive of «أَحْوى». I have perfected these lines and set out the positions of the morphologists on them when I was asked about them, in a place other than this subject, since this one cannot bear it.
The relative adjective (nisba) of يَحْيى is: يَحْيِيّ, dropping the alif by likening it to an additional one, as in حُبْلِيّ from حُبْلى; يَحْيَويّ, by changing (the alif), because it is radical like the alif of مَلْهَويّ, or resembles a radical if it is foreign; and يَحْياويّ, adding an alif before changing its alif into wāw.
Al-nidāʾ (calling) is raising the voice. One says: نادى نُداءً and نداءً, with ḍamma or kasra on the nūn; most sound-words come with ḍamma, as in البُكاء (weeping), الصُّراخ (screaming), الدُّعاء (calling) and الرُّغاء (the camel's grumbling). It was also said: the form with kasra is a maṣdar (verbal noun) and the one with ḍamma a noun; had this been reversed it would have been clearer, because it would agree with its counterparts among maṣdars. Yaʿqūb ibn al-Sikkīt said: "If you put ḍamma on its nūn, you shorten it, and if you put kasra on it, you lengthen it." The root meaning of the material indicates raising.
From it are al-muntadā and al-nādī (the assembly), because people gather in them and raise their voices. Quraysh said: Dār al-Nadwa, because they raised their voices in consultation and dialogue there. فلان أَنْدى صوتاً من فلان means: louder. This is its origin in the language; in customary usage it came to mean the more beautiful of the two in tone and voice. Al-nadā is rain (dew); and from it: نَدِيَ يَنْدَى (to be moist). It is used to express generosity, just as rain, downpour and their sisters are used to express it, by way of metaphor.
His words: {مُصَدِّقاً}: a ḥāl from «يحيى», and it is an anticipated (muqaddara) ḥāl. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is a corroborative ḥāl, according to the state of these prophets, peace be upon them." «بكلمة» is attached to «مصدقاً». Abū al-Sammāl read «بكِلْمَةٍ», with kasra on the kāf and a vowelless lām; it is an eloquent dialectal form. That is because he made the first radical follow the second in its vowel, so two kasras met, and he dropped the second because of heaviness. As for al-kalima, it was said that the plural is meant by it, since what is intended is the Torah, the Gospel and other revealed books of Allah the Exalted; so the plural was expressed by part of it. Similar to this is his words, peace be upon him: «أصدقُ كلمةٍ قالها الشاعر كلمةُ لبيد» ("the truest word a poet said is the word of Labīd"), meaning his words:
1259 - ألا كلُّ شيءٍ ما خلا الله باطِلُ ... وكلُّ نعيمٍ لا مَحَالَةَ زائِلُ
(Indeed, everything except Allah is vain, and every bliss is inevitably passing.)
And the poet al-Ḥuwaydira was mentioned to Ḥassān, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "May Allah curse his kalima," meaning his ode. Further explanation of this will come at the words of the Exalted {إلى كَلِمَةٍ سَوَآءٍ} [Āl ʿImrān: 64].
His words: {مِّنَ الله}: in the position of the genitive as an adjective of كلمة «[Translator's note: the text has لكملة, a slip for لكلمة]», so it is attached to an omitted element, i.e.: of a word coming from Allah. {وَسَيِّداً وَحَصُوراً وَنَبِيّاً} are also ḥāls, like مصدِّقاً. Al-sayyid is fayʿil, the origin being سَيْوِد; there was done [to it] what was done with ميت — how that is done has preceded. Its derivation is from سادَ يسود سِيادة وسُؤْدُدَاً, i.e.: he surpassed his peers in nobility and lordship. And from it is their saying:
1260 - نفسُ عصامٍ سَوَّدَتْ عِصَاما ... وعَلَّمَتْه الكَرَّ والإِقداما
وصَيَّرتَهُ بَطَلاً هُمَاما
(The soul of ʿIṣām made ʿIṣām a lord, taught him attack and boldness, and made him a valiant hero.)
Some said: he was called sayyid because he leads (yasūdu) the mass (sawād) of the people, i.e. their great body and bulk. Its plural on faʿala (sāda) is irregular by analogy but eloquent in usage; the Exalted said {إِنَّآ أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا} [al-Aḥzāb: 67], the origin being سَوَدَة. Faʿala is frequent only for fāʿil, as in كافِر and كَفَرة, فاجِر and فَجَرة, بار and بَرَرة.
Al-ḥaṣūr is faʿūl for intensification, converted from «حاصِر», like ضَرُوب in his words:
1261 - ضَروبٌ بنصْلِ السيفِ سُوقَ سِمانِها ... إذا عَدِموا زاداً فإنَّك عاقِرُ
(Striking hard with the sword-blade the legs of their fat camels: when they lack provisions, you are one who hamstrings (them for food).)
It was also said: rather it is faʿūl in the sense of mafʿūl, i.e. maḥṣūr (restrained); similar are رَكوب meaning مركوب (ridden) and حَلوب meaning مَحْلوب (milked). Al-ḥaṣūr is also one who keeps his secret. Jarīr said:
1262 - ولقد تَسَقَّطَني الوشاةُ فصادَفوا ... حَصِراً بسِرِّك يا أُمَيْمُ ضَنِيناً
(The slanderers sought to catch my slips, but they found me, O Umaym, close with your secret and grudging of it.)
[It is also the miser.] He said:
1263 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... لا بالحَصورِ ولا فيها بِسَآَّرِ
(… neither a miser, nor one who leaves dregs in it.)
The derivation of this root has preceded; its origin is taken from prevention. That is because al-ḥaṣūr is one who does not approach women, either because his nature is so or because he overcomes his self. «من الصالحين» is an adjective of His words «نبياً», so it is in the position of the accusative.

semin-durr:123-123.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {بِبَدْرٍ}: It is attached to «نَصَرَكم», and there are two views on the باء here. The more evident is that it is locative (ẓarfiyya), i.e. "in Badr", as you say "Zayd is in Mecca" (زيد بمكة), meaning "in Mecca". The second is that it is attached to an omitted element, the باء being the bāʾ of accompaniment, so that its position is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. "accompanying Badr". Badr is the name of a watering place between Mecca and Medina; it was so named for its clarity, like the full moon (al-badr); it is also said (it was so named) for its roundness (istidāra); and it is said, after its owner, who was Badr ibn Kalada. It is also said that it is the name of a valley, and also said that it is the name of a well.

And al-tawakkul is of the pattern tafaʿʿul: either from al-wakāla, which is entrusting the matter to someone whose good management and expertise in handling it you trust; or from wakala amrahu ilā fulān ("he left his affair to so-and-so") when he was incapable of it. Ibn Fāris said: "It is the display of incapacity and reliance upon someone else. One says: fulānun wakalatun tukala, meaning incapable, one who leaves his affair to another." The تاء in «تُكَلة» is a substitute for the واو, like tukhama and tujāh.

His saying: {وَأَنْتُمْ أَذِلَّةٌ}: in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the object of «نصركم». And «أَذِلَّة» is the plural of dhalīl (abased). It was formed as a plural of paucity (jamʿ qilla), to indicate their fewness together with this attribute. The regular plural of the adjective of the pattern faʿīl is on fuʿalāʾ, like ẓarīf, ẓurafāʾ and sharīf, shurafāʾ, except that in the doubled (muḍaʿʿaf) root this was abandoned for the sake of lightness. Do you not see what saying dhulalāʾ and khulalāʾ, as plurals of dhalīl and khalīl, leads to of heaviness?

semin-durr:125-125.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {مُسَوِّمِينَ}: like his saying «مُنْزَلين». Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim read it with kasra on the واو, as an active participle, and the rest with fatḥa, as a passive participle. As for the first reading, it may be from al-sawm, which is leaving livestock to graze; the meaning is that they let their horses range, i.e. gave them their free range of running and wheeling and left them so, as one does who lets his livestock pasture in the meadow. Or it may be from al-sawma, which is the mark (ʿalāma), in the sense that they marked themselves or their horses. In the exegesis it is reported that they wore white turbans, except Gabriel, who wore a yellow turban; and it is reported that they were on piebald horses (bulq). Ibn Jarīr preferred this reading on the basis of what is reported in the ḥadīth from him, peace be upon him, on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves (tasawwamū), for the angels have marked themselves."

As for the second reading, it is clear in both of the meanings mentioned. The meaning of al-sawm in it is that Allah sent them out, since the angels were sent from Allah to support His Prophet and the believers. Abū Zayd related: sawwama al-rajulu khaylahu, i.e. he sent them out; and some related: "sawwamtu ghulāmī", i.e. I sent him out. For this reason Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash said: "The meaning of «مُسَوَّمين» is «مُرْسَلين» (sent)." And the meaning of al-sawma in it is that Allah the Exalted marked them, i.e. put a mark on them, namely the turbans; or the angels made their horses a particular kind, namely the piebald, so they marked their horses.

semin-durr:16-16.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {الذين يَقُولُونَ}: its position may be nominative, accusative or genitive. The nominative is in two ways. The first: it is a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted, its implied form being: "those who say such-and-such are answered," or "for them is that good just mentioned." The second: it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, as if it were asked: "Who are these God-fearing ones?" and it was said: "They are those who say thus and so."

The accusative is in one way only, namely accusative by the implied verb أعني ("I mean") or أمدح ("I praise"). This parallels the nominative as khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, and the two are called "nominative by severance" and "accusative by severance". The genitive is in two ways: the first is naʿt (adjective) and the second is badal (substitute). Then, in making it a naʿt or a badal, you have two options: the first is to make it a naʿt of {الذين اتقوا} or a badal of it; the second is to make it a naʿt of {العباد} or a badal of them. Abū l-Baqāʾ considered it weak to make it a naʿt of {العباد}. He said: "Because that would restrict the knowledge of Allah the Exalted; it is permissible, though weak, and the point of it would be to let them know that He knows the measure of their hardship in worship and so repays them for it, as He said: {والله أَعْلَمُ بِإِيمَانِكُمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 25]."

As for the clause {واللهُ بصيرٌ}: it may be parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya), with no grammatical position, if you make {الذين يَقُولُونَ} a follower of {الذين اتقوا}, either as naʿt or as badal; but if you make it nominative or accusative, then it is not.

semin-durr:17-17.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {الصابرين}: if you take {الذين يقولون} to be accusative or genitive in position, according to what has preceded, then {الصابرين} is a naʿt (adjective) of it under both assumptions, so it may be in the position of the accusative or in the position of the genitive. But if you take it to be nominative in position, then {الصابرين} must be accusative by an implied "I mean" (أعني).

{الأسحار} is the plural of سَحَر, with fatḥa or sukūn on the ʿayn (middle letter). The authorities of the language differed about the saḥar: which time is it? A group of them, among them al-Zajjāj, said: "It is the time before the rising of dawn," and from it comes تَسَحَّر (to take the pre-dawn meal), meaning to eat at that time, and أَسْحَرَ when one travels in it. Zuhayr said:

1198 - بَكَرْنَ بُكوراً واسْتَحَرْنَ بسُحْرَةٍ ... فهنَّ ووادي الرَّسِّ كاليدِ للفَم
(They set out early and travelled at the pre-dawn; they and the valley of al-Rass are like the hand to the mouth.)

Al-Rāghib said: "The saḥar is the mingling of the darkness of the end of the night with the light of the day, and it was made a name for that time. One says: 'I met him at the very top of the two saḥars.' The musḥir is the one who goes out at saḥar; the saḥūr is the name of the food eaten at saḥar, and the tasaḥḥur is the eating of it." The mustaḥir is the bird that calls out at saḥar. He said:

1199 - يُعَلُّ به بَرْدُ أنيابِها ... إذا غَرَّدَ الطائرُ المُسْتَحِرْ
(The coolness of its teeth is sipped with it, when the mustaḥir bird sings.)

Some of them said: "أَسْحَرَ الطائر means: the bird cried out and moved about in its crying," and he recited the verse. This, although stated in general terms, only intends what I mentioned, namely crying at saḥar. One also says: أَسْحَر الرجل, meaning: the man entered the time of saḥar, like أَظْهَرَ, meaning: he entered the time of noon (ẓuhr). He said:

1200 - وأَدْلَجَ مِنْ طِيْبَةٍ مسرعاً ... فجاءَ إلينا وقد أَسْحَرَا
(He set out by night from Ṭība in haste, and came to us when he had entered the saḥar.)

Similar to it is also اسْتَحَرَ. Some of them said: "The saḥar is from the last third of the night until the rising of dawn." Some of them also said: "The saḥar, among the Arabs, is from the end of the night, and its rule then continues until the light spreads; all of it is called saḥar." It is said: the saḥar was called saḥar because of its being hidden, and from this the sihr (magic) was called sihr, because of its subtlety and concealment.

The saḥr, with sukūn on the ḥāʾ, is the end of the windpipe of the lung, and from it comes the saying of the Mother of the Believers ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "He died between my saḥr and my naḥr (chest)." It was so named because of its being hidden. Concerning saḥar there is much discussion, with regard to whether it is declined (ṣarf) or not, whether it is inflected or not, and its i'rab or not; the details will come, Allah willing, where it is mentioned, since that is the more fitting place.

His saying: {والصادقين} and what is conjoined to it. If it is asked: how does the wāw enter upon these attributes when all of them belong to one group? There are two answers. The first is that when attributes are repeated, it is permissible to conjoin some of them to others with the wāw, even if the one described by them is one; and the entry of the wāw in such a case is for magnification, because it signals that each attribute is independent in praise. The second answer: that these attributes are distributed among them, so some of them are patient and some truthful, and the one described by them is therefore plural. This is the speech of Abū l-Baqāʾ.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The wāw standing between the attributes indicates their perfection in each one of them." The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "We do not know that conjoining an attribute with the wāw indicates perfection." I (al-Samīn) say: The scholars of rhetoric (bayān) have known it, and the verification of this question has already preceded in the opening of Sūrat al-Baqara, together with what I recited on it from the language of the Arabs. The bāʾ in {بالأسحار} has the meaning of "in".

semin-durr:21-21.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {إِنَّ الذين يَكْفُرُونَ}: since this relative noun was made to include the meaning of a condition, the fāʾ entered its khabar (predicate), namely His saying: فبشِّرْهُم. This is the sound view, I mean that when the mubtadaʾ (subject) is abrogated by "inna", the permissibility of the fāʾ's entry remains, because the meaning has not changed but has increased in emphasis. Al-Akhfash differed and forbade its entry when it is abrogated by "inna"; but the attested usage is a proof against him, as in this verse and as in His saying: {إِنَّ الذين فَتَنُواْ المؤمنين والمؤمنات} [al-Burūj: 10], the verse. Likewise when it is abrogated by "lākinna", as in his saying:

1210 - فوالله ما فَارَقْتُكُمْ عن مَلالةٍ ... ولكنَّ ما يُقْضَى فسوف يكون
(By Allah, I did not part from you out of weariness; but what is decreed will come to be.)
