Likewise when it is abrogated by the fatḥa-vowelled "anna", as in His saying, Exalted is He: {واعلموا أَنَّمَا غَنِمْتُمْ مِّن شَيْءٍ فَأَنَّ للَّهِ [خُمُسَهُ]} [al-Anfāl: 41]. But when it is abrogated by "layta", "laʿalla" and "ka-anna", the fāʾ is impossible according to everyone, because of the change of meaning.

His saying: {وَيَقْتُلُونَ}: Ḥamza read "wa-yuqātilūna" (they fight), from muqātala (fighting), and the rest read "wa-yaqtulūna" like the first. As for Ḥamza's reading, he made the two verbs differ in it, and it agrees with the reading of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd): "wa-qātilū", from muqātala, except that he brought the past form; and it is possible that the imperfect in Ḥamza's reading is for narrating a past state, its meaning being past. As for the rest, it was said of their reading that the verb was repeated only because of the difference of what it attaches to, or it was repeated for emphasis. It was also said that by one of the two killings is meant the taking of the life and by the other the humiliation, and therefore each was mentioned separately; and were it not for that, the construction would have been "wa-yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīna wa-lladhīna yaʾmurūna".

Al-Ḥasan read: "wa-yuqattilūna" with shadda, whose meaning is multiplication. Here it came as {بغيرِ حق} indefinite, while in al-Baqara it is {بِغَيْرِ الحق} [verse 61] definite. It was said: because the sentence here was cast in the mould of a condition, which is general and not specified, it therefore suited it to be indefinite in a context of negation so as to be general; whereas in al-Baqara the verse came concerning particular people, individually identified, and the right for which a person is killed was known to them, so this generality that is here was not intended; so in each place what suits it was brought. His saying: {من الناس}: it is either explicative or partitive, and in both cases it is known that they are from among the people, so it runs in the course of emphasis.

semin-durr:99-99.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {لِمَ تَصُدُّونَ} ("Why do you hinder"): «لِمَ» is attached to the verb after it, and «مَنْ آمن» is the object. As for His saying «يَبْغُونها», it is possible that it is a resumptive clause by which He informed about them, and it is possible that it is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). This is the clearer of the two, because the interrogative clause is followed by another circumstantial clause, namely His saying {وأنتم تَشْهَدون}, so the two clauses agree in having the ḥāl rendered accusative from each of them. Then, if we say that it is a ḥāl, there are two possibilities for its owner: one, that it is the fāʿil (agent) of «تَصُدُّون»; the other, that it is «سبيل الله». Both are permissible only because the clause contains a pronoun referring to each of them.

The majority read «تَصُدُّون» with fatḥa on the tāʾ, from the triliteral صَدَّ يَصُدُّ, which is used both intransitively and transitively. al-Ḥasan read «تُصِدُّون» with ḍamma on the tāʾ, from أَصَدَّ like أَعَدَّ. The explanation is that he made the intransitive «صَدَّ» transitive by the hamza. Dhū l-Rumma said:
1362 - أُناسٌ أَصَدُّوا الناسَ بالسيفِ عنهمُ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(People who turned the others away from them with the sword …) [Translator's note: the second half of the verse is elided in the source.]

As for «عِوَجا», there are two aspects. One: that it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), by taking «تبغون» to mean «تَطْلُبون» (you seek). al-Zajjāj and al-Ṭabarī said: "You seek crookedness for it." The Arabs say «ابغِني كذا» with a conjunctive alif, meaning "seek it for me", and «أَبْغِني كذا» with a cutting alif, meaning "help me in seeking it". al-Anbārī said: "The verb بَغَى is limited to one object when the lām is not with it, as in your saying بَغَيْتُ المال والأجر والثواب ('I sought the wealth, the reward, the recompense'). Here what is meant is: يبغون لها عوجاً ('they seek crookedness for it'); when the lām dropped, the verb acted on what comes after it, just as they said «وَهَبْتُك درهماً», meaning وَهَبْتُ لك ('I gave you a dirham'), and like it «صُدْتُكَ ظَبْياً», meaning صُدْتُ لك ('I hunted a gazelle for you')." The poet said:
1363 - فَتَولَّى غلامُهمْ ثم نادى ... أَظَلِيماً أَصِيدُكم أَمْ حِمارا
(Their servant turned away, then called out: "Shall I hunt you an ostrich, or a wild ass?")
meaning: أَصِيدُ لكم ظَلِيماً. Like it is «جَنَيْتُكَ كَمْأَةً وجَنَيْتُك رُطَباً» where the original is جَنَيْتُ لك ('I gathered for you truffles / fresh dates'); he omitted the lām and made the noun accusative.

The second: that it is a ḥāl from the fāʿil of «يَبْغُونَها», when «تَبْغُون» is taken to mean «تتعَدَّوْن» (you transgress), for البَغْيُ is transgression, and the meaning is: "you transgress against it or in it." al-Zajjāj said: "It is as if He had said: you seek it while being astray."

العِوَج with kasra and العَوَج with fatḥa both mean inclination, but the Arabs distinguished between them: they assigned the kasra form to abstract matters (maʿānī) and the fatḥa form to concrete things (aʿyān). You say: «في دينه وكلامِه عِوَجٌ» with kasra, and «في الجِدارِ عِوَجٌ» with fatḥa. Abū ʿUbayda said: "العِوَج with kasra is inclination in religion, speech and action; with fatḥa it is in a wall and a palm trunk." Abū Isḥāq said: "With kasra, in what you do not see as a body; with fatḥa, in what has a body." The author of al-Mujmal said: "With fatḥa, in everything upright such as a wall; and العِوج, meaning with kasra, is what occurs in a carpet, a religion, a land or a livelihood." So he made the distinction between the two on a different basis from what preceded. al-Rāghib said: "العِوَجُ is turning away from the state of being upright; one says عُجْتُ البعيرَ بزِمامه ('I turned the camel by its halter'), and 'so-and-so does not turn back from anything he intends', that is, he does not return. العَوَج, meaning with fatḥa / is said of what is perceived by sight, such as upright wood and the like, while العِوَج is said of what is perceived by thought and insight, as when a level land has crookedness whose unevenness is known by insight, and like religion and livelihood." I say: this is close to the saying of Ibn Fāris, because he often takes from him.

al-Zamakhsharī raised a question in Sūrat Ṭāhā at His saying {لاَّ ترى فِيهَا عِوَجاً ولا أَمْتاً} [Ṭāhā: 107], the gist of which comes back to this: how was it said عِوَج with kasra of concrete things, when it is only said of abstract matters? He answered there with a good answer whose explanation will come, Allah willing. The question arises only on the saying of Abū ʿUbayda and al-Zajjāj mentioned above; on the saying of Ibn Fāris and al-Rāghib it does not arise.

Among the uses of العِوَج in the sense of inclination, in general, is the saying:
1364 - تَمُرُّون الديارَ ولم تَعُوجوا ... كلامُكُمُ عليَّ إذاً حَرامُ
(You pass by the abodes without stopping; then your speaking to me is forbidden.)
and the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
1365 - عُوجا على الطَّلَلِ المُحيل لأننا ... نبكي الديارَ كما بكى ابنُ حِذَامِ
(Turn aside to the effaced ruin, so that we may weep over the abodes as Ibn Ḥidhām wept.)
that is: "and you did not turn aside", and "turn aside" (two of you). As for their saying «ما يَعيج زيدٌ بالدواء», meaning "Zayd does not benefit from the medicine", it is from another root and another meaning. And العاج is this bone [ivory]; its alif is of unknown origin; we do not know whether it is converted from wāw or yāʾ. In the ḥadīth, he said to Thawbān: «اشترِ لفاطمةَ سِواراً من عاج» ("Buy Fāṭima a bracelet of ivory"). al-Qutaybī said: "العاجُ is al-dhabl [tortoise-shell / turtle shell]." Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī said about a woman:
1366 - فجاءَتْ كخاصِي العَيْر لم تَحْلَ جاجةً ... ولا عاجةً منها تلوحُ على وَشْمِ
(She came like the gelded wild ass; no bead and no bangle of hers appeared shining upon a tattoo.) [Translator's note: gloss given tentatively; the verse is obscure.]
al-Aṣmaʿī said: "العاجةُ is the dhabla [a bracelet of tortoise-shell], and الجاجة is a bead valued at about a fals [small coin]. His saying كخاصي العَيْر is a proverb the Arabs say of one who comes feeling ashamed of a matter, so it is said جاء كخاصِي العَيْر; العَيْر is the donkey; they mean: he came feeling ashamed."

It is also said: عاجَ بالمكانِ and عَوَّج به, meaning he stayed and settled. In the ḥadīth of Ismāʿīl, peace be upon him: «ها أنتم عَائجون», meaning "you are staying." They recited for Jarīr:
1367 - هَلَ انتم عائِجُونَ بِنَا لَغَنَّا ... نَرَى العَرَصاتِ أو أثرِ الخيامِ
(Will you stop with us, that perhaps we may see the courtyards or the traces of the tents?)
al-Harawī recited this verse thus, citing it as evidence for staying, but that is not clear; rather, what is meant by «عائجون» in the verse is "inclining" and "turning". And in the ḥadīth: «ثم عاجَ رأسَه إليها», meaning he turned toward her.

The «ها» in «يَبْغُونها» refers back to سبيل, and سبيل is treated as masculine and feminine, as preceded. An example of the feminine is this verse and His saying, the Exalted: {هذه سبيلي} [Yūsuf: 108], and the saying of another:
1368 - فلا تَبْعَدْ فكلُّ فتى أُناسٍ ... سيصبحُ سالكاً تلك السَّبيلا
(Do not be far removed, for every youth of the people will come to walk that path.)

His saying: {وَأَنْتُمْ شُهَدَآءُ} is a ḥāl: either from the fāʿil of «تَصُدُّون», or from the fāʿil of «تَبْغُون», or it is resumptive, but that is not clear. It was mentioned earlier that «شهداء» is the plural of شهيد or شاهد.

semin-durr:100-100.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {يَرُدُّوكُم}: «رَدَّ» may be taken to include the meaning of «صَيَّر» (to make into), and so take two objects (mafʿūl). Of this is the poet's saying:
1369 - رَمَى الحَِدْثانُ نسوةَ آلِ حرب ... بمِقْدَارٍ سَمَدْن له سُمودا
فَرَدَّ شعورَهُنَّ السُّودَ بِيضاً ... ورَدَّ وجوهَهن البِيضَ سُودا
(Fate struck the women of the house of Ḥarb with a decree before which they stood bewildered; so it turned their black hair white and turned their white faces black.)
It may also be that it is not taken to include that meaning, in which case the second accusative is a ḥāl. His saying {بَعْدَ إِيمَانِكُمْ} may be accusative by «يردُّوكم», or may be attached to «كافرين», and the meaning becomes like the meaning in His saying: {كَفَرُواْ بَعْدَ إِيمَانِهِمْ} [Āl ʿImrān: 90].

semin-durr:101-101.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَأَنْتُمْ تتلى عَلَيْكُمْ آيَاتُ الله}: a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the fāʿil (agent) of «تكفرون», and likewise {وَفِيكُمْ رَسُولُهُ}; that is: how can disbelief be found in you while these two circumstances exist? Iʿtiṣām is refraining (imtināʿ). One says iʿtaṣama and istaʿṣama in one meaning; and iʿtaṣama Zaydun ʿAmran means he prepared for him something by which to hold fast. It is also said: iʿtiṣām is gripping (imsāk), and istaʿṣama bi-kadhā means he held fast to it. al-ʿIṣām is what the waterskin is tied with, and people are named by it. ʿIṣma is used in both senses, because it prevents error and its possessor holds fast to the truth. ʿIṣma is also something like a bracelet, and al-miʿṣam is the place of the ʿiṣma; the whiteness at the wrist is called «عُصْمة» by analogy with it, as if they made the ḍamma of the ʿayn a distinguishing mark. al-Aʿṣam among mountain goats is one with whiteness at its wrists, and it is the swiftest of them in running. He said:
1370 - لو أَنَّ عُصْمَ عَمايتين ويَذْبُلٍ ... سمعا حديثك. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(If the white-wristed mountain goats of ʿAmāyatayn and Yadhbul had heard your talk …) [Translator's note: the rest of the verse is elided in the source.]
In the ḥadīth about women: «لا يَدْخُلُ الجنةَ منهن إلا كالغراب الأَعْصم», and that is the one white in both legs. It is also said: white in both wings; what is meant by that is fewness.

His saying: {فَقَدْ هُدِيَ} is the jawāb al-sharṭ (apodosis). «قد» is brought into the apodosis to indicate expectation, because the one who holds fast is expected to be guided.

semin-durr:76-76.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {بلى} is a reply to their saying "ليس" and an affirmation of what they denied; the discussion of its like has already preceded. And «مَنْ» is either conditional or relative. The link (rābiṭ) in the apodosis clause or the predicate clause is the generality in «المتقين» (the God-fearing); and for one who holds that the link is made by putting the overt noun in the place of the pronoun, he says that here too. It was said: the apodosis or predicate is omitted, its implied form being "يحبه الله" (Allah loves him), and the saying {فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ الْمُتَّقِينَ} points to this omitted element; but there is a strained reading in it that is not needed.
And {بِعَهْدِهِ}: it is permissible that the maṣdar (verbal noun) be annexed to its agent, on the basis that the pronoun refers back to «مَنْ»; or to its object, on the basis that it refers back to «الله». It is also permissible that the maṣdar be annexed to the agent even if the pronoun belongs to Allah the Exalted, and to the object even if the pronoun belongs to «مَنْ»; its meaning is clear once it is considered.

semin-durr:102-102.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {حَقَّ تُقَاتِهِ}: there are two aspects here. [Translator's note: the source gives only one aspect explicitly after the colon; a slash in the text marks a break.] «تقاة» is a maṣdar (verbal noun), and this is a case of annexing an adjective to its qualified noun, since the original is اتقوا الله التقاةَ الحقَّ, that is, the established one, as you say «ضربْتُ زيداً أشدَّ الضَّرْبِ», meaning the severe beating. The verification that «تقاة» is a maṣdar was given at the beginning of the sūra. Here Ibn ʿAṭiyya added that «تُقاة» may be a plural, and in that he opposes the consensus. He said: "It is also valid that «التقاة» in this verse be the plural of fāʿil, even though it is not conjugated from it, so it would be like rumāt and rāmin; or it may be the plural of taqiyy, since fa'īl and fāʿil are on a par. The meaning on this basis would be: fear Allah as it is fitting that those who fear Him, those devoted to Him, should be; and for that reason they were annexed to the pronoun of Allah the Exalted." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "This meaning is rejected by this wording, since the apparent sense of {حَقَّ تُقَاتِهِ} is annexation of an adjective to its qualified noun, as you say «ضربْتُ زيداً شديدَ الضرب», meaning the severe beating; likewise here, meaning: fear Allah with true fear, that is, obligatory and established. But if you make التقاة a plural, the meaning becomes like: اضرِبْ زيداً حقَّ ضِرابِهِ, and this construction does not indicate the meaning 'strike Zayd as it is fitting that his strikers should be'; rather, if one expressed this construction explicitly, one would need, to understand its meaning, to supply things by whose supplying the meaning becomes sound. The supplied form would be: strike Zayd a true striking, as it is fitting that the striking of his strikers be. There is no need that calls for loading the wording with other than its apparent sense and straining to supply things by which a meaning becomes sound that the wording does not indicate."

His saying: {وَلاَ تَمُوتُنَّ إِلاَّ وَأَنْتُمْ مُّسْلِمُونَ} is in form a prohibition against their dying except in this state, but what is meant is that they continue in Islam; for death is unavoidable, so it is as if it were said: persevere in Islam until death. Close to it is what Sībawayh related: «لا أُرَيَنَّك ههنا», meaning "do not be present so that my sight falls upon you." The clause {وَأَنْتُمْ مُّسْلِمُونَ} is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, and the exception is mufarragh (unrestricted) over the general states, that is: do not die in any state of all states except this good state. He brought it as a nominal clause because it is more eloquent and more emphatic, since it contains a repeated pronoun; had it been said «إلاَّ مسلمين», it would not have given this emphasis. The clarification of this construction was given in al-Baqara at His saying, the Exalted: {إِنَّ الله اصطفى لَكُمُ الدين فَلاَ تَمُوتُنَّ إَلاَّ وَأَنْتُم مُّسْلِمُونَ} [al-Baqara: 132].

semin-durr:78-78.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {يَلْوُونَ}: it is a description (ṣifa) of «فريقاً», so it is in the position of accusative. The pronoun is plural by regard to the meaning, because it is a collective noun like القَوْم and الرهط. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "Had it been singular according to the wording it would have been permissible." There is some doubt in this, since one cannot say "القوم جاءني".
The majority read «يَلوون» with fatḥa on the yāʾ, sukūn on the lām, then a wāw with ḍamma and then another, sākin; it is the imperfect of لَوَى, meaning فَتَل (to twist). Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ, and Abū Ḥātim from Nāfiʿ read: يُلَوُّون with ḍamma on the yāʾ, fatḥa on the lām, and shadda on the first wāw, from لَوَّى with doubling; the doubling in it is for intensity and exaggeration, not for transitivization, since had it been for that it would have governed a second object, because it was already transitive to one before that. Al-Zamakhsharī attributed it to the people of Medina, and it is as he said, for these were the chiefs of the readers of Medina.
Ḥumayd read: «يَلُون» with fatḥa on the yāʾ, ḍamma on the lām, followed by a single sākin wāw. Al-Zamakhsharī attributed it to Mujāhid and Ibn Kathīr, and he explained it as follows: the original is «يَلْوُون», like the reading of the majority; then the wāw with ḍamma was replaced by a hamza, which is a regular substitution, as in أُجُوه and أُقِّتت; then the hamza was lightened by casting its vowel onto the sākin before it, which is the lām, and the hamza was dropped. So the pattern of يَلُون remained يَفُون, with the lām and the ʿayn dropped. That is because the lām, which is the yāʾ, was dropped because of the meeting of two sākins, since the original is «يَلْوِيُون» like يَضْربون; the ḍamma on the yāʾ was found heavy and was dropped, so two sākins met, the yāʾ and the wāw of the pronoun, and the yāʾ was dropped because of their meeting; then the wāw that is the ʿayn of the word was dropped for the reason I gave you.
And «ألسنتهم» is the plural of لِسان, and this is according to the dialect of those who make it masculine. As for the dialect of those who make it feminine, saying "هذه لسان", it is pluralized as ألسن, like ذِراع and أَذْرُع, and كِراع and أَكْرُع. Al-Farrāʾ said: "We have not heard it from the Arabs except as masculine." The tongue is used to denote speech, because speech arises from it and in it; and what is meant by it here also is that; and masculine and feminine are both allowed.
And اللَّيّ means الفَتْل (twisting). One says: لَوَيْتُ الثوبَ and لَوَيْتُ عنقه, that is, I twisted it; and the maṣdar is الليُّ and الليَّان. The poet said:
1345 - قد كُنْت دايَنْتُ بها حَسَّانا ... مخافةَ الإِفلاسِ واللَّيَّانا
(I had dealt on credit with Ḥassān through it, for fear of bankruptcy and of procrastination.)
The original is لَوْي and لَوْيان, then the weak-letter change was applied, which is clear from what preceded under «ميِّت» and its class. Then اللَّيّ is applied to evasion and prevarication in arguments and disputation, by likening abstract meanings to bodies.
And {بالكتاب} is attached to يَلْوُون, and this attachment is clear. Abū l-Baqāʾ made it a ḥāl from «الألسنة», saying: "Its implied form is: ملتبسةً بالكتاب or ناطقة بالكتاب." The pronoun in {لِتَحْسَبُوهُ} may refer back to what was indicated by the earlier mention of twisting and distortion, that is: so that you may reckon the distorted part to be of the Torah; and it may refer back to an omitted muḍāf indicated by the meaning, the original being: "they twist their tongues with something resembling the Book, so that you reckon what resembles the Book which they distorted to be from the Book". It would be like His saying, the Exalted: {أَوْ كَظُلُمَاتٍ فِي بَحْرٍ} [النور: 4] and then He said «يَغْشاه»; the original is "أو كذي ظلمات", so the pronoun of «يغشاه» refers back to the omitted «ذي». And {مِنَ الْكِتَابِ} is the second object of the reckoning (ḥusbān). «ليحسبوه» was also read, with the third-person yāʾ, and what is meant by them is also the Muslims, just as the addressees were meant in the reading of the majority; and the meaning is: so that the Muslims may reckon that the distorted part is of the Torah.

semin-durr:82-82.t: His saying, the Exalted: {فَمَنْ تولى}: it is permissible that «مَنْ» be conditional, in which case the فاء in «فأولئك» is its apodosis; and that it be relative, the فاء having been entered because of the resemblance of the mubtadaʾ (subject) to a conditional noun. On the first view the verb after it is in the position of jussive, and on the second it has no position, since it is a ṣila (relative clause). As for «فأولئك», it is likewise in the position of jussive on the first view, and of nominative on the second because it occurs as a khabar (predicate). And «هم» may be a separator (faṣl) or may be a mubtadaʾ. These matters are clear from what has preceded, so I have not gone deeply into explaining them.

semin-durr:83-83.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {أَفَغَيْرَ دِينِ الله يَبْغُونَ}: it has already been mentioned that the majority make the hamza precede the فاء because it must come first in the clause, whereas al-Zamakhsharī leaves it in its place and implies an omitted element before it. Here he allowed two views. One: that the فاء is a conjunction joining one clause to another, the meaning being "فأولئك هم الفاسقون فغيرَ دين الله يبغون", and then the hamza was inserted between the two. The second: that it is conjoined to an omitted element, its implied form being "أيتولَّون فغيرَ دين الله يبغون"; and he put the object «غير» before its verb because it is the more important, in that the denunciation which is the meaning of the hamza is directed at what is worshipped falsely. This is al-Zamakhsharī's statement. The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "There is no precision in it, because the denunciation that is the meaning of the hamza is not directed at essences, but is directed at the actions connected with essences; so what is denounced is the seeking whose object is something other than the religion of Allah. The fronting of the object came only as a matter of latitude, and because يبغون resembles a verse-ending (fāṣila) at the end of the verb." I say: and where is the one meaning from the other?
Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read «يَبْغون» with the yāʾ (third person), as a continuation of His saying {هم الفاسقون}; the rest read it with the second-person tāʾ, as a shift of address (iltifāt).
His saying: {وَلَهُ أَسْلَمَ مَن فِي السماوات} is a ḥāl (circumstantial) clause, that is: how can they seek other than His religion, this being the case?
His saying: {طَوْعاً وَكَرْهاً}: there are two views about them. One: that they are two maṣdars in the position of ḥāl, the implied sense being "طائعين وكارهين" (willingly and unwillingly). The second: that they are two maṣdars not of the same root as the verb. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "because أسلم means انقاد and أطاع (submitted and obeyed)", and the Shaykh followed him in this. There is some doubt in it, in that this holds for «طوعاً» because it agrees with the meaning of the preceding verb, but as for «كَرْهاً», how can this be said of it? And the saying that what is tolerated in the seconds is not tolerated in the firsts does not help here. One says: طاع يَطُوع and أطاع يُطيع, with the same meaning. It was also said: طاعةً: طاعه يَطُوعه means "he submitted to him", أطاعه means "he was pleased with his command", and طاوعه means "he agreed with him".
Al-Aʿmash read «كُرْهاً» with ḍamma; it will come that this is a reading of the Two Brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) in sūrat al-Nisāʾ, and of the Kufans and Ibn Dhakwān in al-Aḥqāf, and we discussed it there. The occurrence of this root in al-Baqara has also preceded.
His saying: {وَإِلَيْهِ يُرْجَعُونَ}: it is permissible that this clause be resumptive, so that it has no position; it was brought only to inform of that, because it contains the sense of great threat and severe warning. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to the clause {وَلَهُ أَسْلَمَ}, so that it is a ḥāl too, and the meaning would be that He rebuked them for seeking other than the religion of Him to whom everyone in the heavens and the earth has submitted, willingly and unwillingly, and to whom their return is.
Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read «يُرْجَعُون» with the third-person yāʾ, which admits several views. First: that the pronoun refers back to «مَنْ أسلم» (those who submitted), which is clear. Second: that it refers back to whom the pronoun of «يَبْغَون» refers in the reading of those who read it in the third person, which is also clear; and there is no iltifāt in these two views. Third: that it refers back to whom the pronoun in «تَبْغَون» refers in the second-person reading, in which case it is an iltifāt. The rest read «تَبْغُون» with the second person; for one who reads «تبغون» with the second person it is clear, and for one who reads it in the third person this is an iltifāt on his part, and it is permissible that it be an iltifāt from His saying: {مَنْ فِي السماوات والأرض}.

semin-durr:84-84.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {قُلْ آمَنَّا بالله}: in this verse there are two possibilities. One: that the one commanded with this utterance, namely «آمنَّا» to the end, is Muḥammad ﷺ; and in that there are two senses. One: that he and his community are commanded with it, and its conjoined element was omitted because the meaning is understood, the implied form being: "Say, O Muḥammad, you and your community: آمنَّا بالله"; this is Ibn ʿAṭiyya's implication. The second sense: that the one commanded with it here is our Prophet ﷺ alone, and he was addressed in the plural wording to honour him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is also possible that he is commanded to speak of himself as kings speak, as an exaltation by Allah of the rank of His Prophet." I say: and this is a fine meaning. The second possibility: that the one commanded with this utterance is those mentioned before, the implied form being: "Say to them: Say آمنَّا"; so «آمنَّا» is accusative as the object of «قُل» on the first possibility, and of the implied «قولوا» on the second, and that implied utterance is accusative in position.
This verse resembles the one in al-Baqara, except that here أنزل is made transitive with «على», and there with «إلى». Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Because both meanings are present, for revelation descends from above and reaches the messengers; so at one time one of the two meanings is brought, and at another the other." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Revelation upon the Prophet of the community is revelation upon it." But there is no benefit in this with respect to seeking the difference. Al-Rāghib said: "He said «على» here only because this was an address to the Prophet ﷺ and it reached him from the Highest Assembly without any human intermediary, so the word «على», which is specific to height, is more fitting for him; whereas there, since it was an address to the community and it reached them through the Prophet ﷺ, the word «إلى», which is specific to conveying, is more fitting. It may also be said: «أنزل عليه» is applied to what the one sent down upon is commanded to convey to others, and «أنزل إليه» to what is specific to him in himself and to which the sending down ends. On that basis He said: {أَوَلَمْ يَكْفِهِمْ أَنَّآ أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الكتاب يتلى عَلَيْهِمْ} [العنكبوت: 51] and said: {وَأَنْزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الذكر لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ} [النحل: 44]; here it is specified with «إلى» since it was specific to the Reminder [which] is the explanation of what was sent down. And this is a statement about what is preferable, not about what is obligatory."
What al-Rāghib mentioned was rejected by al-Zamakhsharī, who said: "And whoever said: «علينا» was said only because of «قل», and «إلينا» because of «قولوا», as a distinction between the Messenger and the believers, because revelation comes to the Messenger by way of seeking knowledge, and comes to them by way of arrival, has been far-fetched. [Do you not see] His saying {بِمَآ أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ} [البقرة: 4], {وَأَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ الكتاب} [المائدة: 48], and His saying: {آمِنُواْ بالذي أُنْزِلَ عَلَى الذين آمَنُواْ} [آل عمران: 72]."
And in al-Baqara: {وَمَا أُوتِيَ النبيون} [الآية: 136], while here «والنبيون», because the wording of the address there is general, and it is a rule of general address to be expansive rather than concise, unlike the address here, which is specific; so it was content here with conciseness rather than prolixity. The remaining words of the verse's clauses have already been discussed in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:124-124.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِذْ تَقُولُ}: There are three views on it. The first: that this adverb is a badal (substitute) for his saying «إذ هَمَّتْ». The second: that it is accusative by «نصركم». The third: that it is accusative by an implied "remember" (اذكر). And is this sentence part of the completion of the story of Badr, which is the view of the majority, so that there is no parenthetical interruption in this discourse; or part of the completion of Uḥud, so that his saying {وَلَقَدْ نَصَرَكُمُ الله} would be a parenthetical clause between the two discourses? It is a well-known disagreement.

His saying: {أَن يُمِدَّكُمْ}: the fāʿil (agent) of «ألن يكفيكم», i.e. "will the supplying of reinforcements by your Lord not suffice you?" When the hamza entered upon the negation, it made it affirmative in the manner of rebuke (inkār). «لن» was used rather than «لا» because it is stronger in negation. In the codex of Ubayy it is «ألا», with «لا» rather than «لن», as if he intended to explain the meaning.

And «بثلاثة» is attached to «يُمِدَّكم». Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read «ثلاثَهْ آلاف» with a quiescent hāʾ in continuous speech (waṣl), and likewise «بخمسهْ آلاف», as if he made waṣl follow the course of pause (waqf). It is weak, because it occurs in two terms of a genitive construct that require connection. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The aspect of this reading is weak, because the muḍāf and the muḍāf ilayhi are like one thing and require connection, the second being the completion of the first, whereas the hāʾ is only a sign of pause, so a pause is awkward in a place that is meant for connection. But something like this has occurred in places in the speech of the Arabs. Among that is what al-Farrāʾ related of their saying "akaltu laḥman shāh" (I ate the meat of a sheep), meaning "laḥma shāh": they stretched the fatḥa until an alif arose from it, as they say in pause "qālā", meaning "qāla". Then they stretch the fatḥa in rhyme-words and similar places of deliberation and steadiness. And among that in poetry is his saying:

1422 - يَنْباع من ذِفْرى غضوبٍ جَسْرَةٍ ... زَيَّافَةٍ مثلِ الفنيق المُكْدَمِ
(It gushes from behind the ear of an ill-tempered, bold she-camel, swaggering in her gait, like the bitten stud-camel.)

He means "yanbaʿu", and stretched it. And similar is the saying of another:

1423 - أقول إذ خَرَّتْ على الكَلْكال ... يا ناقتي ما جُلْت مِنْ مَجَال
(I say, when she fell upon her chest: O my she-camel, you did not roam from any field.)

He means "al-kalkal(i)", and stretched it. And similar is the saying of another:

1424 - فأنتَ من الغوائلِ حين تُرْمَى ... ومن ذمِّ الرجال بمُنْتزاحِ
(You, when shot at, are far from calamities and from the blame of men.)

He means "bi-muntazaḥ". Abū al-Fatḥ said: "If it is permissible for this prolongation to intervene within a single word, then prolongation is permissible between the muḍāf and the muḍāf ilayhi, since they are two." The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said after Ibn ʿAṭiyya's words: "It is piling up and drawing parallels with what is not appropriate. What is appropriate for the justification of this irregular reading is that it is from making waṣl follow the course of waqf: he substituted [hāʾ] for it in waṣl as they substitute it in waqf, and it is found in their speech to make waṣl follow waqf and waqf follow waṣl. As for his saying 'but something like this has occurred in places in the speech of the Arabs', everything he mentioned is only from the category of the prolongation (ishbāʿ) of the vowel, and prolongation of the vowel is not like substituting hāʾ for tāʾ in waṣl. The parallel of this is only their saying "thalathah arbaʿa": he substituted hāʾ for the tāʾ, transferred the vowel of the hamza of "arbaʿa" to it, and dropped the hamza. So he made waṣl follow waqf in the substitution, and made waqf follow waṣl [in the transfer], since the transfer occurs only in waṣl."

It was also read irregularly «بثلاثةْ» with a quiescent tāʾ, which is likewise from making waṣl follow waqf as regards the quiescence. There is disagreement about this tāʾ upon which one now pauses: is it the tāʾ of the feminine which was there and has merely become quiescent, or is it a substitute for the feminine hāʾ which itself was substituted for the tāʾ? This is a disagreement with nothing of benefit beneath it.

And his saying {مِّنَ الملائكة}: it is possible that «مِنْ» is explanatory (lil-bayān), and possible that «من» and its genitive noun are in the position of the genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of «ثلاثة» or of «آلاف».

His saying: {مُنزَلِينَ}: an adjective of «ثلاثة آلاف», and it may be a ḥāl from «الملائكة», but the first is more evident. Ibn ʿĀmir read «مُنَزَّلين» with doubling (tashdīd), and likewise he doubled his saying in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt, {إِنَّا مُنزِلُونَ على أَهْلِ هذه القرية} [verse 34], except that here it is a passive participle and there an active participle. The others lightened both. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read here «مُنَزِّلين» with doubling and kasra on the زاي, as an active voice. And some read it likewise but lightened the زاي, making it from anzala like akrama. The doubling and the hamza both serve for transitivity, so faʿʿala and afʿala are of the same meaning; and it has already been mentioned that al-Zamakhsharī makes the doubling indicate gradual (successive) sending down (tanjīm), and the discussion with him on that has gone before. In the last two readings the object is omitted, i.e. "sending down victory upon the believers and punishment upon the disbelievers".

His saying: «بلى»: a particle of response (ḥarf jawāb), and it is an affirmation of the negation in his saying, the Exalted, {أَلَنْ يَكْفِيكُمْ}; its discussion has already been given at length. And the jawāb al-sharṭ (apodosis) is his saying «يُمْدِدْكُم».

And al-fawr is haste and speed; from it: "fārat al-qidr" (the pot boiled over), when its boiling intensified and what was in it hurried to come out. One says: fāra yafūru fawran. It is used to express anger and fierceness, because the angry man hurries to strike at the one with whom he is angry. So al-fawr is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun), and then it is used to express the state in which there is no delay and no turning aside to anything else.

semin-durr:126-126.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِلاَّ بشرى}: There are three views on it. The first: that it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), and this is a complete exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh), since the estimate is: "and He did not make it for anything of things except for the glad tidings". The conditions for its being accusative are present, namely unity of agent and of time, and its being a maṣdar brought for the cause. The second: that it is a second object of «جَعَل», taking it as a verb of transformation (taṣyīriyya). The third: that it is a badal from the هاء in «جَعَله»; this was said by al-Ḥawfī, who made the هاء refer back to the promise of reinforcement. And al-bushrā is a maṣdar of the pattern fuʿlā, like al-ruj ʿā.

His saying: {وَلِتَطْمَئِنَّ}: There are two views on it. One: that it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to «بشرى». This is if we make it a mafʿūl li-ajlihi. It is genitive with the lām only because one of the conditions of the accusative is deficient, namely the unity of agent: the agent of the making is Allah the Exalted, while the agent of the reassurance is the hearts. Therefore what is conjoined to is accusative, its conditions being complete, and the conjoined is genitive with the lām, its condition being deficient, as has gone before. The estimate: "and He did not make it except for the glad tidings and for the reassurance". The second: that it is attached to an omitted element, i.e. "and that your hearts may be reassured He did that", or "it was such and such".

The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "«وتطمئنَّ» is accusative by an implied «أنْ» after the lām of purpose (lām kay), so it is a conjunction of a noun upon the supposed position of another noun." Then he reported from Ibn ʿAṭiyya that he said: "The lām in «ولتطمئن» is attached to an implied verb indicated by «جعله», and the meaning of the verse is: 'This reinforcement was only so that you might rejoice at it and your hearts be reassured by it.'" The Shaykh said: "It is as if he saw that it is not possible, in his view, for «ولتطمئن» to be conjoined to «بشرى» by position, because it is a condition of conjunction by position, according to our colleagues, that there be a preserver of the position (muḥriz), and there is no preserver here, because the genitive-governing agent is missing. Whoever does not make the muḥriz a condition permits that, and it would be of the category of conjunction by supposition (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-tawahhum)." I say: Some have made the واو in «ولتطمئن» redundant (zāʾida), which suits the school of al-Akhfash; on this the lām is attached to «البشرى», i.e. the glad tidings are the reason for the making, and the reassurance is the reason for the glad tidings, so it is the reason of the reason.

Al-Fakhr al-Rāzī said: "In the mention of the reinforcement there are two aims. One: the entry of joy into their hearts, which is what is meant by {إِلاَّ بشرى}; and the second: the attainment of reassurance through victory so that they do not become cowardly, and this is the original purpose. So he distinguished between these two expressions as a warning of the difference between the two matters, conjoining the verb to the noun, and since the stronger is the attainment of reassurance, he introduced the particle of causation." The Shaykh said: "His words 'conjoining the verb to the noun' are open to dispute, since it is not a conjunction of a verb to a noun, and also his words 'he introduced the particle of causation', for it is not as he said." End of quotation. I say: If the Shaykh means that he did not introduce the particle of causation at all, that is not accepted and cannot be denied; but if he means that he did not introduce it in the sense the Imām intended, then it is easy.

Al-Jurjānī said in his Naẓm: "This is on the interpretation: 'and Allah did not make it except to give you glad tidings and that your hearts be reassured'. And whoever permits the insertion of the واو, which is the school of the Kufans, makes it inserted in «ولتطمئنَّ», so the estimate is: 'and Allah did not make it except glad tidings for you so that your hearts be reassured by it.'"

And the two pronouns in his saying «وما» «جعله» and «به» refer back to the reinforcement understood from the preceding verb, which is his saying «يُمْدِدْكم». It is also said that they refer to the victory; and it is said, to the marking (al-taswīm); and it is said, to the sending down; and it is said, to the number; and it is said, to the promise.

In this verse He said «لكم» and omitted it in Sūrat al-Anfāl, because that one is an abridgement of this one, and it seems that elaboration is more fitting here, because the story is complete here, so it suited the putting of them at ease by direct address. And he placed «به» later here and earlier in Sūrat al-Anfāl, because the address is present here in «لكم», so he made address follow address. And here he brought the two attributes as followers in his saying {العزيز الحكيم}, while he brought them in a resumptive sentence in al-Anfāl in his saying {إِنَّ الله عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ} [verse 10], because when he addressed them here, it was fitting to hasten their glad tidings that He is Mighty and Wise, i.e. that He is not overcome and that all His deeds are perfectly made, wisdom and rightness.

semin-durr:155-155.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {الجمعان}: It was put in the dual even though it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ), and the grammarians have stated explicitly that such a noun is neither dualised nor pluralised except anomalously; (it is dualised here) because the kind (of group) is meant, for the meaning is: the group of the believers and the group of the polytheists. Since that was meant, it was dualised, as in his saying:
1476 - وكلُّ رفيقَيْ كلِّ رحلٍ وإنْ هما ... تعاطَى القَنا قوماً هما أخَوان
(Every two companions of every journey, even if the two of them trade spears against a people, are two brothers.)
The sīn in «استَنْزَلَهم» is for seeking (ṭalab); but the apparent sense is that istafʿala here has the meaning of afʿala, because the story points to it. So the meaning is: he led them to the slip, and it is like istaballa and aballa.

semin-durr:157-157.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَلَئِنْ قُتِلْتُمْ}: The lām is the preparatory lām (al-muwaṭṭiʾa) for an omitted oath, and its response is his saying: {لَمَغْفِرَةٌ}. The apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted because the response of the oath takes its place, as it indicates it. This is what al-Zamakhsharī meant by his saying: «and it fills the place of the apodosis»; he does not mean by that that it is without omission. And the lām is the lām of inception (lām al-ibtidāʾ); it and what follows it are the response of the oath, as has preceded.
As for «مغفرةٌ», there are two views about it. The more evident of them: that it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and the justifiers (for the indefinite being a subject) here are many: the lām of inception; the conjunction upon it in his saying {وَرَحْمَةٌ}; and its being qualified, for his saying {مِّنَ الله} is an adjective of it, attached then to an omitted word; and {خَيْرٌ} is the khabar (predicate) about it. The second: that it is nominative as the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, if by forgiveness and mercy is meant being killed or dying in the way of Allah, because the two are joined to death in the way of Allah. The implied form would then be: "that — that is, dying or being killed in the way of Allah — is forgiveness and mercy; better…", and «خير» would be an adjective, not a khabar. Ibn ʿAṭiyya inclined to this, for he said: «The verse may be understood so that his saying {لَمَغْفِرَةٌ} is a reference to death or being killed in the way of Allah, so he called that forgiveness and mercy since they are joined to it; the implied form comes out as: "that is forgiveness and mercy", and forgiveness is nominative as the khabar of the implied mubtadaʾ, and his saying "خير" is an adjective, not the khabar of a mubtadaʾ.» End of quotation. But the first view is more evident, and «خير» here is in its usual sense of being a comparative (tafḍīl). And from Ibn ʿAbbās: «Better than the earth's fill of red gold.»
And his saying: {وَرَحْمَةٌ}, that is: and a mercy from Allah; its adjective was omitted because the first indicates it. Another omission is necessary to make the meaning sound, its implied form being: "a forgiveness from Allah for you and a mercy from Him for you". He brought forgiveness and mercy as indefinite nouns to announce that the least good and the smallest thing is better than the world and what is in it, which they gather; this is parallel to {وَرِضْوَانٌ مِّنَ الله أَكْبَرُ} [التوبة: 72]. Indefiniteness may indicate fewness. And «ما» in his saying {مِّمَّا يَجْمَعُونَ} is a relative noun with the returning pronoun omitted; it is also permissible that it be a maṣdar (verbal noun) particle, and on that basis the object is omitted, that is: "than your gathering wealth and the like".

semin-durr:160-160.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِن يَنصُرْكُمُ الله فَلاَ غَالِبَ}: A condition (protasis) and its apodosis. His saying {وَإِن يَخْذُلْكُمْ} is the same. This is an iltifāt (shift of person) from the third person to the second; so said the Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān), meaning from the third person in his saying {لِنتَ لَهُمْ}, {لاَنْفَضُّواْ}, and {فاعف عَنْهُمْ واستغفر لَهُمْ وَشَاوِرْهُمْ}. There is room for objection in that. His saying {فَلاَ غَالِبَ} came as the apodosis of the condition, and it is an explicit negation, whereas his saying {فَمَن ذَا الذي}, which implies negation, came as the apodosis of the second condition, out of gentleness toward the believers, in that He stated plainly to them in the first that there is no overcomer, but did not state plainly to them in the second that there is no helper for them; rather He brought it in the form of a question, although its meaning is negation.
And his saying: {فَمَن ذَا الذي}: the like of it has already preceded in al-Baqara, together with people's views on it. As for the hāʾ in «مِنْ بعدِه», there are two views about it. The first, which is the more evident, is that it refers back to Allah the Exalted, and there are two possibilities in that. One: that this is on the omission of a muḍāf (head of a genitive construct), that is: "after His forsaking". The second: that there is no need for that, and the meaning of the speech would be: "If you allow it (reliance) to pass to other than Him, when He has forsaken you, then to whom will you pass, and who will help you?" The second view: that it refers back to the forsaking understood from the verb, which is parallel to {اعدلوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ} [المائدة: 8].
And his saying: {وَعَلَى الله فَلْيَتَوَكَّلِ المؤمنون}: He put the prepositional phrase first only to announce exclusivity, that is: let the believers single out their Lord for reliance upon Him and for entrusting (their affairs), because they know that they have no helper besides Him. This is a fine meaning, mentioned by al-Zamakhsharī. The majority read «ويَخْذُلْكم» with fatḥa on the yāʾ, from «خَذَله» (triliteral), and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read «يُخْذِلْكم» with ḍamma on it, from akhdhala (quadriliteral); the hamza in it is for making a thing so (jaʿl), that is: "He makes you forsaken".

semin-durr:85-85.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ}: the majority read with the two identical letters kept distinct (iẓhār), because there is a separator between them, so they do not really meet; that separator is the yāʾ which was dropped because of the jussive. Two views are reported from Abū ʿAmr on it: keeping them distinct, on the original form and in regard to the original separator; and assimilation (idghām), in regard to the wording, since it is true that they meet in the utterance, and because that separator deserves to be dropped by the jussive-governing agent. This is not specific to this verse; rather, whenever two identical letters meet because a letter was dropped for a reason that required it, both views apply, for example: {يَخْلُ لَكُمْ وَجْهُ أَبِيكُمْ} [يوسف: 9], {وَإِن يَكُ كَاذِباً} [غافر: 28]. A difficulty has been raised against this by cases like {ياقوم مَا لي أَدْعُوكُمْ} [غافر: 41] and {ياقوم مَن يَنصُرُنِي} [هود: 30], for no disagreement is reported from Abū ʿAmr about assimilating these two, whereas analogy would require both views to be permissible, since the first-person yāʾ is a separator by implication.
His saying: {دِيناً}: there are three views on it. One: that it is the object of يَبْتَغِ, and {غَيْرَ الإسلام} is a ḥāl (circumstantial), because originally it is a description of it; so when it was put before it, it was made accusative as a ḥāl.
Second: that it is a tamyīz (specification) of «غير» because of its vagueness, so it was specified just as «مثل», «شبه» and their sisters are specified; and it was heard from the Arabs: "إنَّ لنا غيرَها إبلاً وشاء" (We have other than it, camels and sheep). Third: that it is a badal (substitute) for «غير»; and on these two views, «غيرَ الإسلام» is the direct object of يبتغِ.
His saying: {وَهُوَ فِي الآخرة مِنَ الخاسرين} is like His saying: {وَإِنَّهُ فِي الآخرة لَمِنَ الصالحين} [البقرة: 130] in its i'rab, and what differs between the two in meaning will come. It was said: «أل» is the definite article and not a relative, so it does not prevent what precedes it from being attached to what follows it. This clause may have no position because it is resumptive, and it may be in the position of jussive, conjoined to the apodosis of the condition, which is «فلن يُقْبل», so that non-acceptance and loss follow upon seeking a religion other than Islam.

semin-durr:87-87.t: His saying, the Exalted: {جَزَآؤُهُمْ}: two views are permissible. One: that it is a second mubtadaʾ (subject), and «أنَّ عليهم» to the end is in the position of nominative as the khabar (predicate) of «جزاؤهم», and the clause is the khabar of «أولئك». The second: that «جزاؤهم» is a badal (substitute) of «أولئك», a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), and «أن عليهم» to the end is the khabar of «أولئك». He said here {جَزَآؤُهُمْ أَنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةَ الله}, whereas there it is {أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ} [البقرة: 161] without «جزاؤهم». It was said: because there the report concerned someone who died in disbelief, so Allah decreed the curse upon him; unlike here, for the occasion of revelation is about a people who apostatized and then returned to Islam. The meaning of «جزاؤهم» is: the recompense of their disbelief and apostasy. The reading of al-Ḥasan {والناس أجمعون} [البقرة: 161] and its explanation have preceded.

semin-durr:88-88.t: His saying, the Exalted: {خَالِدِينَ}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun in «عليهم»; the operator in it is "settledness" (istiqrār), or the preposition-and-noun phrase, because it takes the place of the verb; its like has preceded. The pronoun in «فيها» refers to the curse. And {لاَ يُخَفَّفُ} is a ḥāl clause or a resumptive one.

semin-durr:89-89.t: His saying, the Exalted: {إِلاَّ الذين}: a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

semin-durr:92-92.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {لَن تَنَالُواْ}: النَّيْل means attaining a thing and reaching it; it was said that it is a gift; and it was said that it is taking hold of a thing with the hand. One says: نِلْتُه أناله نَيْلاً. The Exalted said: {وَلاَ يَنَالُونَ مِنْ عَدُوٍّ نَّيْلاً} [التوبة: 120]. As for النَّوْل with wāw, its meaning is taking hold; one says: نِلته أنوله, that is, I took hold of it; and أنلته زيداً أنوله إياه, that is, I handed it to him, like your saying: عَطَوْتُه أعطوه meaning I took hold of it, and أعطيته إياه when you handed it to him.
And His saying: {حتى تُنْفِقُواْ} has the meaning of «إلى أن» (until), and «مِنْ» in {مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ} is partitive (tabʿīḍ), which is indicated by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: «بعضَ ما تحبون». In my view this is not a reading but an explanation of the meaning. «ما» is a relative, its returning pronoun being omitted; and the claim that it is an indefinite described noun has no sense, though Abū l-Baqāʾ allowed it, saying: [ "or an indefinite described noun; and it cannot be a maṣdar (verbal noun) because love is not spent; but if love is made to have the meaning of the object, it is permissible according to the opinion of ʿAlī" ] — meaning the implied form remains: "from the thing loved". These two views are weak, and the first is the weaker.
And His saying: {وَمَا تُنْفِقُواْ مِن شَيْءٍ}: its like has preceded in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:94-94.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {مِن بَعْدِ}: two views on it. One: that it is attached to افترى, and this is the apparent one. The second, which Abū l-Baqāʾ allowed: that it is attached to «الكذب», meaning the lie occurring after that. As for what is pointed to by «ذلك», there are three views. One: the settledness of the prohibition mentioned in the Torah, since the meaning is: except what Isrāʾīl (Jacob) forbade himself, and then the Torah forbade it to them as a punishment for them. Second: the recitation (tilāwa), and the masculine demonstrative is permissible because what is meant by it is the explanation of their position. Third: the situation after Isrāʾīl's forbidding it to himself.
And this clause, I mean His saying {فَمَنِ افترى}, may be resumptive and so have no grammatical position; and it may be accusative in position, conjoined to His saying «فَأْتوا بالتوراة», so that it falls within what is to be said. And «مَنْ» may be conditional or relative. He followed its wording in His saying {افترى}, hence the pronoun is singular, and its meaning in His saying {فأولئك} to the end, hence it is plural.

semin-durr:95-95.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {قُلْ صَدَقَ الله}: that is, "say to them". The majority read with the lām of «قُل» kept distinct before the ṣād; Abān ibn Taghlib read it assimilated into it, and likewise he assimilated the lām into the sīn in His saying: {قُلْ سِيرُواْ} [الأنعام: 11]. It will come that Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Hishām assimilated the lām into the sīn in His saying, the Exalted: {بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ} [يوسف: 18].
Abū l-Fatḥ said: "The reason for that is the spreading of these two letters in the mouth and the diffusion of the sound that issues from them, so they came near the point of articulation of the lām, and assimilating it into them became permissible. This is taken from the words of Sībawayh, for Sībawayh said: 'Assimilation' — meaning assimilation of the lām with the ṭāʾ, the ṣād and their sisters — 'is permissible, though it is not as frequent as with the rāʾ, because these letters are set back from it, and they are from the front teeth.'" He said: "And the assimilation is permissible because the end of the lām's point of articulation is close to their point of articulation." End of quotation. Abū l-Baqāʾ said an expression that clarifies what preceded, namely: "because the ṣād has a spreading and the lām has a spreading, such that their edges meet, so they became close to one another." The i'rab of His saying {مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفاً} [البقرة: 135] has already been given, which makes repeating it unnecessary.

semin-durr:20-20.t:
Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ read the yāʾ of {وجهي} with fatḥa, here and in al-Anʿām; the rest read it with sukūn.

His saying: {وَمَنِ اتبعن}: there are several views on the position of {مَنْ}. The first: nominative, conjoined to the tāʾ in {أَسْلَمْتُ}, and this is permissible because of the separation by the object. Al-Zamakhsharī said this and began with it, and so did Ibn ʿAṭiyya. The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "It cannot be taken at its apparent sense, because if it is conjoined to the pronoun, as in 'I ate a loaf and Zayd', it necessarily follows that the two are partners in eating the loaf; and here that is not acceptable, because the meaning is not 'they submitted, and he ﷺ submitted, his face to Allah'; rather the meaning is that he ﷺ submitted his face to Allah, and they submitted their faces to Allah. So what is stronger in the i'rab is that it is conjoined to the pronoun with the object omitted from it, not as a partner in the object of {أَسْلَمْتُ}, the implied form being: 'and whoever follows me, his face'; or that it is a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted because the meaning indicates it, the implied form being: 'and whoever follows me likewise', that is: they submitted their faces to Allah, as you say: 'Zayd fulfilled his vow, and ʿAmr', meaning: and ʿAmr likewise, that is, fulfilled his vow."

I (al-Samīn) say: Partnership is sound in 'I ate a loaf and Zayd' only because it is possible there; but in the like of the noble verse, no one imagines partnership.

The second: it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ with an omitted khabar, as its explanation has preceded. The third: it is accusative as mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment), the wāw meaning "with", that is: "I have submitted my face to Allah along with whoever follows me." Al-Zamakhsharī said this also. The Shaykh said: "From the same side from which conjoining {مَنْ} to the pronoun was ruled out, when the speech is taken at its apparent sense without interpretation, it is ruled out that {مَنْ} be accusative as mafʿūl maʿahu, because when you say 'I ate a loaf and ʿAmr', meaning 'with ʿAmr', that indicates that he shares with you in eating the loaf. Al-Zamakhsharī allowed this view, but it is not permissible, for what we have mentioned, in any case; because the omission of the object is absolutely not allowed when the wāw is the wāw of 'with'." I say: Understanding the meaning and the absence of confusion justify what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. What prevents the meaning from being: "Say: I have submitted my face to Allah, accompanying whoever has also submitted his face to Allah"? This is a sound meaning, with the view of accompaniment.

The fourth: the position of {مَنْ} is genitive, as a coordinate (nasaq) on the name of Allah, blessed and exalted. This i'rab, although its apparent sense is problematic, may be interpreted as meaning: "I made my aim Allah, through faith in Him and obedience to Him, and whoever follows me, through guarding him, and honouring him with his knowledge, his opinion and his companionship."

Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr kept the yāʾ in {اتَّبعني} in continuous reading (waṣl) and dropped it in pause; the rest dropped it in both, in agreement with the written copy. What also made this good is that it is a verse-final (fāṣila) at the head of a verse, like «أَكْرَمَن وأهانَن». On this is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

1208 - وهل يَمْنَعُني ارتيادِي البلا ... دَ مِنْ حَذَرِ الموتِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَنْ
(Does my roaming the lands out of fear of death prevent it from coming?)

Al-Aʿshā also said:

1209 - ومِنْ شانِىءٍ كاسِفٍ وجُهه ... إذا ما انْتَسَبْتُ له أَنْكَرَنْ
(And from a hater, grim of face, who, whenever I trace my lineage to him, disowns me.)

Some of them said: "The dropping of this yāʾ is frequent specifically with the nūn of protection (nūn al-wiqāya); if there is no nūn, then retaining it is the frequent usage."

His saying: {أَأَسْلَمْتُمْ}: its form is a question and its meaning is a command, that is: "submit," like His saying, Exalted is He: {فَهَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُّنتَهُونَ}, that is: "desist." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "He means that there has come to you of the clear proofs what makes submission obligatory and requires its occurrence without fail; so have you submitted yet, or are you still in your disbelief? This is like your saying to one for whom you have summarized the issue and left no avenue of explanation and disclosure untaken: 'Have you understood it or not, may you have no mother?' Among it is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {فَهَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُّنتَهُونَ} [al-Māʾida: 91], after He had mentioned the deterrents from wine and gambling. In this question is exhaustive pursuit and a reproach for obstinacy and lack of fairness, since the fair-minded person, when the proof is made clear to him, does not delay his submission to the truth." This is very fine speech. And His saying: {فَقَدِ اهتدوا}: "qad" entered upon the past verb as an exaggeration of the certainty of the occurrence of the action, as if it had drawn near to occurring.

semin-durr:14-14.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {زُيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ}: the majority read it as passive, and the omitted agent is Allah the Exalted, because of what He set in human natures of love for these things. It was also said that it is Satan. From al-Ḥasan: "Who adorned them? Satan only adorned them, for no one hates them more than their Creator."

Mujāhid read: "zayyana" as active, with {حُبَّ} as an explicit direct object, and the agent is either the pronoun for Allah the Exalted, because His noble mention preceded in His saying, Exalted is He: {والله يُؤَيِّدُ بِنَصْرِهِ} [Āl ʿImrān: 13], or the pronoun for Satan, implied although no mention of him has preceded, because he is the origin of that, so mention of these things announces mention of him. And he annexed the maṣdar (verbal noun) to its object in {حُبّ الشهوات}.

{الشهوات} is the plural of شَهْوة, with sukūn on the ʿayn, which is vowelled in the plural; sukūn is not permitted except by poetic necessity, as in his saying:

1194 - وَحُمِّلْتُ زَفْرَاتِ الضحى فَأَطَقْتُها ... ومالي بزَفْرَات العَشِيِّ يَدَانِ
(I was burdened with the sighs of the forenoon and bore them, but I have no strength for the sighs of the evening.)

with sukūn on the fāʾ. The shahwa is a maṣdar meant as a passive participle, that is, "the things desired" (mushtahayāt), so it is of the type "a just man" (rajulun ʿadl), in which the maṣdar itself is made the thing, as an exaggeration. The shahwa is the inclination of the soul. It is pluralized as shahawāt, as in the noble verse, and as shuhā, like ghuraf. A woman of Banū Naḍr ibn Muʿāwiya said:

1195 - فلولا الشُّهَى واللهِ كنتُ جديرةً ... بأَنْ أتركَ اللَّذاتِ في كلِّ مَشْهَدِ
(Were it not for desires, by Allah, I would be fit to leave pleasures in every gathering.)

The grammarians said: a fʿla form with a defective lām (that is, with fatḥa on the fāʾ and sukūn on the ʿayn) is not pluralized on fuʿal except in three words: kawwa and kuwā, for one who vowels the kāf of kawwa with fatḥa; qarya and qurā; and nazwa and nuzā. The Shaykh added this word to them also, making them four, and he recited the verse. Al-Rāghib said: "The thing desired is sometimes called shahwa, and the faculty by which one desires a thing is sometimes called shahwa; and His saying, Exalted is He: {زُيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ حُبُّ الشهوات} can bear both senses."

His saying: {مِنَ النساء}: in the position of accusative as ḥāl (circumstantial) from {الشهوات}, the implied form being: "the desires being from such and such," so it explains them in meaning. It is also possible that {مِنْ} is for the explanation of the genus, and the saying of al-Zamakhsharī indicates it: "then He explains it with these genera."

His saying: {والقناطير}: the plural of qinṭār. There are two views on its nūn. The first, the view of a group, is that it is original and its pattern is fiʿlāl, like ḥimlāq and qirṭās. The second is that it is additional and its pattern is finʿāl, like qinʿās, which is the strong camel. It was said that its derivation is from qaṭara yaqṭuru, when it flows, because gold and silver are likened to water in the speed of their turning and the frequency of their changing. Al-Zajjāj said: "It is taken from qanṭartu al-shayʾ when you bind it and make it firm, and from it comes the qanṭara (arch) because of the firmness of its binding."

His saying: {مِنَ الذهب} is like His saying "from the women", which has preceded. Dhahab is feminine, and therefore its diminutive is dhuhayba, and its plural is dhahāb and dhuhūb. It was said: "al-dhahab" is in meaning a plural of dhahaba, and its derivation is from dhahāb (going). Al-fiḍḍa is pluralized as fiḍaḍ, and its derivation is from infaḍḍa al-shayʾ, when it scatters. One says "a dhahib man", with kasra on the hāʾ, meaning he saw a vein of gold and was dazed.

His saying: {والخيل}: conjoined to «النساء». Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "not to gold and silver, because they are not called a qinṭār"; imagining the like of that is very remote, so there is no need to point it out.

Concerning {الخيل} there are two views. The first is that it is a plural with no singular from its own wording, its singular rather being "faras" (horse), so it is like "qawm" (people), "rahṭ" (band) and "nisāʾ" (women). The second: that its singular is "khāyil", so it is like rākib and rakb, tājir and tajr, ṭāʾir and ṭayr. On this there is disagreement between Sībawayh and al-Akhfash: Sībawayh makes it a collective noun (ism jamʿ), and al-Akhfash makes it a broken plural. There are two views on its derivation. The first: from ikhtiyāl (haughtiness), which is conceit; it was so named for its haughty gait and the length of its tails. Imruʾ al-Qays said:

1196 - لها ذَنَبٌ مثلُ ذَيْلِ العرو ... سِ تَسُدَّ به فرجَها مِنْ دُبُرْ
(She has a tail like the train of a bride, with which she covers her rear opening.)

The second: from takhayyul (imagining); it was said: because it imagines itself in the form of one greater than it. It was also said: the origin of ikhtiyāl is from takhayyul, which is likening oneself to something, because the haughty person imagines himself in the form of one greater than he in pride. And al-akhyal is the shrike, because its colour changes according to the situation, at one time red, at another green, at another yellow, and on this is the saying:

1197 - كأبي براقِشَ كلَّ لَوْ ... نٍ لونُهُ يَتَخَيَّلُ
(Like Abū Barāqish: every colour his colour takes on.)

Some allowed that it is a lightened form of khayyil with shadda on the yāʾ, like "mayt" for mayyit and "hayn" for hayyin. There is room for consideration in this, because everything in which the lightened form is heard, the heavy form is heard too, whereas this was heard only lightened; and a parallel of this discussion has preceded at the word «الغيب».

Al-Rāghib said: "Al-khayl originally refers to horses and horsemen together. Allah the Exalted said: {وَمِن رِّبَاطِ الخيل} [al-Anfāl: 60]. It is used for each of the two separately, as narrated: 'O horses of Allah, mount!', which is for the horsemen; and his saying, peace be upon him: 'I have pardoned you the zakāt on horses', meaning the mares." There is room for consideration in this, because the people of the language stated explicitly that his saying, peace be upon him: "O horses of Allah, mount!" is either a figurative usage by implication (majāz iḍmār) or a figurative usage by relation (majāz ʿalāqa); and if it were literally for the horsemen, their saying that would not be sound.

His saying: {المسومة}: the origin of taswīm is marking, and the meaning of musawwama is "marked", either by branding or by white patches, as came in the exegesis. It was also said: rather it is from sawwama māshiyatahu, meaning he pastured it, so musawwama means "pastured"; one says "asamtu māshiyatī fa-sāmat" (I pastured my livestock and it grazed). Allah the Exalted said: {فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ} [al-Naḥl: 10], and "sawwamtuhā fa-staʾāmat", so the verb is made transitive sometimes by the hamza and sometimes by doubling. It was also said: rather it is from sīmiyāʾ, which is beauty, so musawwama means "having beauty"; ʿIkrima said this and al-Naḥḥās chose it, saying: "because it is from wasm (marking)." Some have objected to him because of the difference of the two roots. Some have answered him that it is a case of metathesis (maqlūb), so what he said is sound. The verification of that has preceded in His saying {يَسُومُونَكُمْ} [al-Baqara: 49] and His saying, Exalted is He: {بِسِيمَاهُمْ} [al-Baqara: 273].

His saying: {والأنعام}: it is the plural of naʿam, and naʿam is specific to three kinds: camels, cattle and sheep/goats. Al-Harawī said: "Naʿam is both masculine and feminine, and when pluralized it applies to camels, cattle and sheep/goats." The apparent sense of this is that before its being pluralized as anʿām it does not apply to the three kinds, but is specific to one of them. This apparent sense that I have pointed to was stated explicitly by al-Farrāʾ, who said: "Naʿam is camels only; it is masculine and not feminine; you say 'this is a naʿam coming to water'; and it is a plural with no singular from its own wording." Ibn Qutayba said: "The anʿām are camels, cattle and sheep/goats; its singular is naʿam, and it is a plural with no singular from its own wording; they were so named for the softness (nuʿūma) of their gait and their gentleness." In sum, derivation in the names of genera is very rare.

His saying: {والحرث}: its exegesis has preceded. Here it is a maṣdar standing in place of the direct object, so it is singular and was not pluralized as its fellows were. It is permissible to assimilate the thāʾ into the dhāl, although some people considered it weak because it necessitates the joining of two sukūns, the first not being a letter of softness (ḥarf līn). He said: "Unlike {يَلْهَثْ ذلك}, where the thāʾ was assimilated into the dhāl because there is no meeting of two sukūns, since the hāʾ before the thāʾ is vowelled."

This noble verse includes kinds of eloquence and rhetoric. Among them: bringing it in summary form. Among them: making them the desires themselves, as an exaggeration in repelling from them. Among them: beginning with the more important and then the more important, so he put first the women, because they are the most intermingled and in contact with a person, and they are the snares of Satan. He, peace be upon him, said: "I have left behind me no trial more harmful to men than women"; and: "I have not seen any of those deficient in intellect and religion more robbing of the mind of the man than you," and it is narrated: "of the resolute man among you." It was said: "In them are two trials, and in sons one trial; for they frequently cut the bonds of kinship and ties among family, and they are generally the cause of gathering wealth from the lawful and the unlawful, while for the sake of children wealth is gathered; hence he put sons second. In the ḥadīth: 'The child is a cause of miserliness and cowardice.' And because they are branches from them and fruits that grew out of them; and in their saying: 'A man is put on trial by his child.'" They were put before wealth because they are dearer to a man than his wealth. As for putting wealth before children in some places, that is only in a context of favour and benefaction, or of support, assistance and victory, because men are won over by wealth. Then he mentioned the completion of pleasure, which is the splendid mount among all animals; then he mentioned what brings beauty "when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture", as the other verse testifies; then he mentioned that by which their subsistence and the life of their children stands, namely crops and fruits, which includes fruits too. Among them: bringing a wording that signals the intensity of love for these things, where He said "zuyyina", and adornment is beloved in natures.

Among them: building the verb as passive, because the aim is to announce that this has come about. Among them: annexing love to the desires, and the desires are the inclination and yearning toward a thing.

Among them: jinās (paronomasia): «القناطير المقنطرة». Among them: joining what resembles ṭibāq (antithesis) in His saying «والذهب والفضة», because they became opposed in most usage. Among them: describing the qanāṭīr as muqantara, which indicates multiplying them despite their being many in themselves. Among them: mentioning this genus with the root of khayl because of what the wording indicates of embellishing it, and He did not say "horses" (afrās); and likewise His saying «والأنعام», and He did not say camels, cattle and sheep/goats; and because it is greener.

His saying: {ذلك مَتَاعُ}: the pointing with «ذلك» is to what was mentioned before, so the demonstrative is singular though what it points to is plural, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {عَوَانٌ بَيْنَ ذلك} [al-Baqara: 68], where two things had preceded.

His saying: {المآب}: it is a maf'al form from āba yaʾūbu, meaning "he returned"; the origin is maʾwab, so the vowel of the wāw was moved to the silent hamza before it, and the wāw was turned into alif. Here it is an ism maṣdar, that is, "the goodness of the return"; it may also be a noun of place or time. You say: āba yaʾūbu awban, iyāban and maʾāban; awb and iyāb are two maṣdars, and maʾāb is a noun for both.

semin-durr:103-103.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {بِحَبْلٍ} ("by a rope"): al-ḥabl originally is the means (sabab), and everything that connects you to something is a ḥabl. Its origin is in physical bodies, and its use for abstract matters is figurative (majāz); it may then be a case of metaphor (istiʿāra), and it may be a case of simile-allegory (tamthīl). Among the words of the Anṣār, may Allah be pleased with them: «يا رسول الله إنَّ بيننا وبين القوم حبالاً ونحن قاطعوها» ("O Messenger of Allah, between us and the people there are ropes, and we are going to cut them"), meaning covenants and alliances. al-Aʿshā said:
1371 - وإذا تُجَوِّزُها حبالُ قبيلةً ... أَخَذَتْ من الأخرى إليكَ حِبالَها
(When the ropes of one tribe let you pass, you take from the other tribe its ropes towards you.)
meaning covenants. It is said that the reason for this is that when a man travelled he feared, so he took from one tribe a covenant to another and was given an arrow or a rope to keep with him as a sign, so the covenant was called a ḥabl for that reason; but this is a meaning of no worth. Rather the covenant was called a ḥabl because it is a means of reaching the goal. Another said:
1372 - ما زِلْتُ معتصِماً بحبلٍ منكُم ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(I have never ceased holding fast to a rope from you …) [Translator's note: the second half is elided in the source.]
What is meant by ḥabl here is the Qur'an, and in the long ḥadīth: «هو حَبْلُ الله المتين» ("It is the firm rope of Allah").

His saying «جميعاً» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the fāʿil (agent) of «اعتصموا», and «بحبل الله» is attached to it. His saying «ولا تَفَرَّقوا»: al-Bazzī read it with shadda on the tāʾ in continuous recitation; its explanation was given earlier in al-Baqara at His saying {وَلاَ تَيَمَّمُواْ} [al-Baqara: 267]. The others read it with the tāʾ lightened, by omission.

His saying {نِعْمَةَ الله} is a maṣdar (verbal noun) annexed to its agent, since He is the Bestower of favour. «عليكم» may be attached to «نعمة» itself, because this root takes "ʿalā" [as in:] {للذي أَنعَمَ الله عَلَيْهِ} [al-Aḥzāb: 37]; and it may be attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from «نعمة», attached to an omitted word, that is: "established and present upon you."

His saying: {إِذْ كُنْتُمْ}: «إذ» is accusative by «نعمة», as its adverbial; it may also be attached to the "being established" implied by «عليكم», if we say that «عليكم» is a ḥāl from the favour. But if we attach «عليكم» to «نعمة», the first aspect is the only one. al-Ḥawfī allowed it to be accusative by «اذكروا», meaning as a direct object, not as an adverbial of it, because the meaning would be corrupt, as «اذكروا» is future and «إذ» is past.

His saying: {فَأَصْبَحْتُمْ}: aṣbaḥa is one of the sisters of kāna. When it is incomplete (nāqiṣa) it is like kāna in raising the subject and making the predicate accusative; when it is complete (tāmma) it raises a fāʿil and needs nothing more, and if an accusative is found after it, it is a ḥāl. It is complete when it means "entered the morning"; you say «أصبحَ زيد», meaning he entered the morning. Amsā is like it in that. The Exalted said: {فَسُبْحَانَ الله حِينَ تُمْسُونَ وَحِينَ تُصْبِحُونَ} [al-Rūm: 17], and His saying: {وَإِنَّكُمْ لَّتَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مُّصْبِحِينَ} [al-Ṣāffāt: 137]. Among their proverbs: «إذا سَمِعْتُ بسُرى القَيْن فاعلَمْ أنَّه مُصبح» ("If you hear of the night journey of the smith, know that he is staying on in the morning"), because the qayn, who is the blacksmith, might find his craft scarce in the Arab encampments, and so he would say "Tomorrow I am travelling" so that people would bring him their needs, and then he would stay and abandon the journey; so they made it a proverb for one who says / one thing and does otherwise. The meaning is that he is staying in the morning. It can also mean «صار» (became), in both function and meaning, as in his saying:
1373 - فَأَصْبحوا كأنَّهم ورقٌ جَفْ ... فَ فَأَلْوَتْ به الصَّبا والدَّبُورُ
(They became as if they were dry leaves which the east wind and the west wind swept away.)
that is, they became. «إخواناً» is its predicate. They allowed here several possibilities: that it be on its usual footing, indicating that the described is characterised by the attribute at the time of morning; that it mean صار; and that it be the complete one, i.e. "you entered the morning". When it is incomplete, on its usual footing, the clearer view is that «إخواناً» is its predicate.

«بنعمته» is attached to «إخواناً», because of the verbal sense in it, i.e. "you became brothers by His favour"; the bāʾ is of causation. The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] allowed it to be attached to «أصبحتم», and you have known the disagreement in that. Others allowed it to be attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from the fāʿil of «أصبحتم», i.e. "you became brothers, accompanied by His favour", or a ḥāl from «إخواناً», because originally it is an adjective of it. They also allowed «بنعمته» to be the predicate and «إخواناً» a ḥāl, with the bāʾ meaning location (ẓarfiyya). When it means «صار», all these aspects mentioned apply to it; and when it is complete, «إخواناً» is a ḥāl, and for «بنعمته» the aspects given apply, except that of being predicate.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: «فأصبحتم» is an expression for continuity, although the word is specific to a time; this word was given this sense because it is the beginning of the day and in it begins the day's work, so the state a person feels in himself then is, for the most part, the one in which his day continues. Of this is the saying of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ḍubʿ:
1374 - أَصْبَحْتُ لا أَحْمِلُ السِّلاح ولا ... أَمْلِكُ رأسَ البعيرِ إنْ نفرا
(I have become one who cannot carry weapons, nor control the head of the camel if it bolts.)
The Shaykh said: "This which he mentioned, that «أصبح» is for continuity, and the reason he gave, I have not seen any of the grammarians hold; they mentioned only that it is used in the two ways we stated." I say: What Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned is a fine meaning, and if the grammarians have not stated it, it is not to be rejected, because grammarians mostly speak only of what relates to the wording; as for meanings understood from the sense of the speech, they generally have no need to discuss them.

al-Ikhwān is the plural of akh. Ikhwa is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) according to Sībawayh, and a plural according to others. Some said: "Akh in kinship is pluralised as «إخوة», and in religion as «إخوان»; this is the most frequent of their usage. The Exalted said: {إِنَّمَا المؤمنون إِخْوَةٌ} [al-Ḥujurāt: 10]," and this very verse supports what he said, since what is meant here is not brotherhood of kinship; what is meant is brotherhood of religion and friendship. Abū Ḥātim said: "Then the people of Basra said: ikhwa is for kinship and ikhwān for friendship." He said: "This is a mistake; both ikhwa and ikhwān are said of friends and kinsmen. The Exalted said: {إِنَّمَا المؤمنون إِخْوَةٌ}, not meaning kinship, and He said: {أَوْ بُيُوتِ إِخْوَانِكُمْ} [al-Nūr: 61], and this is in kinship." I say: Abū Ḥātim's refutation holds against this unqualified report, but does not apply to the first report, because they restricted it to the most frequent usage.

His saying: {على شَفَا}: the shafā of a thing is its edge and brink. It is a maqṣūr (ending in alif) noun of the wāw-class; its dual is formed with wāw, as in shafawayn; it is written with alif; its plural is ashfāʾ; and it is used annexed to the top of a thing and to its bottom. An example of the first is {شَفَا جُرُفٍ} [al-Tawba: 109], and of the second is this verse. Ashfā ʿalā kadhā means "he came near it", and from it "the sick man was on the verge (ashfā) of death". Yaʿqūb said: "It is said of a man at his death, of the moon at its waning, and of the sun at its setting: «ما بَقي منه أو منها إلا شفا», meaning only a little remains." Some said: what lies between night and day at sunset, when part of it has gone, is called shafā, and he recited:
1375 - أَدْرَكْتُه بلا شَفا أو بشَفا ... والشمسُ قد كادَتْ تكونُ دَنِفا
(I reached him with no remnant, or with a remnant, when the sun had nearly become sickly.)
al-Rāghib said: "al-shifāʾ from illness is arriving at the brink (shafā) of safety, and it became a name for recovery; al-shafā is masculine."

As for the return of the pronoun in «منها», there are several aspects. One: that it refers to «حفرة».
