al-ʿAḍḍ, with ḍamma on the first letter [Translator's note: the source says "ḍamma on the fāʾ"], is fodder of crushed date-stones and the like, and from it: a camel ʿuḍāḍī, i.e. fat, as if related to it; and aʿaḍḍa l-qawm means their camels ate that. al-ʿIḍḍ with kasra is the formidable among men, as if they pictured his biting and severity. A zamanun ʿaḍūḍ is a barren time. al-Taʿḍūḍ is a kind of date, so called for the hardness and difficulty of chewing it.
al-Anāmil is the plural of anmula, which is the fingertips. al-Rummānī said: "Its derivation is from al-naml, this well-known animal [the ant]; it was likened to it for its fineness and the speed of its movement and motion; from it they called the slanderer namil and munmil." Hence he said:
1412 - ولستُ بذي نَيْرَبٍ فيهمُ ... ولا مُنْمِشٍ منهمُ مُنْمِلُ
(I am not one among them given to mischief, nor an agitator or slanderer among them.)
In its mīm both ḍamma and fatḥa occur.
al-Ghayẓ is the maṣdar of ghāẓahu yaghīẓuhu, i.e. he angered him. al-Rāghib explained it as the most intense anger, saying: "It is the heat a person feels from the surging of his heart's blood." He said: when Allah the Exalted is described by it, vengeance is meant. al-Taghayyuẓ is showing rage, and sometimes there is a sound with that. The Exalted said: {سَمِعُواْ لَهَا تَغَيُّظاً وَزَفِيراً} [al-Furqān: 12].
The sentence in His saying «وتؤمنون» is conjoined to «تُحِبُّونهم», so it has the well-known aspects. / al-Zamakhsharī said: "The wāw in «وتؤمنون» is of ḥāl, and its accusative position is from «لا يُحِبُّونكم», i.e. they do not love you while you believe in all your Book, and they, despite that, hate you; so what is the matter with you that you love them when they do not believe in any of your Book?" The Shaykh said: "It is good, except that there is in it, grammatically, something that mars it, namely that he made the wāw in «وتؤمنون» a wāw of ḥāl and its accusative position from «لا يحبونكم», whereas an affirmative imperfect that stands as a ḥāl does not take the wāw of ḥāl. You say «جاء زيدٌ يضحك» and it is not permitted «ويضحك». As for their saying «قمتُ وأَصُكُّ عينَه», it is extremely irregular, and has been interpreted as the implication of a mubtadaʾ, i.e. «وأنا أصُكُّ عينه», so the sentence becomes nominal; and this interpretation is possible here, i.e. «ولا يحبونكم وأنتم تؤمنون بالكتابِ كله», but the better is what we mentioned, that it is a conjunction." He means that it does not require an omission, unlike implying a mubtadaʾ, which is contrary to the basic rule. And there is an omitted sentence indicated by the context, the implied form being: "and you believe in the whole Book, and they do not believe in all of it, but say: we believe in some and disbelieve in some."

His saying: {بِغَيْظِكُمْ}: the bāʾ may be of ḥāl, i.e. "die accompanied by your rage, which does not leave you", and it is a metonymy for the abundance of Islam and its spread, because the more faith increases the more their rage increases. It may also be of causation, i.e. "because of your rage".
His saying {مُوتُواْ}: its form is an imperative and its meaning is a supplication. It is also said that its meaning is a report, i.e. that the matter is so. Some said: "It cannot be in the sense of supplication, because had he been commanded to call upon them with it, they would all have died in that state, for his supplication is not rejected, yet many of them believed after this verse; and it cannot be a report, because had it been a report it would have occurred as reported and none would have believed afterwards. When these two meanings are negated, nothing remains but that its meaning is rebuke and threat, like {اعملوا مَا شِئْتُمْ} [Fuṣṣilat: 40] and «إذا لم تَسْتَح فاصنع ما شئت» ('If you have no shame, do as you wish')." What he said is nothing, because whoever of them believed does not fall under the supplication, if supplication is intended, nor under the report, if reporting is intended.

semin-durr:120-120.t:
The majority read {إِن تَمْسَسْكُمْ} with the feminine form, observing the wording of «حسنة». Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read it with yāʾ, because its femininity is figurative; its analogy is that «وإنْ يصبكم سيئة» also be read in the masculine, but I do not remember anything from him on it.

His saying: {إِنَّ الله عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصدور}: this sentence may be resumptive, the Exalted reporting it because they used to conceal their rage as far as they could, so He mentioned this to them by way of threat. It may also be a sentence of what is said, i.e. "Say to them such and such", in which case it is in the position of accusative by "say". The meaning of His saying «بذات» is "the hidden things that are possessors of the breasts"; so «ذات» here is the feminine of «ذي» meaning "possessor", the qualified noun being omitted and its adjective standing in its place, i.e. "Knowing of the hidden things that are companions of the breasts"; they were made companions of the breasts because of their constant attachment to them and non-separation from them, like "companions of Paradise" and "companions of the Fire".

They disagreed about stopping on this word: is it stopped at with tāʾ or with hāʾ? al-Akhfash, al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Kaysān said: "Stopping is with tāʾ, following the Mushaf's script." al-Kisāʾī and al-Jarmī said: "It is stopped at with hāʾ, because it is the tāʾ of femininity, as in «صاحبه»." Agreement with the script is preferable, since stopping at the explicit feminine tāʾ with tāʾ is established for us, so if we stop here with tāʾ we agree with that dialect and with the script, unlike the reverse.

His saying: {لاَ يَضُرُّكُمْ}: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read «يَضِرْكم» with kasra on the ḍād and jussive rāʾ, as the apodosis of the condition, from ḍārahu yaḍīruhu; one also says ḍārahu yaḍūruhu, so there are two dialectal forms in the middle letter. One says ḍārahu yaḍīruhu ḍayran, so he is ḍāʾir and he is maḍīr; and ḍārahu yaḍūruhu ḍawran, so he is ḍāʾir and he is maḍūr, like qultuhu aqūluhu, so I am qāʾil and he is maqūl.

The others read «يَضُرُّكم» with ḍamma on the ḍād and a doubled rāʾ with ḍamma. In this reading there are several aspects. One: that the verb is nominative and is not the apodosis of the condition, but only indicates the apodosis. That is because it is intended to be put first, the implied form being: "It will not harm you if you are patient and fear Allah; it will not harm you", and the «فلا يضركم», which is the apodosis, was omitted because what precedes indicates it, then what indicates the apodosis was put later. What I have mentioned is the explanation of Sībawayh and his followers. They had to commit this strain only because they saw the lack of jussive in an / imperfect verb where nothing prevents the jussive particle from acting on it. Like it is the saying of another:
1413 - يا أقرعُ بنَ حابسٍ يا أقرعُ ... إنَّك إنْ يَصْرَعْ أخوكَ تُصْرعُ
(O Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, O Aqraʿ, if your brother is thrown, you will be thrown.)
with the last «تُصْرع» in the nominative, and likewise his saying:
1414 - وإنْ أتاهُ خليلٌ يومَ مسألةٍ ... يقولُ لا غائبٌ مالي ولا حَرِمُ
(If a friend comes to him on a day of asking, he says: "My wealth is neither absent nor forbidden.")
with «يقول» in the nominative. However this type is regular, unlike the former, I mean the condition and the response both being imperfect; for what is reported from Sībawayh and his followers is that the jussive is obligatory except in necessity, like «إنْ يُصْرعَ أخوك تُصْرعُ». His explanation of this verse as I have related from him shows that this is not restricted to necessity; so know that.

The second aspect: that the verb is nominative because it occurs after an implied fāʾ, and that and what follows it is in truth the apodosis; whenever a verb occurs after the fāʾ it is nominative, nothing else, as in His saying, the Exalted: {وَمَنْ عَادَ فَيَنْتَقِمُ الله مِنْهُ} [al-Māʾida: 95], the implied form being «فلا يَضُرُّكم». The fāʾ is omitted in a place other than the disputed one, as in the saying:
1415 - مَنْ يَفعلِ الحسناتِ اللهُ يشكُرها ... والشرُّ بالشر عند الله سِيَّانِ
(Whoever does good deeds, Allah thanks them; and evil by evil is the same with Allah.)
that is «فالله يشكرها». I have seen some report this aspect from al-Mubarrad, and there is room for objection in it, since when they recited the verse mentioned they reported from al-Mubarrad that he does not permit the omission of this fāʾ at all, neither in necessity nor otherwise, and they report that he used to say: "The transmission in this verse is rather:
مَنْ يفعلِ الخيرَ فالرحمنُ يَشْكُرُه ...
(Whoever does good, the Merciful thanks him …)"
and they replied to him that when a transmission is sound, another does not impugn it. I have seen some report it from al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī, and this is nearer.

The third aspect: that the vowel is a vowel of assimilation (ḥarakat ittibāʿ). The original is «لا يَضْرِرْكم» with unmerging, because of the sukūn of the second letter by jussive; and it will be mentioned that when two identical letters meet at the end of a verb with the second made sākin by jussive or by pause, the Arabs have two ways: merging (idghām), which is the dialect of Tamīm, and unmerging (fakk), which is the dialect of the Hijaz. But there is no way to merge except with a vowelled letter, so we were forced to vowel the second identical letter, and we vowelled it with the vowel nearest to it, namely the ḍamma on the letter before it, and merged what precedes into it; so it is jussive in implied form, and this vowel is in truth a vowel of assimilation and not a vowel of i'rab, unlike the two earlier aspects, in which it is a vowel of i'rab.

Know that whenever this type is merged, its first letter is either ḍamma-vowelled, fatḥa-vowelled or kasra-vowelled. If ḍamma-vowelled, like the noble verse and their saying «مُدَّ», there are three aspects in the state of merging: ḍamma for assimilation, fatḥa for lightness, and kasra on the basis of the meeting of two sākin letters; so you say muddu, muddа and muddi, ruddu, rudda and ruddi. They recite for this Jarīr's saying:
1416 - فَغُضِّ الطرفَ إنَّك من نُمَيْرٍ ... فلا كعباً بَلَغْتَ ولا كِلابا
(Lower your gaze, for you are of Numayr; you have reached neither Kaʿb nor Kilāb.)
with ḍamma, fatḥa and kasra on the ḍād as I have told you; and it will be mentioned that the verse was recited with the three aspects. If fatḥa-vowelled like ʿaḍḍa, or kasra-vowelled like firra, the final letter has two aspects: fatḥa and kasra, since there is no way for ḍamma; but with something like «فِرَّ» you may say kasra for two reasons, either assimilation or the meeting of two sākin letters, and likewise with fatḥa like «عَضَّ» you have two reasons also, either assimilation or lightness. All this holds when no third-person pronoun is attached to the verb; when a third-person pronoun is attached, like «رُدَّه», there are details and dialectal forms that are long to discuss and it is not fitting to go into them in this kind of work.

ʿĀṣim, in what al-Mufaḍḍal related from him, read with ḍamma on the ḍād and a doubled rāʾ with fatḥa, on the lightness I mentioned to you, / and it is, in their view, a better aspect than ḍamma on the rāʾ.
al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim read «لا يَضُرِّكم» with ḍamma on the ḍād and a doubled rāʾ with kasra, on the meeting of two sākin letters I mentioned to you. It seems that Ibn ʿAṭiyya did not know it as a reading, for he said: "As for the kasra, I do not know it as a reading." al-Zajjāj's expression on that is loose, since it appears from the flow of his speech that it is a reading. I say: I have shown that it is a reading as al-Zajjāj said, and praise be to Allah.

al-Kayd is scheming and guile. al-Rāghib said: "It is a kind of guile, and may be praised or blamed, though it is used more in the blameworthy." Ibn Qutayba said: "Its origin is from hardship, from their saying «فلان يكيدُ بنفسِه», meaning he passes through the pangs of death, and its derivatives." One says kidtu fulānan akīduhu like bʿtuhu abīʿuhu. He said:
1417 - مَنْ يَكِدْني بسيِّءٍ كنتُ منه ... كالشَّجا بين حَلْقِه والوَرِيد
(Whoever schemes against me with evil, I shall be to him like a bone stuck between his throat and his jugular vein.)
Ubayy read «لا يَضْرِرْكم» with unmerging, which is the Hijazi dialect, and on it is His saying, the Exalted: {إِن تَمْسَسْكُمْ حَسَنَةٌ}.
His saying «شيئاً» is accusative like the maṣdars, i.e. "any harm"; a parallel has been given. The majority read «بما يعملون محيطٌ» in the third person, which is clear. al-Ḥasan read it in the second person, either on iltifāt, or on the implication «قل لهم يا محمد» ("Say to them, O Muḥammad").

semin-durr:146-146.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَكَأَيِّن مِّن نَّبِيٍّ}: It is said that this word is a compound of the kāf of comparison and «أيٍّ», and after the compounding there arose in it the meaning of multiplicity understood from the khabar-type «كم». Similar to it in compounding and conveying multiplicity is «كذا» in their saying «له عندي كذا كذا درهماً» ("he has with me so and so many dirhams"); the origin is the kāf of comparison and «ذا», which is a demonstrative; when the two were compounded, the meaning of multiplicity arose in them. The khabar-type «كم», «كأيِّن» and «كذا» are all of one meaning, and we have known compounding to produce another meaning; do you not see that «لولا» acquired a new meaning? «كأيِّن» by right, on this account, should be paused upon without nūn, because tanwīn is dropped in pause; but the Companions wrote it «كأيِّن» with the nūn retained, and so the majority of the readers paused upon it with the nūn, following the codex orthography. Abū ʿAmr, and Sawra ibn Mubārak from al-Kisāʾī, paused upon it as «كأي» without nūn, by analogy. Al-Fārisī gave reasons for pausing with the nūn, which he elaborated at length, among them that when the word was compounded it departed from its like, so the tanwīn was made as if it were an original letter of the structure of the word. It has five dialectal forms. The first: «كَأَيِّنْ», which is the origin, and by it the group read, except Ibn Kathīr. The poet said:

1456 - كَأَيِّنْ في المعاشِر من أُناسٍ ... أخوهُمْ فوقَهم وهمُ كِرامُ
(How many among the tribes are people whose brother is above them while they are noble.)

The second: «كائِنْ» on the pattern of «كاعِنْ», by which Ibn Kathīr and a group read; it is more used than «كَأَيِّن» even though that is the origin. The poet said:

1457 - وكائن بالأباطحِ مِنْ صديقٍ ... يَراني لو أُصِبْتُ هو المُصَابا
(How many a friend in the valley-beds who, were I afflicted, would see himself the afflicted.)

And he said:

1458 - وكائِنْ رَدَدْنا عنكُمُ مِنْ مُدَجَّجٍ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(How many an armoured warrior have we turned back from you ...)

They differed in the justification of this reading. It is transmitted from al-Mubarrad that it is an active participle from kāna yakūnu, so it is kāʾin; Makkī considered this remote, saying: "because «مِنْ» comes after it and because it is built on sukūn." Likewise Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is far from sound, because if it were so it would be declinable (muʿrab) and would not have the meaning of multiplicity." It cannot be said that this is to be charged against al-Mubarrad alone, for this also applies to them (the others), since indeclinability and the meaning of multiplicity are incidental as well, because compounding has been known to produce the like of that, as already said of «كذا» and «لولا» and the like; but a single word being transferred to a meaning and made indeclinable without a cause has no parallel. It is said: the origin of this reading is «كأيِّنْ», like the reading of the group, except that transposition (qalb) entered the word and it became «كائِن» like «جاعِن».

They differed on how it became so by transposition, on four views. The first: the doubled yāʾ was put before the hamza, so its pattern became kaʿlaf, because you put forward the ʿayn and lām, which are the doubled yāʾ; then the second yāʾ was dropped because of its heaviness with the vowel and the doubling, as they said of «أيُّهما»: «أيْهُما»; then the quiescent yāʾ was turned into alif, as they turned it in the like of «آية», the origin being ayya, and as they said ṭāʾī, the origin being ṭayʾī; so the word became kāʾin like jāʿin, as you see, and its pattern is «كَعْفٍ», because the fāʾ was moved back to the place of the lām and the lām was dropped.

The second view: the quiescent yāʾ which is the ʿayn was dropped and the vowelled one which is the lām was put forward, so the hamza, which is the fāʾ, was put back, and the yāʾ was turned into alif because it has a vowel and what precedes it has fatḥa, so it became «كائِن», and its pattern is «كَلْفٍ».

The third view, attributed to al-Khalīl: one of the two yāʾs was put in the position of the hamza and given the vowel of the hamza, namely fatḥa, and the hamza became quiescent in the position of the yāʾ; the yāʾ took a vowel with fatḥa before it, so it was turned into alif, and two quiescents met, the alif turned from yāʾ and the quiescent hamza after it, so the hamza was given kasra on the basis of the meeting of two quiescents; and one of the two yāʾs remained final, and the tanwīn removed it after its vowel was stripped, like the yāʾ of qāḍin and ghāzin.

The fourth view: the vowelled yāʾ was put forward and turned into alif, and the other remained quiescent and the tanwīn dropped it, like qāḍin; its pattern on these two views is also «كَلْفٍ», because of the dropping of the ʿayn and the postponement of the fāʾ, the operations differing only.

The third dialect: «كَأْيِن» with a light yāʾ after the hamza, on the pattern kaʿyin, by which Ibn Muḥayṣin and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī read. Its aspect is that the origin is «كَأَيِّن» like the reading of the group; the second yāʾ was dropped for heaviness, so two quiescents met, the yāʾ and the tanwīn, so the yāʾ was given kasra for the meeting of two quiescents; then the hamza was made quiescent for lightness because of the heaviness of the word by compounding, so it became like a single word, as they made «فهو» and «فهي» quiescent.

The fourth dialect: «كَيْئِن», with a quiescent yāʾ followed by a hamza with kasra; this is the transposition of the reading before it, and some read by it.

The fifth dialect: «كَئِنْ» on the pattern kaʿ in, which al-Dānī reported as a reading from Ibn Muḥayṣin also. The poet said:

1459 - كَئِنْ مِنْ صديقٍ خِلْتُه صادقَ الإِخا ... أبانَ اختباري أنَّه لي مُداهِنُ
(How many a friend I thought truthful in brotherhood; my testing made clear that he was flattering me.)

There are two views on it. One: that he dropped the two yāʾs at once because of the blending of the two words through compounding; the second: that he dropped one of the two yāʾs as explained above, then dropped the other because it met the tanwīn while quiescent; and its pattern on this is «كَفٍ», with the ʿayn and lām dropped from it.

They differed about «أيٍّ»: is it originally a maṣdar or not? A group held that it is not a maṣdar, and this is the apparent meaning of Abū al-Baqāʾ's statement, for he said: "The origin of «كأيِّن» is «أي», which is part of a whole, to which the kāf of comparison was added." In his describing «أي» as being part of a whole there is something to consider, because it is not in the sense of part of a whole; yes, when it is annexed to a definite it takes the ruling of «بعض» (part) in agreement of the khabar and the return of the pronoun, as in «أيُّ الرجلين قام؟» and you do not say «قاما»; but it is not that of «بعض» at all.

Ibn Jinnī held that it is originally the maṣdar of awā yaʾwī, when something is gathered and joined, the origin being awy, like ṭawā yaṭwī ṭayyan, the origin being ṭawy: the yāʾ and wāw met, one of them preceded by sukūn, so the wāw was turned into yāʾ and assimilated into the yāʾ. It is as if Ibn Jinnī looked to the meaning of the root, the gathering, which «أيّ» indicates, for it is for generality, and generality entails gathering.

Is this kāf which enters upon «أي» attached to something, like other prepositions, or not? The sound view is that it is not attached to anything at all, because with «أي» the two became equivalent to a single word, «كم», so it is not attached to anything; for that reason its original meaning, comparison, was abandoned.

Al-Ḥawfī claimed that it is attached to a governor, and his text must be cited so that you may stand upon it, for it is strange speech. He said: "As for the governor in the kāf, if we take it according to the ruling of the origin it is carried on the meaning, the meaning being: 'there afflicted you something like the affliction of those prophets before and their companions'; and if we carry the ruling on the transfer to the meaning of «كم», the governor is by the estimate of inchoation and it is in the position of the nominative, «قُتِل» being the khabar, and «مِنْ» attached to the meaning of residing; and the first estimate is clearer, to carry the speech on the wording rather than the meaning, because of what is necessary of the genitive in «أي»; and if «أي» is in its normal way in treating the wording, «مِنْ» is attached to what the kāf is attached to of the meaning indicated." End.

The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) chose that «كأيِّنْ» is a simple word, not compounded, and that its final nūn is part of the word itself, not tanwīn, because these earlier claims have no evidence standing upon them. The Shaykh took the easier route in that, while the grammarians mentioned these things to preserve their principles, along with the benefits added to that and the sharpening and exercising of the mind. This is what concerns «كأيِّن» in terms of its singularity.

As for what concerns it in terms of syntax, its position is nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and there are four views on its khabar. The first: that it is «قُتِل», for in it is a nominative pronoun governed by it referring back to the mubtadaʾ, the estimate being: "many of the prophets were killed". Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "The good form is that the pronoun refer to the wording of «كأيِّنْ», as you say «مئة نبي قُتِل» (a hundred prophets was killed), the pronoun being for the hundred, since it is the mubtadaʾ. If you say: were it so you would have made it feminine and said «قُتِلَتْ». It is said: this is carried on the meaning, because the estimate is: 'many of the men was killed'." End. As if he means by "not good" its referring back to the wording «نبي». On this, «معه ربِّيُّون» is a sentence in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun in «قُتِل» [and it is preferable because it is of the class of singulars, and the origin of the ḥāl, khabar and attribute is to be singular]. It is possible that «معه» alone is the ḥāl and «رِبِّيُّون» its fāʿil, and there is no need here of the wāw of ḥāl, because the pronoun is the link, I mean the pronoun in «معه»; and it may be a ḥāl from «نبي», although it is indefinite, because it is specified by the description then; Makkī mentioned it; and the adverbial phrase operates here because it relies on the owner of the ḥāl.

The Shaykh said: "It is a narration of a past state (ḥikāyat ḥāl māḍiya), and for that reason «ربِّيُّون» is nominative through the adverbial phrase even though the governor is past, because it narrates the past state, as in His saying, the Exalted, {وَكَلْبُهُمْ بَاسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ} [al-Kahf: 18]; and this is according to the Basrans, whereas al-Kisāʾī makes the active participle devoid of «ال» govern absolutely." There is something to consider in it, because we do not concede that the adverbial phrase is attached to an active participle so that what he said, of interpreting the active participle as a past state, would be necessitated; rather we claim that it is attached to a verb whose estimate is: "there rested with him Rabbis".

The second view: that «قُتِل» is a sentence in the position of the genitive as a naʿt of «نبي», and «معه ربيون» is the khabar, and you have the two earlier views in making it a ḥāl, I mean if you wish you may make «معه» a fronted khabar and «ربيون» a postponed mubtadaʾ, the sentence being the khabar of «كأين»; and if you wish you may make «معه» alone the khabar and «ربيون» its fāʿil, because the adverbial phrase relies on the possessor of a khabar.

The third view: that the khabar is omitted, its estimate being «في الدنيا» ("in the world") or «مضى» ("passed") or «صائر» ("become") and the like. On this his saying «قتل» is in the position of the genitive as an attribute of «نبي», and «معه ربيون» a ḥāl from the pronoun in «قتل» as the explanation preceded; it is also possible that «معه ربيون» is a second attribute of «نبي», it being described with two attributes: its being killed and its having Rabbis with it.

The fourth view: that «قُتِل» is empty of the pronoun, attributed to «ربيون»; in this sentence there are then two possibilities. One: that it is the khabar of «كائن»; the second: that it is in the position of the genitive as an attribute of «نبي», the khabar being omitted as has gone before; and the claim of omitting the khabar is weak because the speech is self-sufficient without it. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It may be that «قُتِل» is an attribute of «ربيين», so there is no pronoun in it on this, and the sentence is an attribute of «نبي»; and it may be a khabar, so there become four views on the khabar; and it may be an attribute of «نبي» with the khabar omitted as we mentioned." As for his saying "an attribute of «ربيين»", he means that being killed is among their attributes in meaning. And his saying "so there become four views", he means with the views he mentioned earlier. His saying "so there is no pronoun in it on this, and the sentence is an attribute of «نبي»" is an error, because it leaves the mubtadaʾ without a khabar. If you say: he claims this only because he estimates an omitted khabar; I say: he mentioned that as another view where he said: "It may be an attribute of «نبي» with the khabar omitted as we mentioned."

The attribution of «قُتِل» to the pronoun of the prophet is supported by the fact that the story is on account of the battle of Uḥud and the believers' dispute when it was said that Muḥammad had died, killed; this is supported by his saying {أَفإِنْ مَّاتَ أَوْ قُتِلَ} [Āl ʿImrān: 144]; to this went Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ṭabarī and a group; and from Ibn ʿAbbās on His saying {وَمَا كَانَ لِنَبِيٍّ أَنْ يَغُلَّ} [Āl ʿImrān: 161]: "The prophet is killed, so how would he not be betrayed?" Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Jubayr and a group held that the killing was of the Rabbis; they said: because no prophet has ever been killed in battle. Al-Zamakhsharī supported this with the reading «قُتِّل» with doubling, meaning that multiplicity does not arise with a single one, who is the prophet. What al-Zamakhsharī mentioned was preceded to it by Ibn Jinnī, and the interpretation of this will come.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr read «قُتِل» as a passive; Qatāda likewise, except that he doubled the تاء; and the rest of the seven read «قاتَل». Each of these verbs can take as its subject the pronoun of «نبي» and can take «ربِّيِّين», as the detail has preceded. Ibn Jinnī said: "In the reading «قُتِّل» with doubling it is necessary that the verb be attributed to the overt noun, I mean «ربيين»." He said: "because there is no multiplicity in a single one." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is not impossible that it contain the pronoun of the first, because it is in the sense of a group." End. He means that by «من نبي» the genus is meant, so the multiplicity is in relation to the multiplicity of persons, not in relation to each individual, since killing is not multiplied in each individual. This answer that Abū al-Baqāʾ gave was sensed by Abū al-Fatḥ, who answered it. He said: "If it is said: it is attributed to «نبي» in regard to the meaning of «كم», the answer: the wording has spread in the singular in His saying {مِّن نَّبِيٍّ}, and the singular pronoun in «معه» indicates that what is meant is the exemplification by one, so the speech has gone out of the meaning of «كم»." He said: "This reading strengthens the statement of those who said that «قُتِل» and «قاتَل» are attributed to the Rabbis."

The Shaykh said: "It is not apparent, because «كأين» is like «كم», and when you say «كم مِنْ عانٍ فككتُه» ('how many a captive have I freed'), [using the singular], you have regarded its wording, and its meaning is plural; and when you say «فَكَكْتُهم» you have regarded the meaning. So there is no difference between «قُتل معه ربيون» and «قُتِل معهم رِبِّيُّون». Regarding the wording at times and the meaning at others is permissible in «كم» and «كأين» only because their meaning is 'a group' (jamʿ), and for «جمع» that is permissible. The Exalted said: {أَمْ يَقُولُونَ نَحْنُ جَمِيعٌ مُّنتَصِرٌ سَيُهْزَمُ الجمع وَيُوَلُّونَ الدبر} [al-Qamar: 44-45], so He regarded the wording in His saying «منتصِرٌ» and the meaning in His saying «يُوَلُّون»."

Some preferred the reading «قاتل» because of His saying after that {فَمَا وَهَنُواْ}; he said: "If they were killed, how would they be described by this? Only the living are described by this." The answer: its meaning is "some of them were killed", as you say "the sons of so-and-so were killed in such-and-such a battle, then they were victorious". Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The reading of those who read «قاتل» is more general in praise, because it includes those who were killed and those who remained; and it seems good to me on this reading that the verb be attributed to the Rabbis, and on the reading «قُتِل» that it be attributed to «نبي»." The Shaykh said: "Rather «قُتِل» is more praising and more eloquent for the aim of the address, for «قُتِل» entails fighting, without the converse."

And His saying {مِّن نَّبِيٍّ} is a tamyīz for «كأيِّن», because it is like the khabar-type «كم». Some claimed that its genitive with «مِن» is obligatory, and for this nothing but that has come in the Revelation; and this is the most frequent and prevalent, as he said. Its tamyīz has come accusative, he said:

1460 - اطرُدِ اليأسَ بالرجاء فكائِنْ ... آلِماً حُمَّ يُسْرُهُ بعدَ عُسْرِ
(Drive despair away with hope, for how many a sufferer has had ease decreed for him after hardship.)

And another said:

1461 - وكائِنْ لنا فَضْلاً عليكم ورحمةً ... قديماً ولا تَدْرُون ما مَنُّ مُنْعِمِ
(How many a favour and mercy have we shown you of old, and you do not know what a benefactor's bestowal is.)

As for its being genitive by annexation, it is impossible because its end is tanwīn, which does not stay with annexation.

And al-rabbiyyūn is the plural of «رِبِّي», which is the scholar, ascribed to al-rabb (the Lord); its rāʾ was given kasra only as a change in the ascription (nisba), like «إمْسِيّ» with kasra, ascribed to «أَمْس». It is also said: it was given kasra by assimilation; and it is said: there is no change in it, and it is ascribed to al-ribba, which is the group. This reading with kasra on the rāʾ is the reading of the majority. ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan read «رُبِّيُّون» with ḍamma on the rāʾ, which is from a change in the ascription if we say it is ascribed to al-rabb; it is also said: there is no change, and it is ascribed to al-rubba, which is the group, and it has two dialects: kasra and ḍamma. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the narration of Qatāda, read «رَبِّيُّون» with fatḥa on it, on the origin if we say it is ascribed to al-rabb, otherwise it is from a change in the ascription if we say it is ascribed to al-ribba. Ibn Jinnī said: "The fatḥa is the dialect of Tamīm." Al-Naqqāsh said: "They are those who increase knowledge, from their saying rabā yarbū, when it increases." This is an oversight on his part, because of the difference of the two roots, since that one is of rāʾ, bāʾ and wāw, and this of rāʾ and a doubled bāʾ. And «كثير» is an attribute of «ربّيّون» although it is in the singular wording, because its meaning is plural.

His saying: {فَمَا وَهَنُواْ}: the pronoun in «وَهَنوا» refers back to the Rabbis as a whole if «قُتِل» is attributed to the pronoun of the prophet; likewise in the reading «قاتل», whether attributed to the pronoun of the prophet or to the Rabbis; and if it is attributed to the Rabbis, the pronoun refers back to some of them, as has already gone before in the discussion of preferring the reading «قاتل».

The majority read «وَهَنوا» with fatḥa on the hāʾ, and al-Aʿmash and Abū al-Sammāl with kasra on it; they are two dialects: wahana yahinu like waʿada yaʿidu, and wahina yawhanu like wajila yawjalu. It is also related from Abū al-Sammāl and ʿIkrima: «وَهْنوا» with sukūn on the hāʾ, which is a lightening of faʿila because it is a guttural letter, like naʿm and shahd for naʿima and shahida.

And «لَمَّا» is attached to «وَهَنوا», and «وما» may be a relative noun, a maṣdar particle, or an indefinite noun with a description. The majority read «ضَعُفوا» with ḍamma on the ʿayn, and it was read «ضَعَفوا» with fatḥa on it, which al-Kisāʾī reported as a dialect.

And His saying {وَمَا استكانوا}: there are three statements on it. The first: that it is istafʿala from al-kawn, and al-kawn is humiliation, its origin being istakwana; the vowel of the wāw was transferred to the kāf, then the wāw was turned into alif. [Translator's note: the source gives no label for the second view; the statement of al-Azharī and Abū ʿAlī that follows appears to be the second.] Al-Azharī and Abū ʿAlī said: "It is from the saying of the Arabs «بات فلان بِكَيْنَةِ سوءٍ» on the pattern of «جفنة», i.e. in a bad state", so its alif on this is from a yāʾ, and the origin is istakyana, and what was done with the yāʾ is what was done with its sister.

The third: al-Farrāʾ said: "Its pattern is iftaʿala from al-sukūn, but the fatḥa was extended and an alif was generated from it, as in his saying:

1462 - أعوذُ باللهِ من العَقْرابِ ... الشَّائِلاتِ عُقَدَ الأَذْنَابِ
(I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions, raising the knots of their tails.)

he means al-ʿaqrab al-shāʾila (the scorpion raising [its tail])." Al-Farrāʾ was refuted in that this alif is retained in all the inflections of the word, like istakāna yastakīnu, so he is mustakīn and mustakān ilayhi, istikāna; and in that extension (ishbāʿ) occurs only in necessity. Neither of the two is binding on him: as for the extension, it occurs in the seven readings, as will pass you; and as for the retention of the alif in the inflections of the word, it is also no proof, because an augment may be fixed; do you not see that the mīm in tamandala and tamadraʿa is augmented, and yet it is retained in all the inflections of the word? They said: tamandala yatamandalu tamandulan, so he is mutamandil and mutamandal bihi, and likewise tamadraʿa, both from al-nadl and al-dirʿ. Abū al-Baqāʾ's wording is better in the refutation, for he said: "because the word in all its inflections has retained its ʿayn, and extension is not on this pattern."

He did not mention what the abasement and weakness are attached to; He did not say "they did not weaken against such and such, nor abase themselves to such and such", either for the sake of working with it, or to limit to the two verbs, like {كُلُواْ واشربوا} [al-Baqara: 60], so that it should include whatever is suitable for them.

semin-durr:173-173.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {الذين قَالَ لَهُمُ الناس}: The aspects in it are those that preceded for the «الذين» before it, except its being nominative as a mubtadaʾ.
His saying: {فَزَادَهُمْ إِيمَاناً}: There are three aspects regarding the agent of «زاد». The most evident: that it is a pronoun referring back to the maṣdar understood from «قال», that is: "the saying of such-and-such increased them in faith", like {اعدلوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ للتقوى} [المائدة: 8]. The second: that it refers to what was said, namely {إِنَّ الناس قَدْ جَمَعُواْ لَكُمْ فاخشوهم}, as though it were said: "They said this speech to them, and it increased them in faith." The third: that it refers to «الناس», when a single individual is meant, as is transmitted in the story and the occasion of revelation, namely Nuʿaym ibn Masʿūd al-Ashjaʿī. Al-Zamakhsharī transmitted these three aspects. The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) considered the last two weak. He said: "because the first (the saying) does not increase faith except through uttering it, not in itself, and because the second: when the wording of the plural is applied figuratively to a single person, the pronouns run according to that plural, not according to the singular. You say 'his temples have turned grey (shābat)' taking the plural into account, and it is not permissible to say 'his temple has turned grey (shāba)' taking 'his parting has turned grey' into account."
There is room for objection in what the Shaykh said, because what was said is that by which, in truth, the increase of faith came about. As for his saying "they run according to the plural, not the singular", it is not conceded. What supports it is that they have stated explicitly that it is permissible to take into account the wording of the plural that occurs in place of the dual at one time and its meaning at another, so they allowed: "the heads of the two rams — I cut them (qaṭaʿtuhunna) and I cut them (qaṭaʿtuhumā)." If that is established for the plural occurring in the place of the dual, let it be permissible for what occurs in the place of the singular. One could distinguish between the two, namely that taking into account the meaning of duality expressed by the wording of the plural is permissible only because of its nearness to it, in that each of the two involves joining a thing to its like, unlike the singular, which is distant from the plural for lack of joining, so taking the meaning of the dual into account in that does not entail taking the meaning of the singular into account.
His saying: {وَقَالُواْ حَسْبُنَا الله}: He conjoined «قالوا» to «فزادهم», and the sentence after the saying is in the position of accusative by it. It has already preceded that «حَسْب» has the meaning of an active participle, that is «مُحْسِب», meaning "sufficient", and for that reason its annexation is not a pure annexation, at His saying in al-Baqara {فَحَسْبُهُ جَهَنَّمُ} [الآية: 206].
And His saying: {وَنِعْمَ الوكيل}: the one specified for praise is omitted, that is: Allah.

semin-durr:174-174.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {بِنِعْمَةٍ}: There are two views about it. One: that it is attached to the verb itself, the bāʾ being the bāʾ of transitivity. The second: that it is attached to an omitted word as a ḥāl from the pronoun in «انقلبوا», and the bāʾ on this is for accompaniment, as though it were said: "so they returned involved with a favour and accompanied by it".
His saying: {لَّمْ يَمْسَسْهُمْ سواء}: This sentence is also in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, and there are two views about its ḥāl-owner. One: that it is the agent of «انقلبوا», that is: "they returned safe from harm". The second: that it is the latent pronoun in «بنعمة» if it is a ḥāl, the implied form being: "so they returned blessed, free from harm"; and the operator in it is the operator in «بنعمة», so the two are nested ḥāls. When a ḥāl occurs as an imperfect negated with «لم» and contains a pronoun of the ḥāl-owner, the entry of the wāw and its absence are both permissible. Of the first is His saying, the Exalted: {أَوْ قَالَ أُوْحِيَ إِلَيَّ وَلَمْ يُوحَ إِلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ} [الأنعام: 93], and the saying of Kaʿb:
1493 - لا تَأْخُذَنِّي بأقوالِ الوشاةِ ولم ... أُذْنِبْ وإنْ كَثُرَتْ فِيَّ الأقاويلُ
(Do not seize me for the words of the slanderers, when I have not sinned, even if the sayings about me are many.)
and of the second is this verse and His saying: {وَرَدَّ الله الذين كَفَرُواْ بِغَيْظِهِمْ لَمْ يَنَالُواْ خَيْراً} [الأحزاب: 25], and the saying of Qays ibn al-Aslat:
1494 - وأضرِبُ القَوْنَسَ يوم الوغى ... بالسيفِ لم يَقْصُرْ به باعِي
(And on the day of battle I strike the crown of the helmet with the sword, my arm not falling short with it.)
By this the error of the master Ibn Kharūf is known, where he claimed that the wāw is obligatory in the like of this, whether there is a pronoun in the sentence or not.
His saying: {واتبعوا}: Two aspects are allowed in this sentence. One: that it is a conjunction upon «انقلبوا». The second: that it is also a ḥāl from the agent of «انقلبوا», and it would be on the implying of «قد», that is: "and they had followed".

semin-durr:175-175.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِنَّمَا ذلكم الشيطان}: «إنما» is a particle restrained from operating by «ما»; discussion of it has already preceded at the beginning of this book. There are five aspects in the i'rab of this sentence. One: that «ذلكم» is a mubtadaʾ and «الشيطان» its khabar, and {يُخَوِّفُ أَوْلِيَاءَهُ} is a ḥāl, on the evidence of an explicit ḥāl occurring in a construction like this, as in {وهذا بَعْلِي شَيْخاً} [هود: 72] and {فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خَاوِيَةً} [النمل: 52].
Second: that «الشيطانُ» is a badal or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition), and «يُخَوِّفُ» is the khabar; Abū l-Baqāʾ mentioned it. Third: that «الشيطان» is an adjective of the demonstrative noun, and «يُخَوِّفُ» the khabar, with «الشيطان» meaning Nuʿaym or Abū Sufyān; al-Zamakhsharī mentioned it. The Shaykh said: "He said 'by Satan is meant Nuʿaym or Abū Sufyān' only because it cannot be an adjective if Iblīs is meant, since then it would be a proper name by predominance (ʿalam bi-l-ghalaba) like al-ʿAyyūq, for it is originally an adjective which then came to predominate for Iblīs." There is room for objection in this. Fourth: that «ذلكم» is a mubtadaʾ with its khabar, and «يُخَوِّف» a resumptive sentence, an explanation of his satanic nature, and what is meant by Satan is the one who discourages the believers. Fifth: that «ذلكم» is a mubtadaʾ, «الشيطانُ» a second mubtadaʾ, and «يُخَوِّف» the khabar of the second, and the second with its khabar is the khabar of the first; so said Ibn ʿAṭiyya. He said: "This i'rab is better for the harmony of the meaning than making «الشيطان» the khabar of «ذلكم», because that comes out in meaning as a remote metaphor."
The Shaykh rejected this i'rab from him if the pronoun in «أولياءه» refers back to Satan, because the sentence occurring as the khabar lacks a link tying it to the mubtadaʾ, and it is not the mubtadaʾ itself in meaning, as in "the constant refrain (hijjīrā) of Abū Bakr: lā ilāha illā llāh"; and if it refers back to «ذلكم», and by «ذلكم» something other than Satan is meant, it is permissible, and it becomes parallel to: "Hind is Zayd, whose slave she beats (yaḍribu ʿabdahā)", and the meaning is: "This caravan or Abū Sufyān, the Satan, frightens you — you, his supporters", that is, the supporters of the caravan or the supporters of Abū Sufyān.
As for what «ذلكم» points to, is it an entity or a meaning? There are two possibilities. One: that it points to specific people such as Nuʿaym, Abū Sufyān and their followers, as has preceded. The second: that it points to everything that took place of the reports of the caravan, the sending of Abū Sufyān and the alarm of those who were alarmed; and on this supposition a muḍāf must be omitted, that is: "the doing of Satan", and al-Zamakhsharī implied it as "the saying of Satan", that is, his earlier saying, which is {إِنَّ الناس قَدْ جَمَعُواْ لَكُمْ فاخشوهم}. On either supposition, I mean the reference being to persons or to meanings, the predication of Satan about «ذلكم» is figurative, because the persons mentioned and the meanings of sayings and actions proceeding from the disbelievers are not Satan himself; it is permissible only because they were due to him and his whispering.
His saying: {يُخَوِّفُ أَوْلِيَاءَهُ}: Its position in i'rab has preceded. The doubling in it is for transitivity, since before the doubling it takes one object and by the doubling it acquires a second, and it belongs to the chapter of aʿṭā, so it is permissible to omit its two objects or one of them, for restriction and brevity. In the noble verse it admits several aspects. One: that the first object is omitted, its implied form being "he frightens you with his supporters"; this implication is strengthened by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd of this verse in that way. By his supporters here are meant the disbelievers, and a muḍāf must be omitted, that is: "the evil of his supporters", because persons are not feared. The second: that the second object is the omitted one and «أولياءه» is the first, the implied form being: "he frightens his supporters with the evil of the disbelievers"; and by his supporters on this aspect are meant the hypocrites and those with disease in their hearts who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the going out. The meaning is: his frightening by means of the disbelievers is achieved only for the hypocrites, who are his supporters, whereas as for you, his frightening does not reach you. The third, which some mentioned: that both objects are omitted and «أولياءه» is accusative by dropping the preposition, the implied form being "he frightens you with evil through his supporters", the bāʾ being causal, that is "because of his supporters", so they are the instrument of frightening. It is as though this speaker saw the reading of Ubayy and al-Nakhaʿī, «يُخَوِّف بأوليائه», and thought that the reading of the majority is like it originally, then the bāʾ was dropped; and it is not so. Rather the analysis of the majority's reading is as has preceded, as there is no need to claim what is not necessary. As for the reading of Ubayy, the bāʾ may be redundant, as in the saying:
1495 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... سُودُ المَحاجِرِ لا يَقْرَأْنَ بالسُّوَرِ
(… black around the eyes, they do not recite the sūras [the first half of the verse is elided in the source])
in which case it is like the majority's reading in meaning; and it may be causal with the two objects omitted as its exposition has preceded.
His saying: {فَلاَ تَخَافُوهُمْ}: There are three aspects regarding the accusative pronoun. The most evident: that it refers back to his supporters, that is: "do not fear the supporters of Satan", this if by supporters the disbelievers of Quraysh are meant. The second: that it refers back to «الناس» in His saying {إِنَّ الناس قَدْ جَمَعُواْ لَكُمْ}, if by his supporters the hypocrites are meant. The third: that it refers back to Satan in meaning. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "The pronoun was made plural only because Satan is a genus." The yāʾ in His saying «وخافونِ» is among the extra ones: Abū ʿAmr kept it in continuous reading and dropped it in pause, on his principle, and the rest drop it throughout.
His saying: {إِن كُنتُمْ مُّؤْمِنِينَ}: Its apodosis is omitted, or is fronted according to those who hold that; and this belongs to the manner of inciting and arousing, otherwise they are already clothed in faith.

semin-durr:176-176.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَلاَ يَحْزُنكَ الذين}: Nāfiʿ read «يُحْزِنْك» with ḍamma on the imperfect letter, from «أحزن» (quadriliteral), throughout the Qurʾān, except the one in His saying {لاَ يَحْزُنُهُمُ الفزع الأكبر} [الأنبياء: 103], for there he is like the group. The rest read it with fatḥa on the yāʾ, from «حَزَنه» (triliteral). It was said: both are from the category in which faʿala and afʿala come with one meaning; and it was said: with a difference in meaning, so «حَزَنَه» means he placed grief in him, like «دَهَنه» and «كَحَله», that is, he placed oil and kohl in it, and «أحزنتُه» when I made him grieved; and like «حَزَنَه» and «أَحْزَنَه» are «فَتنَه» and «أَفْتَنَه». Sībawayh said: "Some of the Bedouins said: aḥzantu the man and aftantuhu, that is, I made him grieved and tempted." It was also said: ḥazantuhu means I originated grief in him, and aḥzantuhu means I exposed him to grief; so said Abū l-Baqāʾ. The derivation of this word and what was said about it has already preceded in al-Baqara. It also preceded that one says "the man grieved (ḥazina)" with kasra, and when they want to make it transitive they make it so with fatḥa and say "ḥazantuhu", like "his eye turned (shatirat) and Allah turned it (shatarahā)". The truth is that ḥazanahu and aḥzanahu are two widespread dialects, both being established by continuous transmission, although Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "aḥzana is a rare dialect."
Among the wonders of what happened is that Nāfiʿ, may Allah have mercy on him, reads this root from «أحزن» except for the one in al-Anbiyāʾ, as has preceded, and that his shaykh Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ reads it from the triliteral «حَزَنه» except for the one in al-Anbiyāʾ; and this is from combining the two dialects, and recitation is a Sunna that is followed.
It is also read «يُسارعون» with fatḥa and imāla. And al-Naḥwī read «يُسْرعون», from asraʿa, throughout the Qurʾān [Translator's note: the source says only "al-Naḥwī" (the grammarian); the reader intended is not specified]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The reading of the group is more eloquent, because the one who races another is more diligent than the one who hurries alone."
His saying: «شيئاً»: There are two views about it. One: that it is a maṣdar, that is: "they will not harm him any harm". The second: that it is accusative by dropping the preposition, that is: "they will not harm him in anything", and so is every place resembling it; the two aspects hold in it.

semin-durr:81-81.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَإِذْ أَخَذَ}: concerning the operator in this adverbial there are several views. One: «اذكر» (remember), if the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. The second: «اذكروا» (remember, plural), if it is an address to the People of the Book. Third: «اصطفى», so that it is conjoined to the preceding «إذ»; there is remoteness in it, indeed impossibility because of its remoteness. Fourth: that the operator in it is «قال» from His saying «قال أأقررتم», which is very clear.
And {مِيثَاقَ} may be annexed to its agent or to its object. In the codex of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh, and in their readings: «ميثاقَ الذين أوتوا الكتاب», like what is at the end of the sūra; and likewise from Mujāhid ibn Jabr, who said: "The scribe erred." This is an error by whoever said it, whoever he was, and I do not think it is sound from Mujāhid, for the likes of Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ recited to him, and neither of them transmitted anything of that from him.
The meaning according to the famous reading is sound, and people have mentioned several views about it. One: that the speech is on its apparent sense and that Allah the Exalted took covenants from the prophets that they would confirm one another and support one another, in the sense that each one charges his people to support the prophet who comes after him and not to forsake him; this is reported from a group. Second: that the covenant is annexed to its agent, and the one on whom the covenant is taken is not mentioned because the meaning is understood, the implied form being: "the covenant of the prophets upon their communities"; this is supported by the reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh, and also by His saying: {فَمَنْ تولى بَعْدَ ذلك}. Third: that it is on the omission of a muḍāf (annexed noun), its implied form being: "the covenant of the communities of the prophets" or "of their followers"; supported by what supported the previous, and also by His saying: {ثُمَّ جَآءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ}.
Fourth: al-Zamakhsharī said: "That what is meant is the People of the Book, and that it is a rebuttal of their claim by way of mockery of them, because they used to say: we are more entitled to prophethood than Muḥammad ﷺ, for we are people of a Book and from us were the prophets." What he said is very remote; how could He call them prophets in mockery of them when there was no indication there to make that clear?
His saying: {لَمَآ آتَيْتُكُم}: the majority read «لَما» with fatḥa on the lām and light mīm; Ḥamza alone with kasra on the lām; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan read لَمَّا with fatḥa and shadda.
As for the reading of the majority, there are five views in it. One: that «ما» is a relative with the meaning of «الذي», and it is an object of an omitted verb, and that verb is the response to the oath, the implied form being: "By Allah, you will surely convey what We gave you of a book". This speaker said: because the lām of the oath occurs only upon a verb, so when this lām indicated the verb, it was dropped. Then the Exalted said: «ثم جاءكم رسول», and he is Muḥammad ﷺ. He said: "On this implied form the composition is straight." I say: this view should not be allowed at all, since it is impossible to say, in a like construction, «واللهِ لزيداً», meaning: "By Allah, you will surely strike Zayd."
The second view, which is the saying of Abū ʿAlī and others: that the lām in «لَما» is the response to His saying {مِيثَاقَ النبيين}, because it runs the course of an oath; so it is the lām of ibtidāʾ (inception) with which the oath is met, and «ما» is an inceptive relative mubtadaʾ and «آتيناكم» is its ṣila (relative clause), the returning pronoun being omitted, its implied form being: آتيناكموه, omitted because its conditions are fulfilled; and «من كتاب» is a ḥāl (circumstantial), either from the relative or from its returning pronoun. His saying {ثُمَّ جَآءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ} is conjoined to the ṣila, and then there must be a link tying this clause to what precedes it, for what is conjoined to a ṣila is a ṣila. They differed about that. Some of them held that it is omitted, its implied form being: «ثم جاءكم رسول به», so «به» was dropped because of the length of the speech and because the meaning indicates it. This is not permissible, because whenever the returning pronoun is governed by a preposition it is not omitted except under conditions that have preceded, which are lacking here; and these people claimed that this is Sībawayh's school, with what you already know about it. Among them are those who said: the link was achieved here by the overt noun, because this overt expression, His saying «لِما معكم», applies to His saying «لِما آتيناكم»; so it is like: «أبو سعيد الذي رَوَيْتُ عن الخِدْريّ، والحَجَّاج الذي رأيتُ ابنُ يوسف», and the poet said:
1348 - فيا رَبَّ ليلى أَنْتَ في كلِّ موطن ... وأنت الذي في رحمةِ اللهِ أَطْمَعُ
(O Lord of Laylā, you are in every situation, and you are the one in whose mercy I place hope.)
They mean: "from him", "I saw him", and "in his mercy". This has occurred in the mubtadaʾ and khabar, as in His saying, the Exalted: {إِنَّ الذين آمَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ الصالحات إِنَّا لاَ نُضِيعُ أَجْرَ مَنْ أَحْسَنَ عَمَلاً} [الكهف: 30]. This is the opinion of Abū l-Ḥasan, and a discussion about it has preceded. Among them are those who said: the returning pronoun is the pronoun of settledness (istiqrār) that operates in «مع», and «لتؤمِنُنَّ به» is the response of an implied oath, and this implied oath and its response are the khabar of the mubtadaʾ which is «لَما آتيتكم»; the hāʾ in «به» refers back to the mubtadaʾ and not to «رسول», lest the clause occurring as a khabar be devoid of a link tying it to the mubtadaʾ.
Third: as preceded, except that the lām in «لما» is the preparatory lām (lām al-tawṭiʾa), because taking the covenant has the sense of administering an oath, and in «لتؤمِنُنَّ به» is the lām of the response to the oath. This is al-Zamakhsharī's statement. Then he said: "«ما» may be the one containing the sense of condition, with «لتؤمِنُنَّ» filling the place of the response of both the oath and the condition; and it may be with the meaning of «الذي»." What he said is open to doubt, in that the preparatory lām occurs only with conditional particles, and it comes mostly with «إنْ»; with a relative, no. Had he allowed the lām to be preparatory and also to be for ibtidāʾ, and then mentioned the two views for «ما», we would have assigned each to what suits it.
Fourth: that the lām is the preparatory one and «ما» after it is conditional, its position being accusative as the direct object of the verb after it, which is «آتيتكم»; this verb is future in meaning because it is within the sphere of the condition, and its position is jussive; and the implied form is: "By Allah, whatever thing I give you of such and such, you will surely be such and such."
And His saying: {مِّن كِتَابٍ} is like His saying: {مَا نَنسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ} [البقرة: 106], and its statement has preceded. His saying: {ثُمَّ جَآءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ} is conjoined to the verb before it, so there must be a link in it tying it to what it is conjoined to. And «لتؤمِنُنَّ» is the response to His saying {أَخَذَ الله مِيثَاقَ النبيين}, the response of the condition being omitted, the response of the oath standing in its place; and the pronoun in «به» refers back to «رسول». Thus said the Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān). There is some doubt in it, since it is its returning to the conditional noun, and then it does not need an implied link; this is as preceded in the second view. A like of it in speech is that you say: «أَحْلِفُ باللهِ لأَيَّهم رأيتُ ثم ذهب إليه رجلٌ قُرَشي لأُحْسِنَنَّ إليه», meaning to the man; and this view is al-Kisāʾī's school.
He said: Sībawayh asked al-Khalīl about this verse and he answered that «ما» is in the position of «الذي», and the lām entered «ما» as it enters «إنْ» when you say: «واللهِ لَئِنْ فَعَلْتَ لأفعلنَّ»; so the lām that is in «ما» is like this one in «إنْ», and the lām in the verb is like this one in the verb here. This is al-Khalīl's text. Abū ʿAlī said: "Al-Khalīl did not mean by his saying 'it is in the position of «الذي»' that it is a relative, but that it is a noun just as «الذي» is a noun," and he established that it may be a particle, as it came as a particle in His saying: {وَإِنَّ كُلاًّ لَّمَّا لَيُوَفِّيَنَّهُمْ} [هود: 111], {وَإِن كُلُّ ذَلِكَ لَمَّا مَتَاعُ الحياة} [الزخرف: 35]. And Sībawayh said: "And like that: {لَّمَن تَبِعَكَ مِنْهُمْ لأَمْلأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ} [الأعراف: 18]; the lām entered only with the intention of an oath."
A group held that it is conditional, such as al-Māzinī, al-Zajjāj, al-Zamakhsharī and al-Fārisī. The Shaykh said: "There is a subtle conjecture in it. The sum of what he mentioned is that if they intend to explain the meaning, it is possible to say it; and if they intend to explain the i'rab, it is not sound, because each of the two, I mean the condition and the oath, demands a response on its own, and it is not possible that this be taken to serve both; for the condition requires it by way of operation, so it is in the position of jussive, whereas the oath requires it by way of conceptual connection without operation, so it has no position in i'rab; and it is impossible for a thing to have a position in i'rab and have no position in i'rab." I say: this difficulty and its answer have preceded.
Fifth: that its original is «لَمَّا» with shadda on the mīm and it was lightened; this is the saying of Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and the explanation of the doubled reading will come, from which it will be known.
Ḥamza read «لِما» with kasra on the lām and also a light mīm, and there are four views in it. One, the strangest of them: that the lām has the meaning of «بعد» (after), as in the saying of al-Nābigha:
1349 - تَوَهَّمْتُ آياتٍ لها فَعَرَفْتُها ... لستةِ أعوامٍ وذا العامُ سابعُ
(I made out her signs and recognized them after six years, and this year is the seventh.)
He means: "I recognized them after six years". This is transmitted from the author of al-Naẓm, and I do not know what impelled him to it. How does this form a coherent speech, since the implied form becomes: "And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets after what We gave you", and who is the addressee of that?
Second: that the lām is for cause, and this is what should not be turned from; it is attached to «لتؤمِنُنَّ», and «ما» is then maṣdariyya. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Its meaning is: because of My giving you part of the Book and wisdom, and then because of the coming of a confirming messenger, you will surely believe in him; on the basis that «ما» is maṣdariyya, and the two verbs with it, I mean «آتيناكم» and «جاءكم», are in the sense of two maṣdars, and the lām enters for cause. The meaning: Allah took their covenant that they believe in the Messenger and support him because I gave you wisdom, and because the Messenger who commands you to believe in him and support him agrees with you and does not oppose you." The Shaykh said: "The apparent sense of this causation he mentioned and of the implied form he implied is that it is a cause for the act sworn upon. If he means this apparent sense, it contradicts the apparent sense of the verse, for the apparent sense of the verse requires that it be a cause for taking the covenant and not for what it relates to, which is belief; so the lām is attached to 'taking', whereas on the apparent sense of al-Zamakhsharī's implication it is attached to His saying «لتؤمِنُنَّ به». This is impossible, in that the lām with which the oath is met does not let what follows it operate in what precedes it; you say: «والله لأضربَنَّ زيداً», and it is not allowed: «والله زيداً لأضربنَّ». On this it is not allowed that the lām in «لِما» be attached to «لتؤمننَّ». Some grammarians allowed that the object of the response, if it is an adverbial or a genitive phrase, may precede it, and made of that:
1350 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . عَوْضُ لا نَتَفَرَّقُ
([the verse is incomplete in the source; the second half ends:] "... ever shall we not part")
and His saying, the Exalted: {عَمَّا قَلِيلٍ لَّيُصْبِحُنَّ نَادِمِينَ} [المؤمنون: 40]. On this it is permissible that it be attached to His saying «لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ»; and in this question there is a detail that is mentioned in the science of grammar." I say: as for the lām's attachment to لتؤمِنُنَّ from the aspect of meaning, it is more apparent than its attachment to 'taking', and it is clear; so nothing remains except what he mentioned of the prohibition of putting the object of the response that is accompanied by the lām before it, which is known; and al-Zamakhsharī may be among those who see it as permissible.
Third: that the lām is attached to 'taking', that is: "because of My giving you such and such, I took the covenant from you", with the omission of a muḍāf in the speech, its implied form being: "for the regard of what I gave you".
Fourth: that it is attached to «الميثاق» because it is a maṣdar, that is: "we took a covenant upon them for that". These views relate to the lām. As for [«ما»], it has three views. One: that it is maṣdariyya, and its treatment according to al-Zamakhsharī has preceded. The second: that it is a relative with the meaning of «الذي» and its returning pronoun is omitted, and «ثم جاءكم» is conjoined to the ṣila, the link of it with the relative being either omitted, its implied form being «به», which is Sībawayh's opinion, or by the overt noun taking the place of the pronoun, which is al-Akhfash's opinion, or the pronoun of settledness that «معكم» contains, and the verification of that has preceded. The third: that it is an indefinite described noun, the clause after it being its description and its returning pronoun omitted, and «ثم جاءكم» conjoined to the description, with the discussion of the link being as preceded in it as a ṣila, except that putting the overt noun in place of the pronoun in the description is impossible: if you said «مررت برجلٍ قام أبو عبد الله», with «قام أبو عبد الله» as an adjective of «رجل» and the link being «أبو عبد الله», since he is the man in meaning, it would not be allowed, though it is allowed in the ṣila and the khabar according to those who hold that; so the return of an omitted pronoun is necessarily intended.
The response of His saying {وَإِذْ أَخَذَ الله مِيثَاقَ} is His saying {لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِ} as preceded, and the pronoun in «به» refers back to «رسول»; and separation between the oath and the object of the oath by such a preposition-and-noun phrase is permissible: if you said «أقسمتُ للخير الذي بلغني عن عمرٍو لأحْسِنَنَّ إليه» it would be allowed.
And His saying: {مِّن كِتَابٍ وَحِكْمَةٍ}: either a ḥāl from the relative or from its returning pronoun, or a clarification of it. So in Ḥamza's reading it is impossible that «ما» be conditional, just as in the reading of the majority it is impossible that it be maṣdariyya.
As for the reading of Saʿīd and al-Ḥasan, there are several views in it. One: that «لَمَّا» here is adverbial, with the meaning of «حين» (when). Then those who say it is adverbial differed in their implication of its response. Al-Zamakhsharī held that the response is implied, of the kind of the response of the oath, so he said: "«لَمَّا» with shadda has the meaning of «حين», that is: when I gave you part of the Book and wisdom and then there came to you a confirming messenger, belief in him and supporting him became obligatory upon you." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It appears that this «لمَّا» is adverbial, that is: when you were in this state, chiefs of the people and their best, the covenant was taken from you, since it is taken from the leaders; so it comes, on this meaning, like the meaning in Ḥamza's reading." Ibn ʿAṭiyya thus implied its response from the kind of what preceded it. What the two went to is a weaker school, held by al-Fārisī, while the majority, Sībawayh and his followers, are against it; and the verification of this disagreement has preceded, so there is no need to mention it. Al-Zajjāj said: "That is, when He gave you the Book and wisdom, He took the covenant from you, and «لمَّا» comes down to the sense of requital, as you say: when you came to me, I honoured you." No adverbial status of «لَمّا» nor anything else is taken from this wording, except that it supports Ibn ʿAṭiyya's implication of its response from the kind of what preceded it, unlike al-Zamakhsharī's implication.
Second: that «لَمَّا» is a particle of necessity due to necessity (ḥarf wujūb li-wujūb); its evidence has preceded and that it is Sībawayh's school, and its response is as preceded from the implications of Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Zamakhsharī. In Ibn ʿAṭiyya's saying "so it comes, on the meaning, like the meaning in Ḥamza's reading" there is some doubt, since Ḥamza's reading contains a cause and this reading contains no cause; unless it is said that since «لَمَّا» needs a response, it resembled the cause and its effect, because when you say «لَمَّا جِئْتَني أكرمتُك», it is equivalent to "I honoured you because of your coming to me", so from this aspect it is like Ḥamza's reading.
Third: that the original is «لَمِنْ ما», and the nūn was assimilated into the mīm because it is near it, assimilation being obligatory here; and when three mīms came together, the mīm of «مِنْ», the mīm of «ما», and the mīm that turned from the nūn of «مِنْ» for the assimilation, heaviness arose in the utterance. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "So they dropped one of them." The Shaykh said: "There is vagueness in it," and Ibn ʿAṭiyya specified it, that the dropped one is the first. I say: there is doubt in it, because the heaviness arose only from what follows the first, so the sound course in its like is the dropping of the seconds, for example «تَنَزَّل» and «تَذَكَّرون»; and Abū l-Baqāʾ mentioned that the dropped one is the second, saying: "because of its weakness in being a substitute and the repetition's arising by it."
And this «مِنْ» in «لَمِنْ ما» is redundant in an affirmative context according to the opinion of Abū l-Ḥasan al-Akhfash. This is Abū l-Fatḥ's explanation, and there is some doubt in it with regard to his claim of the redundancy of «مِنْ», for the construction is awkward on that, and the meaning remains unclear.
Fourth: that the original is also «لَمِنْ ما», and what has preceded was done to it, of the substitution, the assimilation and then the dropping, except that «مِنْ» is not redundant but causal. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Its meaning is 'because of what I gave you, you will surely believe in him', and this is somewhat like Ḥamza's reading in meaning." I say: this view is more eminent than what preceded it for its freedom from the claim of the redundancy of «مِنْ» and for the clarity of its meaning. The Shaykh said: "This explanation is extremely remote, and the speech of the Arabs should be held free of the like of it coming in it, so how much more the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic! Ibn Jinnī used to engage heavily in contrived explanation in the speech of the Arabs. And it is necessary in this «لَمّا», on what al-Zamakhsharī established, that the lām in «لِمنْ ما آتيناكم» be redundant and not be the preparatory lām, because the preparatory lām enters only conditional particles and not a preposition; if you said «أُقسم بالله لمِنْ أجلك لأضربن زيداً» it would not be allowed. It was called preparatory only because it prepares what is suitable to be a response for the condition for the oath, so the response of the condition then becomes omitted because the response of the oath indicates it." I say: he himself had earlier said that «ما» in this reading may be a relative with the meaning of «الذي» and that the lām with it is preparatory for the oath, and here he restricted it so that it enters only conditional particles; so one of the two matters is necessarily his, and I have presented that this is the difficulty for one who makes «ما» a relative and the lām preparatory.
Nāfiʿ read «آتيناكم» with the pronoun of one who magnifies himself, and the rest «آتيتكم» with the pronoun of the speaker alone, which agrees with what is before and after it of the singular form in His saying {وَإِذْ أَخَذَ الله}, and after it «إصري» comes.
In His saying «آتيتكم» or «آتيناكم», on both readings, there are two iltifāts (shifts). One: the departure from the third person to the first person in His saying «آتينا» or «آتيتُ», because before it is the mention of the Majestic Name in His saying {وَإِذْ أَخَذَ الله}. The second: the departure from the third person to the second person in His saying «آتيناكم», because an overt noun preceded it, which is «النبيين»; for had it followed the requirement of the preceding of the Majestic Name and the prophets, the construction would have been: "And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets, 'for what He gave them of such a book'". Some of them said: "There is doubt in it, because the like of this is not called iltifāt in their terminology; rather it is called hikāyat al-ḥāl (narration of the situation), and its like is your saying: حلف زيد ليفعلنَّ ولأفعلن; the third person is in regard to the preceding of the overt noun, and the first person is a narration of the oath-taker's words, and the noble verse is of this kind."
And the original of لتؤمِنُنَّ به ولتنصُرُنَّه is لتؤمنونَنّ ولتنصرونَنّ: the first nūn is the sign of the nominative, and the doubled one after it is for emphasis; the succession of three like letters was found heavy, so they dropped the nūn of the nominative because it is not as strong as the one for emphasis; with its dropping two sākins met, so the wāw was dropped because of the meeting of two sākins.
ʿAbd Allāh read «مُصَدِّقاً» in the accusative as a ḥāl from an indefinite; Sībawayh made it analogical, although the well-known view from him is the opposite, and what made it good here is that the indefinite is equal in force to a definite, in that a specific person is meant by it, namely Muḥammad ﷺ. The lām in «لَما» is redundant, because the operator is a derivative (furūʿ), which is مُصَدِّق, and the original is: مُصَدِّقٌ ما معكم.
His saying: {قَالَ أَأَقْرَرْتُمْ}: the agent of «قال» may be the pronoun of Allah the Exalted, which is the apparent, or the pronoun of the prophet who is one of the prophets, addressing his community with that; and what the acknowledgement relates to is omitted, that is: "Did you acknowledge all of that?" The interrogative on the first view is figurative, since what is meant by it is confirmation and emphasis upon them, because of its impossibility for the Creator the Exalted; and on the second it is a true interrogative. And «إصْري»: on the first the yāʾ belongs to Allah the Exalted and on the second to the prophet.
The majority read «إصري» with kasra on the hamza, and it is the most eloquent; Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim in one transmission read «أُصْري» with ḍamma on it. The ḍamma form may be a dialect of the kasra form, which is the apparent, and may be the plural of إصار, and like it أُزُر as the plural of إزار. The discussion of it was given in full toward the end of al-Baqara.
And His saying: {أَقْرَرْنَا}, that is, "we acknowledged belief in him and his support". In the speech there is also an omitted clause, omitted because what preceded indicates it, since the implied form is: "They said: We acknowledged, and we took Your covenant upon all of that."
And His saying: {فاشهدوا}: this فاء is conjoined to an implied clause, its implied form being: "He said: Did you acknowledge? Then bear witness"; and its like is: «أَلقِيتَ زيداً»? He said: «لَقِيتُه». He said: «فَأَحسِنْ إِليه»; the implied form is: "Did you meet Zayd? Then be good to him." So what has the فاء is part of what is said, and it cannot be all of what is said because of the فاء; do you not see that in His saying «قال: أأقررتم» and His saying «قالوا: أقررنا», since they were all of what is said, he did not enter the فاء? The Shaykh said this, and the meaning is clear without it.
His saying: {مِّنَ الشاهدين}: this is the khabar, because it is the focus of the benefit. As for His saying «معكم», it may be a ḥāl, that is: "and I am among the witnesses, accompanying you", and may be accusative by «الشاهدين» as an adverbial of it, according to those who allow that; and it is impossible that it be the khabar, since the benefit by it is incomplete in this situation. The clause of His saying {وَأَنَاْ مَعَكُمْ مِّنَ الشاهدين} may have no position because it is resumptive, and may be in the position of accusative as a ḥāl from the agent of «فاشْهدوا».

semin-durr:121-121.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَإِذْ غَدَوْتَ}: the governing element of «إذ» is implied, its implied form being «واذكر إذ غدوت» ("and remember when you set out in the morning"), so it is accusative as a direct object, not as an adverbial. Some allowed it to be conjoined to «فئتين» in His saying {قَدْ كَانَ لَكُمْ آيَةٌ فِي فِئَتَيْنِ} [Āl ʿImrān: 13], i.e. "there was for you a sign in two groups and in when you set out in the morning"; but this should not be dwelt on.

al-Ghudūw is going out at the beginning of the day. One says ghadā yaghdū, i.e. he went out in the morning (ghudwa). Some use it in the sense of ṣāra (became), in which case it is incomplete, raising the subject and making the predicate accusative, and on this is his saying, peace be upon him: «لو توكلتم على الله حَقَّ توكُّلهِ لرزقكم كما يَرزق الطيرَ تَغْدُو خِماصاً وتروُح بِطاناً» ("If you relied on Allah with true reliance, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry and return in the evening full").

His saying {مِنْ أَهْلِكَ} is attached to «غَدَوْتَ», and for «من» there are two aspects. The clearer is that it is for the beginning of the extent, i.e. "from among your family". Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "Its position is accusative; the implied form is «فارقْتَ أهلك» (you left your family)." What he said is neither an explanation of i'rab nor of meaning, for the meaning is other than he mentioned. The second: that it means "with", i.e. "with your family"; neither wording nor meaning supports this.

His saying: {تُبَوِّىءُ}: the sentence may be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the fāʿil (agent) of «غدوت», and it is a prospective ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara), i.e. "intending to settle the believers", because the time of setting out is not the time of settling. It may also be a concurrent one, since the time is wide.
Tubawwiʾu means "to lodge", and it takes two objects, one directly and the other by a preposition, which may be omitted, as in this verse. An example of its not being omitted is His saying, the Exalted: {وَإِذْ بَوَّأْنَا لإِبْرَاهِيمَ مَكَانَ البيت} [al-Ḥajj: 26]. Its origin is from al-mabāʾa, which is the place of return. He said:
1418 - وما بَوَّأ الرحمنُ بَيْتَك منزلاً ... بشرقيِّ أجيادِ الصَّفا والمُحَرَّمِ
(The Merciful has not lodged your house in a dwelling to the east of Ajyād, al-Ṣafā and al-Muḥarram.)
and another said:
1419 - كم مِن أخٍ لي صَالحٍ ... بَوَّأْتُه بيدَيَّ لَحْدا
(How many a righteous brother of mine have I lodged with my own hands in a grave.)
The derivation of this word was given earlier. It is also said: "The lām in his saying «لإبراهيم» is redundant, and on this it takes two objects by itself."
Maqāʿid is the plural of maqʿad, and what is meant here is the place of sitting. Qaʿada can mean ṣāra in proverbs especially. al-Zamakhsharī said: "Qaʿada and qāma have been broadened until they were made to function as ṣāra." The Shaykh said: "As for making qaʿada function as ṣāra, some of our colleagues said that this occurred only in a single irregular expression in a proverb, in their saying «شَحَذَ شَفْرَته حتى قَعَدَتْ كأنها حَرْبة» ('He sharpened his blade until it became like a spear'); and likewise he criticised al-Zamakhsharī for explaining His saying, the Exalted, {فَتَقْعُدَ مَذْمُوماً} [al-Isrāʾ: 22] in the sense of «فتصيرَ», because making qaʿada function as ṣāra is not regular." I say: what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned is correct, that qaʿada can mean ṣāra beyond what this critic indicated; Abū ʿUmar al-Zāhid related from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that the Arabs say «قَعد فلان أميراً بعد أن كان مأموراً», i.e. he became.
Then the Shaykh said: "As for making qāma function as ṣāra, I know of no one who counted it among the sisters of kāna, or made it mean ṣāra, except Ibn Hishām al-Khaḍrāwī, who mentioned, regarding the poet's saying: /
1420 - على ما قام يَشْتِمُني لئيمٌ ... كخِنْزيرٍ تَمَرَّغَ في رماد
(Upon what ground does a base fellow begin to revile me, like a pig wallowing in ashes?)
that it is among the verbs of approximation." I say: other grammarians make it redundant, and that too is irregular.
The majority read «تُبَوِّىءُ», making it transitive by doubling. ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd] read «تُبْوِىءُ» with sukūn on the bāʾ, making it transitive by hamza, so it is the imperfect of abwaʾa like akrama. Yaḥyā ibn Wathāb read «تُبْوي» like ʿAbd Allāh's reading, except that he eased the hamza by turning it into yāʾ, so its wording became like that of «تُحْيي», as they say «تُقْري» for «تُقْرىء». ʿAbd Allāh read «للمؤمنين» with the genitive lām, like {وَإِذْ بَوَّأْنَا لإِبْرَاهِيمَ} [al-Ḥajj: 26]. It was mentioned that there are two views about this lām. The apparent is that it makes the verb transitive, because before doubling and hamza it is not transitive by itself. It may be that he made it include here the meaning of «تُهَيِّىء» (to prepare) and «ترتِّب» (to arrange).
al-Ashhab read «مقاعدَ القتالِ» annexing it to «القتال». As for the lām in «للقتال» in the reading of the majority, there are two aspects. The clearer: that it is attached to «تُبَوِّىء» as the lām of cause. The second: that it is attached to an omitted element because it is an adjective of «مقاعد», i.e. "seats that are present and prepared for fighting". It cannot be attached to «مقاعد», though it is a derived noun, since it is a noun of place, and nouns of place do not govern.

semin-durr:122-122.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِذْ هَمَّتْ}: for this adverbial there are several aspects. One: that it is a badal (substitute) from «إذ غَدَوْتَ», so the governing element of it is the governing element of the substituted. Second: that it is an adverbial of «غَدَوْتَ». Third: that it is an adverbial of «تُبَوِّىءُ»; these aspects require historical transmission regarding the identity of the two times. Fourth: that the governing element is «عليم» alone, mentioned by Abū l-Baqāʾ.
